Weapons having no effect on memory
Better identification of perpetrators when weapons are present

reviewQueue.prompt: Schema theory proposes that knowledge is organized in:
choices: Random, unconnected bits
Structured mental FRAMEWORKS that organize experience and guide perception, memory, and understanding of new information
Only visual images
Alphabetical order
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Bartlett, Piaget, Rumelhart: schemas are cognitive structures organizing knowledge about objects, events, people, and situations. They guide encoding, retrieval, and interpretation. Restaurant schema: expect to be seated, order, eat, pay.

Why others are wrong:

reviewQueue.prompt: The mood congruency effect demonstrates that:
choices: Mood never affects cognition
People in a particular mood tend to ENCODE and RECALL information CONSISTENT with that mood
Only positive moods affect memory
Mood effects are always harmful
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Bower: mood congruent processing — depressed mood → better encoding and retrieval of negative information; happy mood → better processing of positive information. This creates a self-reinforcing cycle in depression.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Mood SIGNIFICANTLY influences cognitive processes including attention, memory, and judgment
(C) BOTH positive and negative moods produce congruent processing effects
(D) Mood congruency can be beneficial (positive mood → positive processing) or detrimental (negative mood → negative spiral)
references: Bower, G. H. (1981). Mood and memory. American Psychologist, 36(2), 129–148. https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.36.2.129

reviewQueue.prompt: Elaborative rehearsal differs from maintenance rehearsal in that:

Maintenance rehearsal is always superior
Elaborative rehearsal only involves repetition
reviewQueue.rationale:

(C) Elaborative rehearsal produces SUPERIOR long-term memory — maintenance is inferior for LTM

reviewQueue.prompt: Tversky and Kahneman showed that people often estimate the probability of an event happening based on how easily examples of that event come to mind. This is known as:
choices: The representativeness heuristic
The availability heuristic
Anchoring and adjustment
Confirmation bias
reviewQueue.rationale:
The availability heuristic is a mental shortcut where judgments of frequency or probability are based on how easily instances can be retrieved from memory. Because plane crashes are highly publicized, people often overestimate their frequency and fear flying more than driving, despite driving being statistically more dangerous.

Why others are wrong:
• The representativeness heuristic involves judging the likelihood of something belonging to a category based on how closely it matches a typical prototype of that category.
• Anchoring and adjustment involves relying too heavily on an initial piece of information (the 'anchor') and insufficiently adjusting from it.
• Confirmation bias is the tendency to seek out, interpret, and remember information that confirms one's pre-existing beliefs.

reviewQueue.prompt: According to the fundamental attribution error, when making judgments about another person's behavior, observers tend to:
choices: Overestimate situational factors and underestimate dispositional factors
Overestimate dispositional factors and underestimate situational factors
Attribute the person's success to situation and failure to disposition
Evaluate people from their own in-group more positively
reviewQueue.rationale:
The fundamental attribution error is the pervasive tendency for observers to underestimate the impact of situational (external) influences and overestimate the impact of dispositional (internal/personality) factors when explaining the behavior of others. (E.g., assuming someone cut you off because they are a jerk, rather than because they are rushing to the hospital).

Why others are wrong:
• Overestimating situational factors while underestimating disposition describes what people often do for their OWN behavior (part of the actor-observer bias).
• Attributing success to disposition and failure to situation describes the self-serving bias, which applies to evaluating oneself.
• Evaluating your in-group more positively describes in-group favoritism/bias, not attribution theory specifically.

reviewQueue.prompt: A person with anterograde amnesia would have the greatest difficulty with which of the following tasks?
choices: Riding a bicycle they learned to ride years ago
Remembering the name of their first grade teacher
Learning the layout of a hospital they moved into after their injury
Tying their shoelaces
reviewQueue.rationale:
Anterograde amnesia is the inability to form new declarative/explicit memories after the brain injury or event that caused the amnesia. Therefore, learning new spatial layouts, names of new people, or daily events post-injury is extremely impaired.

Why others are wrong:
• Old motor skills (bicycle riding, shoelace tying) are implicit/procedural memories and are famously preserved in standard amnesic patients.
• Remembering a childhood teacher relies on retrograde memory (memories formed before the injury), which is largely intact in pure anterograde amnesia.

reviewQueue.prompt: In operant conditioning, a 'variable-ratio' schedule of reinforcement typically produces:
choices: A low, steady rate of responding
A scalloped response pattern with a pause after reinforcement
A high, steady rate of responding with little to no pause after reinforcement
Rapid extinction of the behavior
reviewQueue.rationale:
A variable-ratio (VR) schedule provides reinforcement after an unpredictable number of responses (e.g., slot machines). This produces the highest, most steady rate of responding among the four basic schedules and is highly resistant to extinction, as you never know exactly when the next payoff will happen.

Why others are wrong:
• A low, steady rate is more characteristic of a variable-interval (VI) schedule.
• A scalloped pattern (pause after reinforcement then increasing rate) is the hallmark of a fixed-interval (FI) schedule.
• Variable-ratio schedules are highly resistant to extinction, whereas continuous reinforcement (CRF) leads to rapid extinction when reinforcement stops.

reviewQueue.prompt: Ebbinghaus's famous 'forgetting curve' demonstrated that:
choices: Forgetting proceeds at a constant, linear rate over time.
Most forgetting occurs very rapidly immediately after learning, then levels off.
Forgetting only occurs if interference is introduced.
Meaningful material is forgotten faster than nonsense syllables.
reviewQueue.rationale:
Ebbinghaus used nonsense syllables to study memory. His forgetting curve showed that a massive amount of information is forgotten very quickly (within the first hour or day), but the rate of forgetting then slows down significantly, leaving a baseline amount of retained information over time.

Why others are wrong:
• Forgetting is a logarithmic/exponential decay curve, not a linear, constant rate.
• Interference (proactive/retroactive) contributes to forgetting, but Ebbinghaus found decay occurred simply over time without intentionally introduced interference.
• Ebbinghaus found (and modern research confirms) that meaningful material is retained much better and longer than nonsense syllables.

reviewQueue.prompt: Which theory of emotion posits that physiological arousal and the cognitive interpretation (labeling) of that arousal must occur simultaneously for an emotion to be experienced?
choices: James-Lange theory
Cannon-Bard theory
Schachter-Singer Two-Factor theory
Cognitive Appraisal theory (Lazarus)
reviewQueue.rationale:
The Schachter-Singer Two-Factor Theory argues that emotion requires two components: physiological arousal and a cognitive label applied to that arousal based on environmental cues. Without the cognitive interpretation of the arousal, no specific emotion is strongly experienced.

Why others are wrong:
• James-Lange posits that emotion is directly caused by the perception of physiological changes (arousal leads to emotion: 'I am afraid because I am shaking').
• Cannon-Bard argues that a stimulus simultaneously triggers both physiological arousal and the subjective experience of emotion, independently of each other.
• Lazarus's Cognitive Appraisal theory emphasizes that the cognitive appraisal of a stimulus comes first and determines if there will be physiological arousal and emotion at all.

reviewQueue.prompt: The phenomenon where later learning impairs the recall of previously learned information is called:
choices: Proactive interference
Retroactive interference
Decay
Repression
reviewQueue.rationale:
Retroactive interference occurs when new learning works backward to disrupt the retrieval of older, previously learned information (e.g., studying French this week makes it harder to remember the Spanish you studied last week).

Why others are wrong:
• Proactive interference is the opposite: old learning interferes with recalling new information (e.g., writing last year's date on a new check).
• Decay is forgetting simply due to the passage of time without rehearsal.
• Repression is a psychoanalytic defense mechanism involving the unconscious blocking of traumatic memories.

reviewQueue.prompt: According to Yerkes-Dodson law, optimal performance on a highly complex or difficult task is usually achieved when physiological arousal is:
choices: Very low
Moderate to moderately low
Very high
Fluctuating rapidly
reviewQueue.rationale:
The Yerkes-Dodson law forms an inverted-U curve representing the relationship between arousal and performance. For simple, well-learned tasks, a relatively high level of arousal is optimal. But for complex, novel, or difficult cognitive tasks, a lower level of arousal is optimal because high arousal creates distracting anxiety and cognitive overload.

Why others are wrong:
• Very low arousal generally results in poor performance (boredom, inattention) across all task types.
• Very high arousal (panic/stress) severely impairs complex task performance.
• Rapidly fluctuating arousal impairs sustained attention and focus.

All cognitive biases are successfully eliminated through rigorous clinical training

reviewQueue.prompt: Transfer-appropriate processing theory suggests memory is best when:
choices: The initial stimulus encoding phase is explicitly extremely deep
The type of processing at encoding matches the type at retrieval
Specific formal individual target items are robustly restudied
Explicit cognitive retrieval immediately tracks basic encoding
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Transfer-appropriate processing (Morris et al.): memory performance depends on the match between encoding and retrieval processes. Semantic encoding helps semantic tests; phonological encoding helps phonological tests. Goes beyond levels of processing.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Deep encoding often helps, but match matters more
(C) Repetition helps but doesn't guarantee appropriate transfer
(D) Timing matters, but the encoding-retrieval match is the key principle

reviewQueue.prompt: Encoding specificity (Tulving) states that:
choices: The original encoding context is fundamentally irrelevant to the probability of successful memory retrieval
Retrieval is statistically most effective when the retrieval context closely matches the encoding context
Only exclusively visual encoding stimuli can be preserved over significantly delayed retrieval intervals
Declarative episodic memory remains structurally perfect assuming complete conscious encoding focus
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Encoding specificity: cues effective at retrieval are those that were processed during encoding. If you study while sad, sad mood at test improves recall (mood-dependent memory). State-dependent learning is a related phenomenon.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Experimental context is deeply, highly relevant — the matching principle is the absolute core claim.
(C) All encoding operational modalities routinely follow this precise contextual matching principle.
(D) Biological memory is intrinsically reconstructive and highly fallible across time scales.

reviewQueue.prompt: The serial position effect shows:
choices: All items within a continuous sequential list possess perfectly equal memorability across time domains
Items at the beginning (primacy effect) and end (recency effect) of an extended list are remembered best
Only items strategically positioned in the exact middle of a sequence achieve permanent consolidation
Exceedingly long qualitative verbal lists practically cannot be consciously memorized under any condition
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Primacy effect: early items are rehearsed more and transferred to LTM. Recency effect: last items are still in STM. Middle items (asymptote) are recalled worst. Delayed recall eliminates recency but preserves primacy.

Why others are wrong:
(A) The classical U-shaped recall curve graphically shows wildly unequal memorability.
(C) Middle temporal items are statistically recalled consistently WORST.
(D) Extended lists can be effectively memorized; sequential position drastically affects relative ease.

reviewQueue.prompt: Bronfenbrenner's Ecological Systems Theory identifies nested levels including:
choices: Only the immediate microsystem of family and school without broader contextual influences
Microsystem, mesosystem, exosystem, macrosystem, and chronosystem — from immediate to broadest
Only a simple genes-versus-environment dichotomy without differentiated contextual system levels
Only school-based influences on child development without consideration of other ecological contexts
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Bronfenbrenner: nested systems. Microsystem (immediate environments — family, school). Mesosystem (interactions between microsystems). Exosystem (indirect influences — parent's workplace). Macrosystem (culture, laws). Chronosystem (historical time/transitions).

Why others are wrong:
(A) Five distinct nested ecological systems are identified.
(C) The model is far more complex than the nature-nurture dichotomy.
(D) School is one microsystem among many influences on development.

reviewQueue.prompt: Neural pruning during adolescence primarily involves:
choices: Growing entirely new brain regions that were not present during earlier childhood development
Elimination of unused synaptic connections, strengthening frequently used pathways ('use it or lose it')
No meaningful neurological brain changes occurring during the entire adolescent developmental period
Only myelination of existing neural axons without any corresponding synaptic connection elimination
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Synaptic pruning: adolescent brain loses ~40% of synapses. Experience-dependent: frequently used connections strengthen (LTP), unused ones are eliminated. PFC is last to mature (mid-20s), explaining adolescent risk-taking, emotion regulation difficulties, and executive function development.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Pruning removes unused connections rather than growing new brain regions.

reviewQueue.prompt: Leon Festinger's cognitive dissonance theory predicts that a person who is paid $1 (vs. $20) to lie about a boring task will:

Show no change in attitude

reviewQueue.prompt: In-group bias refers to:
choices: Explicit baseline preference for targeted individuals outside one's group
The tendency to favor members of one's own group over out-group members
Systematically objective and strictly equal treatment of distinct groups
Pervasive baseline bias directed specifically against one's group members
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) In-group bias (in-group favoritism): preferential treatment, more positive evaluations, and greater resource allocation to members of one's own groups. It occurs even in minimal group paradigms (Tajfel).

Why others are wrong:
(A) Preferring out-group members = out-group favoritism, which is rare and usually occurs in marginalized groups
(C) Equal treatment of all groups = absence of bias, the opposite
(D) Bias against one's own group = in-group derogation, which can occur in stigmatized groups but is not 'in-group bias'

reviewQueue.prompt: According to the social comparison theory (Festinger), people compare themselves to others primarily to:
choices: Routinely feel superior to specific others
Evaluate their own abilities and opinions
Conform precisely to standard group norms
Reduce any internal cognitive dissonance
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Festinger (1954): people have a fundamental drive to evaluate their abilities and opinions. When objective standards are unavailable, they compare with similar others (lateral comparison).

Why others are wrong:
(A) Feeling superior = downward social comparison (comparing with worse-off others), only one type of comparison
(C) Conformity is a separate process — comparison is about self-evaluation, not necessarily adjusting to norms
(D) Reducing dissonance is Festinger's OTHER major theory, separate from social comparison theory

reviewQueue.prompt: Stereotype threat (Steele & Aronson) refers to:
choices: Explicit conscious hostile prejudice uniquely directed toward a specific targeted group
The risk of confirming a negative stereotype about one's group, which impairs performance
The systematic explicit use of generalized stereotypes to safely predict active behavior
Broad explicit structural discrimination occurring specifically within corporate hiring
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Stereotype threat: awareness of a negative stereotype about one's group creates anxiety and cognitive load that impairs performance on the stereotyped dimension. E.g., women performing worse on math tests when gender is made salient.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Conscious prejudice = explicit bias; stereotype threat is about the TARGET experiencing the threat, not the prejudiced person
(C) Using stereotypes to predict behavior = profiling or statistical discrimination, not stereotype threat
(D) Hiring discrimination = institutional racism/sexism, a different phenomenon from the performance-impairing effects of stereotype threat

reviewQueue.prompt: Acculturative stress is MOST likely when an individual adopts which acculturation strategy?
choices: Integration approach
Assimilation concept
Marginalization path
Separation framework
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (C) Marginalization (rejecting both original culture AND host culture) produces the highest acculturative stress and poorest psychological outcomes. The individual lacks cultural support from both communities.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Integration (maintaining original culture while adopting host culture) is associated with the BEST outcomes and lowest stress
(B) Assimilation (adopting host culture, abandoning original) produces moderate stress but maintains host culture support
(D) Separation (maintaining original culture, rejecting host) provides cultural support from the heritage community, producing less stress than marginalization

reviewQueue.prompt: Microsaggressions are:

Brief, commonplace exchanges that communicate derogatory messages to marginalized groups
Explicitly intentional and formally verifiable severe hate crimes conveying prejudice
Explicitly constructed continuous explicit verbal insults routinely given beyond context
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Microaggressions (Sue, 2007) are subtle, often unintentional slights — verbal, behavioral, or environmental — that communicate hostile or derogatory messages to members of marginalized groups.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Overt discrimination = macro-level or explicit; microaggressions are subtle and often unconscious
(C) Hate crimes are criminal acts; microaggressions are everyday interactions, usually not criminal
(D) Microaggressions can be behavioral (clutching a purse), environmental (only White faces in marketing), or verbal — not just verbal insults

reviewQueue.prompt: Groupthink (Janis) is MOST likely when:
choices: Group members freely disagree
The group is highly cohesive with a directive leader and insulation from outside opinions
Members have diverse backgrounds
The group encourages devil's advocacy
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Janis's antecedents of groupthink: high cohesion, directive leadership, insulation from experts, lack of systematic procedures, and high stress with low hope for alternatives. E.g., Bay of Pigs, Challenger disaster.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Free disagreement PREVENTS groupthink — dissent is the antidote
(C) Diverse backgrounds reduce groupthink by introducing different perspectives
(D) Devil's advocacy is a REMEDY for groupthink, not a condition that promotes it

A counselor's narrow, culturally biased view that fails to consider diverse perspectives
Being fully immersed in one's own culture for identity development
A stage in the acculturation process
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Cultural encapsulation (Wrenn, 1962): counselors who substitute stereotypes for real understanding, assume their own worldview is universal, and fail to adapt interventions for diverse clients. A key concept in multicultural counseling.

reviewQueue.prompt: Social facilitation (Zajonc) occurs when:
choices: The presence of others impairs performance on all tasks
The presence of others enhances performance on simple/well-learned tasks but impairs complex tasks
People always perform better alone
Groups are always more productive than individuals
reviewQueue.rationale:

Why others are wrong:
(A) Others' presence enhances performance on SIMPLE tasks — impairment only occurs on complex ones
(C) People sometimes perform better with an audience (social facilitation of simple tasks)
(D) Group productivity versus individual depends on the task and process losses (coordination, motivation)

choices: People always help in emergencies

Bystanders always intervene
Helping behavior is entirely determined by personality

Make accurate attributions about others
Attribute all behavior to luck

Why others are wrong:
(A) Attributing own behavior to dispositions = opposite of the actor-observer bias (we tend to use situational attributions for ourselves)
(C) The FAE produces INACCURATE attributions by ignoring situational factors
(D) Attributing everything to luck would be an external attribution bias, not the FAE

Independent individual decision-making processes without any group conformity or social influence
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Janis's groupthink: cohesive groups under stress suppress dissent, create illusion of unanimity, self-censor, and use mindguards — producing defective decision-making (e.g., Bay of Pigs, Challenger disaster).

reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Relative deprivation: dissatisfaction results from perceived discrepancy between what one has and what one's reference group has. Explains why economic growth doesn't always increase happiness, and why inequality fuels social unrest.

(C) Genetic predisposition relates to set-point theory, not relative deprivation.
(D) Physical deprivation is absolute deprivation — relative deprivation is about social comparison.

Correct: (B) Bandura's social cognitive theory: behavior (B), personal factors (P — cognitions, emotions, biological events), and environment (E) operate as interacting determinants. Each influences and is influenced by the others.

Accurate perception of group diversity
Favoring outgroups over ingroups
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Outgroup homogeneity bias: 'They're all alike.' We perceive greater variability within our ingroup (because we know more members individually) and see outgroup members as more homogeneous than they actually are.

Why others are wrong:

(C) The effect is a BIAS — it's an inaccurate perception of outgroup uniformity

Complete absence of morality

Diffuse responsibility across many people
Assuming someone else will help

Always agreeing with others
Ignoring others' experiences

Prejudice to accurate perception only
Prejudice to purely cognitive factors

(C) Scapegoating involves MISPERCEPTION — attributing blame incorrectly to outgroups

Aggression is never triggered by situations

reviewQueue.prompt: The Robbers Cave experiment (Sherif) demonstrated:
choices: That intergroup conflict cannot be resolved

That prejudice is entirely innate
That separation always reduces conflict
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Sherif et al. (1961): Phase 1 — in-group formation. Phase 2 — intergroup competition created intense hostility. Phase 3 — superordinate goals (common problems requiring cooperation) reduced conflict. Foundation for realistic conflict theory.

Why others are wrong:

(C) The study showed prejudice arising from competitive SITUATIONS, not innate disposition
(D) Mere separation didn't reduce conflict — cooperative interdependence was needed
references: Sherif, M., Harvey, O. J., White, B. J., Hood, W. R., & Sherif, C. W. (1961). Intergroup conflict and cooperation: The Robbers Cave experiment. University of Oklahoma Press.

Random chance
Only individual differences
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Sherif: when groups compete for scarce resources (jobs, territory, power), intergroup hostility develops. The Robbers Cave experiment demonstrated that competition → conflict, and superordinate goals → cooperation.

(A) Realistic conflict theory emphasizes SITUATIONAL factors (resource competition), not personality

All contact automatically reduces prejudice
Separation between groups is maintained
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Allport (1954): mere contact is insufficient — sometimes it increases prejudice. Four conditions optimize contact: equal status between groups, common goals, cooperative interdependence, and institutional support/social norms favoring equality.

Why others are wrong:

(C) Contact WITHOUT Allport's conditions can worsen prejudice

reviewQueue.prompt: According to Festinger's cognitive dissonance theory, people are most likely to change their attitudes when they:

Engage in behavior contrary to their beliefs with insufficient external justification
Observe a high-status role model expressing a different attitude

reviewQueue.rationale:
Festinger's classic $1 vs $20 experiment showed that people who were paid $1 (insufficient justification) to lie about a boring task experienced cognitive dissonance. To resolve this internal discomfort, they changed their internal attitude to believe the task was actually interesting. Those paid $20 had sufficient external justification for the lie and did not change their attitude.

reviewQueue.prompt: In social psychology, 'social loafing' is defined as:

The decline in individual performance when observed by a crowd
The tendency for groups to make riskier decisions than individuals
The loss of personal identity in a large crowd
reviewQueue.rationale:

• Groups making riskier decisions is 'risky shift' (a type of group polarization).

reviewQueue.rationale:

reviewQueue.rationale:

Correct: (B) Type C (anxious-resistant/ambivalent, ~10-15%): intense distress at separation, ambivalent behavior at reunion (clinging but also pushing away/angry), difficulty being soothed, limited exploration. Associated with inconsistent caregiving.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Easy comfort at reunion = secure attachment (Type B)
(C) Indifference to caregiver's absence = avoidant attachment (Type A)
(D) Organized, coherent responses are typical of secure, avoidant, or resistant attachment — DISorganized responses characterize Type D
references: Ainsworth, M. D. S., Blehar, M. C., Waters, E., & Wall, S. (1978). Patterns of attachment. Erlbaum.

reviewQueue.prompt: Puberty onset is primarily triggered by:
choices: Social pressure
Activation of the HPG axis: hypothalamus releases GnRH, stimulating pituitary release of gonadotropins (LH, FSH)
Cognitive development alone
Random biological chance
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Puberty begins with reactivation of the HPG axis: hypothalamus releases GnRH → anterior pituitary releases LH and FSH → gonads produce sex hormones (estrogen, testosterone) → secondary sexual characteristics develop.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Social pressure doesn't directly trigger the hormonal cascade of puberty
(C) Cognitive development is a consequence of brain maturation during puberty, not the trigger
(D) Puberty timing is influenced by genetics, nutrition, and body composition — it's not random

reviewQueue.prompt: Lev Vygotsky's key contribution to developmental psychology was emphasizing:
choices: Universal biological stages of development
The social and cultural context of cognitive development — learning is fundamentally a social process
That development occurs independently of social interaction
Only hereditary factors in intelligence
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Vygotsky's sociocultural theory: cognitive development is driven by social interaction, cultural tools (language, signs), and collaborative learning with more knowledgeable others (MKOs) within the zone of proximal development.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Universal biological stages = more aligned with Piaget (though Piaget also recognized social factors)
(C) Vygotsky argued the OPPOSITE — development is fundamentally social and interactive
(D) Vygotsky emphasized culture and social interaction, not just hereditary factors
references: Vygotsky, L. S. (1978). Mind in society: The development of higher psychological processes. Harvard University Press.

reviewQueue.prompt: Egocentrism in Piaget's preoperational stage means:
choices: Being selfish
The inability to take another person's perspective — assuming everyone sees and experiences the world as they do
Having no emotions
Being narcissistic clinically
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Piaget's egocentrism: a COGNITIVE limitation (not personality flaw) — preoperational children cannot mentally represent another person's viewpoint. The three mountains task demonstrates this: children describe what THEY see, not what another person sees.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Egocentrism is a cognitive limitation, not a character flaw of selfishness
(C) Egocentrism is about perspective-taking, not emotional capacity
(D) Narcissism is a personality construct — Piaget's egocentrism is a normal developmental stage
references: Piaget, J., & Inhelder, B. (1956). The child's conception of space. Routledge & Kegan Paul.

reviewQueue.prompt: The activity theory of aging proposes that:
choices: Older adults should disengage from society
Older adults who remain socially active and engaged maintain higher life satisfaction and well-being
Activity has no effect on aging
Only physical activity matters in aging
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Activity theory: successful aging involves maintaining roles, relationships, and activities from earlier life. Replacing lost roles with new ones promotes life satisfaction. Contrasts with disengagement theory.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Disengagement from society = disengagement theory (Cumming & Henry), which activity theory challenges
(C) Activity theory specifically argues that activity HAS significant positive effects on aging
(D) Social, cognitive, and physical activity ALL contribute — not just physical
references: Havighurst, R. J. (1961). Successful aging. The Gerontologist, 1(1), 8–13. https://doi.org/10.1093/geront/1.1.8

reviewQueue.prompt: Strange Situation procedure (Ainsworth) is used to assess:

Attachment style in infants (12-18 months) through a series of separations and reunions with the caregiver and a stranger
Intelligence in preschoolers
Motor development in newborns
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) The Strange Situation: eight episodes of caregiver-infant separations and reunions designed to activate the attachment system. Key behavioral indicators: separation protest, stranger wariness, reunion behavior, and exploration patterns.

Why others are wrong:

(C) It measures attachment, not intelligence — intelligence is measured by Bayley Scales, Wechsler tests, etc.

choices: Building actual scaffolds
Providing temporary, structured support that is graduallyremoved as the learner gains competence
Doing the work for the student permanently
Testing students repeatedly
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Scaffolding: the MKO (more knowledgeable other) provides guided support — hints, demonstrations, breaking tasks into steps — then systematically withdraws support as the learner becomes capable of independent performance.

Why others are wrong:

(C) Scaffolding is TEMPORARY — the goal is independent performance, not permanent dependency

reviewQueue.prompt: Disorganized attachment (Main & Solomon, Type D) is characterized by:

Easy comfort at reunion
Strong exploration behavior

Correct: (B) Type D (disorganized/disoriented, ~15%): paradoxical behaviors — approaching while averting gaze, freezing, stereotypies, fear/apprehension of the caregiver. Associated with caregiver abuse, neglect, or frightening behavior.

choices: Preoperational stage
Sensorimotor stage (approximately 8-12 months, fully by 18-24 months)
Formal operational stage
Concrete operational stage
reviewQueue.rationale:

Why others are wrong:

references: Piaget, J. (1954). The construction of reality in the child (M. Cook, Trans.). Basic Books.

choices: Extreme distress at separation

Crying inconsolably at reunion
Disorganized, contradictory behaviors
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Type A (avoidant, ~20-25%): little distress at separation, actively avoids or ignores caregiver at reunion, willingly approaches strangers. Associated with emotionally unavailable or rejecting caregiving. The child learns to suppress attachment needs.

(C) Crying inconsolably at reunion = resistant/ambivalent attachment (Type C)
(D) Disorganized, contradictory behaviors = disorganized attachment (Type D)

reviewQueue.prompt: Harlow's surrogate mother studies demonstrated:
choices: That food is the only basis for attachment
That CONTACT COMFORT (soft, tactile stimulation) is MORE important than food in attachment formation
That attachment is impossible with surrogates
That only human mothers can form attachments
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Harlow: infant monkeys preferred the soft, cloth-covered surrogate over the wire surrogate that provided food. Contact comfort was the primary determinant of attachment, challenging the cupboard theory (attachment = food association).

Why others are wrong:
(A) The studies specifically DISPROVED the idea that food is the sole basis for attachment
(C) Monkeys DID form attachments to the cloth surrogate — though these attachments were insufficient for normal development
(D) The studies showed attachment can form with non-living surrogates (though quality differs from human caregivers)

reviewQueue.prompt: Emerging adulthood (Arnett) refers to:
choices: Early childhood
A developmental period from approximately ages 18-25 characterized by identity exploration, instability, self-focus, and feeling 'in-between'
Only middle adulthood
Late adulthood
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Arnett (2000): emerging adulthood (~18-25) is a distinct period in industrialized societies. Features: identity exploration (love, work, worldviews), instability, self-focused, feeling in-between (not adolescent, not fully adult), and optimism/possibilities.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Early childhood = Erikson's initiative vs. guilt stage (~3-6 years)
(C) Middle adulthood = generativity vs. stagnation (~40-65)
(D) Late adulthood = integrity vs. despair (~65+)
references: Arnett, J. J. (2000). Emerging adulthood: A theory of development from the late teens through the twenties. American Psychologist, 55(5), 469–480. https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.55.5.469

6-8 months of age and peaks around 12-15 months
5 years of age
Only in adulthood
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Stranger anxiety: distress in response to unfamiliar people, emerging ~6-8 months (coinciding with development of object permanence and specific attachment). Peaks ~12-15 months, then gradually declines.

(C) By age 5, stranger anxiety has typically resolved
(D) Stranger anxiety is a normal infant developmental phenomenon

reviewQueue.prompt: Continuity vs. discontinuity in development refers to the debate about whether:
choices: Development always stops at age 18
Development occurs gradually and continuously OR through distinct, qualitatively different stages
Only nature matters in development
Development is the same across all cultures
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Continuity: development is gradual, quantitative change (like growing taller). Discontinuity: development involves qualitatively distinct stages (like a caterpillar → butterfly). Piaget's theory is discontinuous; information processing is continuous.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Development continues throughout the lifespan — it doesn't stop at 18
(C) Nature vs. nurture is a SEPARATE developmental debate
(D) Cultural universality vs. specificity is a SEPARATE developmental question
references: Lerner, R. M. (2002). Concepts and theories of human development (3rd ed.). Erlbaum.

reviewQueue.prompt: Diana Baumrind's authoritative parenting is associated with:
choices: Poor child outcomes
The BEST child outcomes: high self-esteem, social competence, academic success, and emotional regulation
Rebellious children
Excessively dependent children
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Authoritative parenting (high warmth + high demands) consistently predicts the best developmental outcomes across cultures. Children show: higher self-esteem, better academic performance, fewer behavioral problems, greater social competence.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Authoritative parenting predicts the BEST outcomes, not poor ones
(C) Rebellious behavior is more associated with authoritarian parenting (excessive control provokes reactance)
(D) Excessive dependence is more associated with permissive parenting (insufficient demands for self-regulation)
references: Baumrind, D. (1991). The influence of parenting style on adolescent competence and substance use. Journal of Early Adolescence, 11(1), 56–95. https://doi.org/10.1177/0272431691111004

reviewQueue.prompt: Concrete operational thinking (Piaget, ages ~7-11) is characterized by:
choices: Abstract hypothetical reasoning
Logical thinking about CONCRETE, tangible events — including conservation, classification, and seriation
No logical abilities
Only sensorimotor intelligence
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Concrete operations: children can think logically about concrete objects and events. Achievements: conservation, reversibility, decentration, classification, seriation, transitivity. Limitation: can't yet reason about ABSTRACT hypotheticals.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Abstract hypothetical reasoning = formal operational stage (~12+)
(C) Children at this stage HAVE logical abilities — specifically for concrete problems
(D) Sensorimotor intelligence = the first stage (birth to ~2 years)
references: Piaget, J. (1965). The child's conception of number. W. W. Norton.

reviewQueue.prompt: Formal operational thinking (Piaget, ~12+) enables:
choices: Only concrete reasoning about physical objects
ABSTRACT, hypothetical-deductive reasoning, systematic scientific thinking, and considering possibilities beyond the present
No advanced thought
Only language development
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Formal operations: abstract thought, hypothetical reasoning ('what if?'), systematic hypothesis testing, combinatorial logic, and propositional reasoning. Not everyone reaches this stage — influenced by education and cultural context.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Concrete reasoning = concrete operational stage (~7-11)
(C) Formal operations represents the MOST advanced stage in Piaget's theory
(D) Language development spans all stages — formal operations specifically adds abstract reasoning
references: Inhelder, B., & Piaget, J. (1958). The growth of logical thinking from childhood to adolescence. Basic Books.

reviewQueue.prompt: Ainsworth's attachment theory proposes that the INTERNAL WORKING MODEL:
choices: Has no lasting effects
Creates mental representations of SELF and OTHERS that guide expectations in future relationships throughout the lifespan
Only affects infant behavior
Changes completely every year
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Internal working models: mental representations formed from early attachment experiences. A model of SELF (worthy/unworthy of love) and OTHERS (reliable/unreliable). These models guide relationship expectations and behavior across the lifespan.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Internal working models have SIGNIFICANT lasting effects on relationship patterns
(C) Internal working models influence relationships from infancy through adulthood
(D) While internal working models CAN change (through new relationships, therapy), they show considerable stability
references: Bretherton, I. (1992). The origins of attachment theory: John Bowlby and Mary Ainsworth. Developmental Psychology, 28(5), 759–775. https://doi.org/10.1037/0012-1649.28.5.759

reviewQueue.prompt: Erikson's generativity vs. stagnation stage (~40-65) involves:
choices: Developing basic trust
The need to contribute to the next generation through parenting, mentoring, work productivity, or community involvement
Achieving a sense of identity
Developing intimacy in relationships
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Generativity: concern for establishing and guiding the next generation. Achieved through parenting, mentoring, creative production, and community contribution. Failure → stagnation (self-absorption, lack of purpose).

Why others are wrong:
(A) Basic trust → trust vs. mistrust (infancy, stage 1)
(C) Sense of identity → identity vs. role confusion (adolescence, stage 5)
(D) Intimacy → intimacy vs. isolation (young adulthood, stage 6)
references: Erikson, E. H. (1950). Childhood and society. W. W. Norton.

reviewQueue.prompt: Piaget's assimilation involves:
choices: Modifying existing schemas to fit new information
Incorporating new information INTO existing schemas — interpreting new experiences using current cognitive frameworks
Rejecting all new information
Creating entirely new schemas each time
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Assimilation: fitting new experiences into existing schemas. A child who knows 'dog' calls a cat a 'dog' — assimilating the new animal into the existing 'four-legged animal' schema.

Why others are wrong:
(A) MODIFYING schemas = accommodation (the complementary process)
(C) Assimilation INCORPORATES new information — it doesn't reject it
(D) Assimilation uses EXISTING schemas rather than creating new ones each time
references: Piaget, J. (1952). The origins of intelligence in children (M. Cook, Trans.). International Universities Press.

reviewQueue.prompt: Piaget's accommodation involves:
choices: Fitting new information into existing schemas
MODIFYING or creating new schemas to fit information that doesn't fit existing frameworks
Ignoring conflicting information
Never changing one's understanding
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Accommodation: changing existing schemas or creating new ones when new information can't be assimilated. The child learns 'cat' is different from 'dog' — modifying the schema to create a separate category.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Fitting into existing schemas = assimilation
(C) Accommodation involves ENGAGING with conflicting information, not ignoring it
(D) Accommodation is specifically about CHANGING understanding when necessary
references: Piaget, J. (1952). The origins of intelligence in children (M. Cook, Trans.). International Universities Press.

reviewQueue.prompt: Disengagement theory (Cumming & Henry) proposes that:
choices: Older adults should stay maximally active
Aging naturally involves MUTUAL withdrawal between older adults and society — viewed as functional and adaptive by proponents
Disengagement has no effect on well-being
All older adults want to remain engaged
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Disengagement theory (1961): mutual, natural withdrawal between aging individuals and society. Criticized as too passive and universalized — activity theory and SOC model provide alternative perspectives emphasizing continued engagement.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Maximum activity = activity theory (the competing perspective)
(C) Disengagement proponents claimed it was adaptive for well-being (though critics disagree)
(D) Individual differences exist — some prefer disengagement, others prefer continued engagement
references: Cumming, E., & Henry, W. E. (1961). Growing old: The process of disengagement. Basic Books.

reviewQueue.prompt: The zone of proximal development (Vygotsky) represents:
choices: Tasks a child can already do independently
The gap between what a child can do ALONE and what they can do with GUIDED ASSISTANCE from a more knowledgeable other
Tasks completely beyond the child's capacity
Only physical development milestones
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) ZPD: the space between independent performance and assisted performance. Learning occurs most effectively within the ZPD — tasks that are challenging but achievable with appropriate scaffolding from a more knowledgeable other (MKO).

Why others are wrong:
(A) Already independent tasks are BELOW the ZPD — no learning benefit from instruction there
(C) Tasks completely beyond capacity are ABOVE the ZPD — even with help, the child can't succeed
(D) The ZPD applies to COGNITIVE and social development, not just physical milestones
references: Vygotsky, L. S. (1978). Mind in society: The development of higher psychological processes. Harvard University Press.

Achieving intimacy with a partner
Reviewing one's life with acceptance
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Identity vs. role confusion (~12-18): adolescents explore who they are across domains (occupation, ideology, relationships, sexuality). Successful resolution → coherent identity; failure → role confusion, identity diffusion.

(A) Trust in caregivers → trust vs. mistrust (infancy)
(C) Intimacy with a partner → intimacy vs. isolation (young adulthood)
(D) Life review → integrity vs. despair (late adulthood)

reviewQueue.prompt: Cross-sectional research designs in developmental psychology:

Compare DIFFERENT age groups at ONE point in time — faster and cheaper but confound age with cohort effects
Eliminate all confounds
Are the same as longitudinal designs
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Cross-sectional: compare different age groups simultaneously. Advantage: quick, inexpensive. Disadvantage: cohort effects — differences between age groups may reflect generational differences, not developmental changes.

Why others are wrong:

(C) Cross-sectional designs specifically INTRODUCE cohort effects as a confound
(D) Cross-sectional and longitudinal designs are fundamentally different approaches

choices: Only one research methodology
BOTH cross-sectional AND longitudinal approaches — allowing researchers to separate age, cohort, and time-of-measurement effects
No developmental data
Only qualitative methods
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Schaie's sequential designs: combining cross-sectional and longitudinal data collection allows researchers to disentangle age effects (developmental), cohort effects (generational), and time-of-measurement effects (historical).

Why others are wrong:
(A) Sequential designs specifically COMBINE multiple methodologies
(C) Sequential designs are specifically designed TO collect developmental data more effectively
(D) Sequential designs use quantitative methods to compare multiple cohorts over time

reviewQueue.prompt: Moral development in Gilligan's care perspective emphasizes:

That only men have morality
That morality doesn't develop

(C) Gilligan argued BOTH men and women have moral development — they may emphasize different perspectives

reviewQueue.prompt: The goodness-of-fit model (Thomas & Chess) proposes:
choices: That temperament is the only factor in development
Child outcomes depend on the MATCH between the child's temperament and the demands/expectations of the environment — particularly caregiving style
That all temperaments produce the same outcomes
That environment is the only factor
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Thomas & Chess: optimal development occurs when there's a good 'fit' between the child's temperament (easy, difficult, slow-to-warm-up) and environmental demands/expectations. A 'difficult' child with patient, flexible parenting can thrive.

Why others are wrong:
(A) The model emphasizes the INTERACTION of temperament and environment, not temperament alone
(C) Different temperaments produce different outcomes depending on environmental fit
(D) Both temperament AND environment matter — the model is explicitly interactionist
references: Thomas, A., & Chess, S. (1977). Temperament and development. Brunner/Mazel.

reviewQueue.prompt: Kohlberg's conventional level of moral reasoning involves:

Conforming to social expectations and maintaining the social order — 'good boy/nice girl' orientation and law-and-order reasoning
Abstract universal principles
Punishment avoidance
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Conventional level: Stage 3 (interpersonal concordance — seeking approval, 'good boy/nice girl') and Stage 4 (law and order — maintaining social system, duty, rules). Most adults reason at this level.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Self-interest = preconventional level (Stage 2: instrumental purpose)
(C) Abstract universal principles = postconventional level (Stage 6)
(D) Punishment avoidance = preconventional level (Stage 1: punishment-obedience)

reviewQueue.prompt: The preconventional level of moral reasoning (Kohlberg) is characterized by:
choices: Social conformity
SELF-CENTERED reasoning — avoiding punishment (Stage 1) and seeking personal reward (Stage 2)
Universal ethical principles
Maintaining social order
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Preconventional: Stage 1 (punishment/obedience — 'I'll get in trouble') and Stage 2 (instrumental/exchange — 'What's in it for me?'). Typical of young children but also found in some adults.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Social conformity = conventional level
(C) Universal ethical principles = postconventional Stage 6
(D) Maintaining social order = conventional Stage 4
references: Kohlberg, L. (1981). Essays on moral development: Vol. 1. The philosophy of moral development. Harper & Row.

reviewQueue.prompt: Internalizing disorders in children include:
choices: Only conduct problems
Anxiety, depression, withdrawal, and somatic complaints — problems directed INWARD
Only aggression
Only attention problems
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Internalizing disorders: emotional distress directed inward. Includes anxiety disorders, depression/dysthymia, social withdrawal, and psychosomatic problems. Often underdiagnosed because symptoms are less disruptive and less visible.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Conduct problems = externalizing disorders
(C) Aggression = externalizing disorder
(D) Attention problems are often classified separately or with externalizing problems (ADHD)

reviewQueue.prompt: Externalizing disorders in children include:
choices: Only depression
ADHD, conduct disorder, oppositional defiant disorder, and aggression — problems directed OUTWARD
Only anxiety
Only learning disabilities
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Externalizing disorders: behavioral problems directed outward/toward the environment. Includes ADHD, ODD, conduct disorder, aggression, and rule-breaking behavior. More easily identified than internalizing problems because they're disruptive.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Depression = internalizing disorder

reviewQueue.prompt: The standard error of measurement (SEM) is used to:
choices: Determine test validity
Calculate the confidence interval around an individual's true score
Establish test-retest reliability
Assess cultural bias in test items
reviewQueue.rationale: The SEM estimates the range within which an individual's true score likely falls. It is calculated from the test's reliability coefficient and standard deviation: SEM = SD × √(1 - reliability). Higher reliability results in smaller SEM, indicating more precise measurement. The 95% confidence interval is approximately ±2 SEMs around the observed score.

reviewQueue.rationale: The Flynn effect (Flynn, 1984) refers to the substantial and sustained increase in IQ scores worldwide over the 20th century (approximately 3 IQ points per decade). This necessitates periodic re-norming of IQ tests to maintain accurate standard scores.

reviewQueue.prompt: In classical test theory, an observed score is comprised of:
choices: The true score only
The true score plus measurement error
The standard deviation plus the mean
The reliability coefficient times the validity coefficient
reviewQueue.rationale: Classical test theory (CTT) posits that any observed score (X) equals the true score (T) plus error (E): X = T + E. Error is assumed to be random and normally distributed with a mean of zero. This model underlies reliability estimation — if errors are small and random, the observed score closely approximates the true score. Higher reliability means less error and more accurate measurement.

reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Content validity = whether test items adequately represent the full content domain. Established through expert review, analysis of curriculum standards, and systematic item sampling — not statistical procedures.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Correlating with a criterion = criterion validity (predictive or concurrent)
(C) Factor analysis examines internal structure, related to construct validity
(D) Test-retest correlation measures reliability (temporal stability), not validity

reviewQueue.prompt: IQ scores have a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of:
choices: Exactly 10
Exactly 15
Exactly 20
Exactly 25
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Standard IQ scores (deviation IQ): mean = 100, SD = 15. This means ~68% of scores fall between 85-115, and ~95% between 70-130. Used by WAIS, WISC, and most modern intelligence tests.

Why others are wrong:
(A) SD of 10 = T-scores (which have mean = 50, SD = 10)
(C) SD of 20 would spread scores too widely — 84th percentile would be IQ 120 and 98th would be 140
(D) SD of 25 is not used in any standard IQ scoring system

reviewQueue.prompt: The Rorschach Inkblot Test is classified as a:
choices: Highly structured standardized personality measure
Performance-based (projective) personality measure
Standardized objective neuropsychological measure
Comprehensive valid cognitive intelligence measure
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) The Rorschach is a performance-based (projective) test where examinees describe what they see in ambiguous inkblots. Scored using the Exner Comprehensive System or R-PAS, which provide empirical scoring.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Structured inventories (MMPI, PAI) use standardized questions — the Rorschach uses ambiguous stimuli
(C) Neuropsychological tests (Halstead-Reitan, WCST) assess brain-behavior relationships, not personality
(D) Intelligence tests (WAIS, WISC) measure cognitive abilities — the Rorschach assesses personality and thought processes

reviewQueue.prompt: Concurrent validity is demonstrated when:
choices: Test scores reliably accurately predict distinct future outcomes
Test scores correlate with a criterion measured at the same time
The specific test superficially appears to measure what it claims
All specific formal test items are completely internally consistent
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Concurrent validity: the test correlates with a criterion measured at approximately the SAME TIME. E.g., a new depression scale correlating with the BDI-II administered simultaneously.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Predicting future outcomes = predictive validity (criterion validity with a time lag)
(C) Appearing to measure what it claims = face validity (not a true form of validity)
(D) Internal consistency = reliability (Cronbach's alpha, split-half), not validity

reviewQueue.prompt: An intelligence test with a reliability of .95 means that:
choices: The test is statistically explicitly effectively perfectly fully valid explicitly 95% of the time directly
95% of the score variance is due to true score variance
The structured evaluated test absolutely incorrectly completely falsely fails independently 5% of the time
95% of studied diverse individuals will continuously correctly specifically score the same on strict retest
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Reliability = proportion of observed score variance attributable to true score variance. A reliability of .95 means 95% of score differences reflect actual ability differences, with only 5% due to measurement error.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Reliability ≠ validity — a test can be highly reliable but not valid (consistently measuring the wrong thing)
(C) 'Failing 5%' confuses reliability with test failure rates — the 5% is error variance, not failure
(D) Individual retest scores will vary due to the 5% error; reliability is about the overall proportion of variance, not individual constancy

reviewQueue.prompt: A T-score of 70 on the MMPI-2 clinical scales is considered:
choices: Objectively formally placed perfectly securely tightly uniformly fully and safely within normal limits
Clinically significant/elevated
Categorically statistically securely completely comprehensively firmly thoroughly reliably exactly below typical averages
Objectively flawlessly statically smoothly completely distinctly perfectly rigorously cleanly universally average expectations
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) On the MMPI-2, T-scores ≥ 65 are considered clinically significant, and T ≥ 70 is clearly elevated. Since T-scores have mean = 50 and SD = 10, a T of 70 is 2 SDs above the mean.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Normal limits on MMPI-2 clinical scales are generally T < 65
(C) T = 70 is ABOVE average (2 SDs above the mean), not below
(D) Average would be T = 50 (the mean for T-scores)

reviewQueue.prompt: In item response theory (IRT), item difficulty is defined by:
choices: Expert opinion
The ability level at which 50% of examinees answer correctly
The number of words in the item
How long it takes to answer
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) In IRT, item difficulty (b parameter) = the ability level (theta) at which 50% of examinees answer correctly. Higher b values = harder items that require greater ability for a 50% success rate.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Expert opinion relates to content validity, not the statistical item parameter in IRT
(C) Word count affects reading load but isn't the IRT definition of difficulty
(D) Response time is a separate parameter studied in some IRT extensions but isn't the difficulty parameter

reviewQueue.prompt: Response sets on personality inventories include:
choices: Only honest responding
Acquiescence (yea-saying), social desirability, and random responding
Perfect test-taking strategies
Only malingering
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Response sets are systematic tendencies unrelated to item content: acquiescence (tendency to agree), social desirability (giving socially acceptable answers), nay-saying, random responding, and extreme responding.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Honest responding is the goal, not a response set — response sets are BIASES in responding
(C) Perfect strategies don't exist for well-designed personality measures with validity scales
(D) Malingering is ONE type of response set but not the only one — social desirability and acquiescence are equally important

Only verbal and performance scores
A personality profile

Neuropsychological functioning

reviewQueue.prompt: An ipsative interpretation of test scores compares:
choices: The individual to a normative group
The individual's scores to their OWN pattern of strengths and weaknesses
Two different tests to each other
Group averages across studies
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Ipsative = comparing an individual's scores to their OWN profile. E.g., noting that a person's Verbal Comprehension is a relative strength compared to their own Processing Speed, regardless of normative standing.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Comparing to a normative group = normative interpretation
(C) Comparing different tests = concurrent validity analysis
(D) Comparing group averages = meta-analytic or between-studies comparison

choices: Depression
ADHD symptoms and related behavior problems
Autism spectrum disorder
Intellectual disability

Correct: (B) The Conners scales are the gold standard for assessing ADHD. They include parent, teacher, and self-report versions measuring inattention, hyperactivity/impulsivity, and associated behavioral problems.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Depression is assessed by the BDI-II, PHQ-9, or HDRS
(C) ASD is assessed by ADOS-2, ADI-R, or SRS-2
(D) Intellectual disability is assessed by IQ tests (WAIS/WISC) + adaptive behavior scales (Vineland)

reviewQueue.prompt: Ceiling effects occur when:
choices: Scores cluster at the bottom of the distribution
A test is too easy and most scores cluster at the top
Scores are normally distributed
The test has perfect reliability
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Ceiling effects: when a test is too easy for the population, scores pile up at the maximum, preventing differentiation among high-ability examinees. This reduces variability, reliability, and validity.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Scores clustering at the bottom = floor effect (the opposite problem)
(C) Normal distribution = no ceiling or floor effects
(D) Perfect reliability is unrelated to ceiling effects — ceiling effects actually REDUCE reliability by restricting range

reviewQueue.prompt: Construct validity is supported by:
choices: High test-retest reliability alone
Convergent and discriminant evidence showing the test relates to theoretically similar and dissimilar constructs appropriately
The test appearing valid to examinees
Item difficulty analysis only
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Construct validity (the overarching validity concept) requires convergent evidence (correlates with measures of similar constructs) AND discriminant evidence (doesn't correlate with measures of unrelated constructs).

Why others are wrong:
(A) Reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity — a reliable test can be invalid
(C) Appearing valid to examinees = face validity (not a formal type of validity)
(D) Item difficulty relates to test construction, not the broader construct validity question

17-90 years
Birth to 2 years
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) The Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children, Fifth Edition (WISC-V) is normed for ages 6:0-16:11. It provides Full Scale IQ and five primary index scores.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Ages 2-5 = WPPSI (Wechsler Preschool and Primary Scale of Intelligence)
(C) Ages 17-90 = WAIS (Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale)
(D) Birth to 2 = Bayley Scales of Infant Development (developmental assessment, not IQ)

reviewQueue.prompt: When a distribution is negatively skewed, the tail points:
choices: To the right (higher scores)
To the left (lower scores)
Equally in both directions
No direction — it's perfectly normal
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Negative skew: the tail extends to the LEFT (toward lower scores). Most scores cluster at the high end. This occurs with easy tests (most people score high, few score very low). Mean < Median < Mode.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Tail to the right = positive skew (most scores are low, with a few very high scores)
(C) Equal in both directions = a normal, symmetric distribution (no skew)
(D) A negatively skewed distribution is definitionally NOT normal

reviewQueue.prompt: The Thematic Apperception Test (TAT) is:
choices: An objective personality inventory
A projective test where examinees create stories about ambiguous pictures
A cognitive ability test
A behavioral observation checklist
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) The TAT (Murray, 1935) presents ambiguous pictures and asks examinees to tell a story (what's happening, what led up to it, what will happen next). Responses reveal underlying needs, conflicts, and interpersonal patterns.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Objective inventories (MMPI, PAI) use structured items — the TAT uses ambiguous stimuli
(C) The TAT measures personality dynamics, not cognitive abilities
(D) Behavioral checklists (CBCL, BASC) are standardized rating forms, not projective story-telling tasks

reviewQueue.prompt: The coefficient of determination (r²) represents:
choices: The correlation between two variables
The proportion of variance in one variable explained by the other
The reliability of a test
The significance level of a study
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) r² = the squared correlation coefficient. If r = .60, then r² = .36, meaning 36% of the variance in one variable is explained by (shared with) the other. The remaining 64% is unexplained.

Why others are wrong:
(A) The correlation itself is r, not r²; r² transforms it into variance explained
(C) Reliability is measured by test-retest, internal consistency, or inter-rater coefficients, not r²
(D) The significance level (p-value) is a separate inferential statistic

reviewQueue.prompt: A percentile rank of 84 means:
choices: The person answered 84% of items correctly
The person scored higher than 84% of the normative sample
The person scored in the 84th stanine
The person needs 84 points to pass
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Percentile rank = the percentage of the norm group that scored AT OR BELOW a given score. A percentile of 84 means the person outperformed 84% of the normative sample (approximately 1 SD above the mean).

Why others are wrong:
(A) Percentile rank ≠ percent correct; it's a norm-referenced score comparing to the sample
(C) Stanines range from 1-9; percentile 84 corresponds to approximately stanine 7
(D) Percentile rank has nothing to do with passing scores or cut points

reviewQueue.prompt: Actuarial (statistical) prediction differs from clinical prediction in that it:
choices: Relies on subjective clinical judgment
Uses empirically derived formulas and algorithms to make predictions
Is always less accurate
Doesn't use data
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Actuarial prediction uses statistical formulas combining predictor variables with empirically established weights. Research consistently shows actuarial methods are equal to or better than clinical judgment for most prediction tasks.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Subjective judgment = clinical prediction, not actuarial
(C) Actuarial methods are generally MORE accurate than clinical judgment (Meehl, 1954; Grove et al., 2000)
(D) Actuarial methods are heavily data-driven — they rely entirely on empirical data and statistical relationships

reviewQueue.prompt: Restricted range in a sample will cause the correlation coefficient to:
choices: Increase
Decrease (underestimate the true relationship)
Stay the same
Become negative
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Range restriction reduces the observed correlation because there's less variability in scores — if everyone scores similarly on the predictor, there's little variability to covary with the criterion.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Restriction reduces, not increases, the correlation (correction for attenuation formulas adjust for this)
(C) Range restriction systematically affects correlations — they don't stay the same
(D) Restriction attenuates magnitude without necessarily changing direction (sign) of the correlation

reviewQueue.prompt: The standard error of measurement (SEM) indicates:
choices: The arithmetic mean average test score across the entire normative standardization sample
The expected range of score fluctuation around a true score due to random measurement error
The degree to which a test measures what it purports to measure as a validity coefficient
The total number of participants included in the original normative standardization sample
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) SEM estimates how much an individual's observed score might vary from their true score due to random measurement error. A smaller SEM indicates more precise measurement. SEM = SD × √(1 - reliability).

Why others are wrong:
(A) Average test score = mean, a central tendency measure.
(C) Validity refers to whether the test measures what it claims — SEM addresses measurement precision.
(D) Normative sample size is a test development characteristic, not related to SEM.

flags.detail: No citation or reference overlay is attached.

reviewQueue.prompt: The Rorschach Inkblot Test using the Exner Comprehensive System provides:
choices: Only subjective clinical impressions without any standardized scoring procedures or normative data
Standardized scoring procedures with normative data, established reliability, and valid clinical indices
A complete diagnosis based on a single inkblot response without need for full administration
Computer-generated personality profiles that require no clinical interpretation expertise at all
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Exner developed a standardized, empirically-based scoring system for the Rorschach with normative data, established reliability, and valid indices, moving it beyond purely clinical impression.

Why others are wrong:
(A) The Exner system specifically provides OBJECTIVE, standardized scoring.
(C) Rorschach interpretation uses patterns across ALL responses, never a single response.
(D) Computer scoring assists but interpretation requires clinical expertise.

reviewQueue.prompt: Regression to the mean explains why:
choices: Extreme scores on initial testing tend to move toward the population average upon subsequent retesting
All scores remain perfectly stable and unchanged across repeated administrations without any variation
Test-retest reliability coefficients are always perfect at 1.0 indicating zero random measurement error
Normal distributions don't apply to psychological tests because scores are uniformly distributed
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (A) Regression to the mean: extreme scores (very high or very low) on initial testing tend to move toward the population mean on retesting. This is a statistical phenomenon, not necessarily reflecting real change.

Why others are wrong:
(B) Scores fluctuate — they don't all remain perfectly stable.
(C) No test has perfect reliability — measurement error always exists.
(D) Normal distributions are widely used in psychological testing.

reviewQueue.prompt: Ecological validity of a neuropsychological assessment refers to:
choices: Whether the assessment was administered in an outdoor naturalistic environmental setting
Whether test performance accurately predicts real-world functional abilities and daily living skills
Whether the test exclusively uses naturalistic stimuli that closely resemble real-world objects
Whether the test was originally developed through a field study research methodology approach
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Ecological validity in neuropsychological assessment: whether test scores meaningfully predict a patient's ability to function in daily life (driving, managing finances, living independently).

Why others are wrong:
(A) The 'ecological' doesn't refer to outdoor environments — it refers to real-world applicability.
(C) Natural stimuli may increase ecological validity but don't define it.
(D) Field study development relates to research methodology, not clinical validity.

reviewQueue.prompt: Item response theory (IRT) differs from classical test theory in that IRT:
choices: Is significantly and mathematically substantially simpler to effectively implement in broad practice
Models the probability of a correct response as a function of both item parameters and person ability
Does not require rigorous complex advanced formal statistical mathematical analytical computations
Functions completely correctly and exclusively only with highly unstructured projective assessments
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) IRT models the relationship between a latent trait (ability) and the probability of endorsing an item using item characteristic curves. Parameters include difficulty, discrimination, and guessing. Unlike CTT, IRT properties are sample-independent.

Why others are wrong:
(A) IRT is MORE complex than CTT, requiring larger samples and specialized software
(C) IRT is heavily statistical — it uses maximum likelihood estimation and complex mathematical models
(D) IRT works primarily with ability and achievement tests, not projective assessments

reviewQueue.prompt: The WAIS-V measures:
choices: Academic achievement
Adult intelligence across multiple cognitive domains
Personality traits
Adaptive behavior
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) The Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale (WAIS-V, ages 16-90) provides Full Scale IQ and index scores across cognitive domains including Verbal Comprehension, Visual Spatial, Fluid Reasoning, Working Memory, and Processing Speed.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Academic achievement → WJ-IV Achievement, WIAT-4
(C) Personality traits → MMPI-2, PAI, NEO-PI-3
(D) Adaptive behavior → Vineland-3, ABAS-3
references: Wechsler, D. (2024). Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale–Fifth Edition (WAIS-V): Technical and interpretive manual. Pearson.

reviewQueue.prompt: Split-half reliability involves:
choices: Administering the test on two occasions
Dividing the test into two halves and correlating scores between them
Having two raters score the same test
Comparing scores across different tests
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Split-half reliability: divide a test into two comparable halves (odd/even items), score each half separately, and correlate. The Spearman-Brown formula corrects the correlation to estimate full-test reliability.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Two occasions = test-retest reliability
(C) Two raters scoring = inter-rater reliability
(D) Comparing different tests = alternate forms reliability
references: Anastasi, A., & Urbina, S. (1997). Psychological testing (7th ed.). Prentice-Hall.

reviewQueue.prompt: Predictive validity is demonstrated when:
choices: The test correlates with a criterion measured at the SAME time
Test scores predict a FUTURE criterion (e.g., GRE scores predicting graduate school grades)
The test has high face validity
Items are reviewed by experts
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Predictive validity: test scores obtained NOW predict performance on a criterion measured in the FUTURE. Time interval between predictor and criterion is the key distinction from concurrent validity.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Criterion measured at the same time = concurrent validity
(C) Face validity is whether the test APPEARS to measure what it claims — not predictive validity
(D) Expert review = content validity
references: Cronbach, L. J. (1990). Essentials of psychological testing (5th ed.). Harper & Row.

reviewQueue.prompt: Divergent validity (discriminant validity) is established when a test:
choices: Correlates highly with measures of the same construct
Shows LOW correlations with measures of theoretically DIFFERENT constructs
Correlates with a future criterion
Has high internal consistency
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Discriminant/divergent validity: the test does NOT correlate with measures of constructs it should be theoretically distinct from. A depression scale should NOT correlate highly with a measure of reading ability.

Why others are wrong:
(A) High correlation with same construct = convergent validity (the complement of discriminant)
(C) Future criterion correlation = predictive validity
(D) Internal consistency = reliability, not discriminant validity
references: Campbell, D. T., & Fiske, D. W. (1959). Convergent and discriminant validation by the multitrait-multimethod matrix. Psychological Bulletin, 56(2), 81–105. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0046016

Is only for children

reviewQueue.prompt: Response bias in testing includes:
choices: Only accurate responding
Acquiescence (yea-saying), social desirability, malingering, and extreme responding
Only test-retest effects
No systematic patterns
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Response biases are systematic patterns of responding unrelated to test content: acquiescence (agreeing regardless), social desirability (looking good), malingering (looking bad), extreme responding, and central tendency.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Accurate responding indicates ABSENCE of response bias
(C) Test-retest effects relate to reliability, not response bias
(D) Response biases ARE systematic patterns — that's what makes them biases

reviewQueue.prompt: A raw score by itself is:

Meaningless without a frame of reference (norms or criterion standards)
The most important score type

Correct: (B) A raw score (e.g., 45 correct) has no inherent meaning without context. It must be converted to a standardized score (IQ, T-score, percentile) using norms, or compared to a criterion (pass/fail threshold) to be interpretable.

Why others are wrong:
(A) A raw score of 45 tells you nothing about performance level without norms or criteria
(C) Standardized/normed scores are more interpretable than raw scores for most purposes
(D) Raw scores must be CONVERTED to percentiles — they are not percentiles themselves

reviewQueue.prompt: Malingering on psychological tests involves:
choices: Answering honestly
Deliberately faking or exaggerating symptoms for external incentive (financial gain, avoiding prosecution)
Random responding
Trying one's hardest
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Malingering: intentional fabrication or exaggeration of symptoms motivated by external incentives. Detected through validity scales (F, Fb, Fp on MMPI-2), symptom validity tests (TOMM), and inconsistency indicators.

reviewQueue.prompt: Sensitivity of a diagnostic test reflects:
choices: How specific the test is to one condition
The test's ability to correctly identify individuals WHO DO HAVE the condition (true positive rate)
The test's ability to identify those without the condition
The test's reading level
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Sensitivity = true positives / (true positives + false negatives). High sensitivity = few missed cases. A sensitive test is good for RULING OUT a condition (SnNOut: Sensitivity rules out Negative).

Why others are wrong:
(A) How specific to one condition = specificity (true negative rate), not sensitivity
(C) Identifying those WITHOUT the condition = specificity
(D) Reading level refers to test accessibility, not diagnostic accuracy
references: Groth-Marnat, G., & Wright, A. J. (2016). Handbook of psychological assessment (6th ed.). Wiley.

reviewQueue.prompt: Specificity of a diagnostic test reflects:
choices: How sensitive the test is

reviewQueue.prompt: According to Beck's Cognitive Model, the 'cognitive triad' of depression consists of negative views about:
choices: The past, the present, and the future
The self, the world (environment), and the future
Id, ego, and superego

reviewQueue.rationale:
Aaron Beck proposed that depression is maintained by a negative cognitive triad: (1) negative views of the self ('I am worthless'), (2) negative views of the world/environment ('Everything is unfair and hostile'), and (3) negative views of the future ('Things will never get better').

Why others are wrong:
