reviewQueue.prompt: Bipolar I disorder is distinguished from Bipolar II disorder primarily by:
choices: The severity and duration of the depressive episodes
The presence of psychotic symptoms during depression
The occurrence of a full manic episode vs. only hypomanic episodes
The rapid cycling between moods
reviewQueue.rationale:
The defining feature of Bipolar I is the occurrence of at least one full manic episode (lasting at least 1 week, causing marked impairment to functioning, or requiring hospitalization). Bipolar II requires at least one major depressive episode AND at least one hypomanic episode (lasting at least 4 days, noticeable by others, but NOT causing severe impairment or requiring hospitalization). If there is ever a full manic episode, the diagnosis automatically becomes Bipolar I.

Why others are wrong:
• Depressive episodes are required for Bipolar II, but their severity alone doesn't differentiate it from Bipolar I (which also has severe depressions).
• Psychotic symptoms can occur in severe depression in both disorders; however, psychosis during a 'high' automatically qualifies it as full mania (Bipolar I).
• Rapid cycling (4+ episodes per year) is a specifier that can be applied to either type.

reviewQueue.prompt: Factitious Disorder is characterized by:
choices: Feigning physical or psychological symptoms for an external reward like money or avoiding work
A genuine belief that one has a serious illness despite medical reassurance
Intentional production or feigning of symptoms solely to assume the 'sick role', without external incentives
Neurological symptoms (like paralysis) with no identifiable organic cause due to an unconscious conflict
reviewQueue.rationale:
Factitious Disorder (previously Munchausen's) involves intentionally producing, falsifying, or exaggerating symptoms. Crucially, the motivation is internal—a psychological need to be cared for and assume the 'sick role'—rather than obtaining a tangible external reward.

Why others are wrong:
• Feigning for external reward (money, avoid jail/work, getting drugs) is Malingering, which is a V-code for behavior, not a psychiatric disorder.
• Genuine but false belief in having an illness is Illness Anxiety Disorder (hypochondriasis).
• Unconscious neurological symptoms (paralysis, blindness) without physical cause is Conversion Disorder (Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder).

reviewQueue.prompt: Measurement invariance in assessment means:
choices: Statistical absolute certainty that zero measurement error structurally exists within the instrument
A given test demonstrably measures the identical theoretical construct in the exact same way across groups
Every demographic group inevitably achieves the exact identical mean raw score during administration
Only a single, highly standardized form of the measurement instrument exists globally to prevent bias
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Measurement invariance (factorial invariance): the test's factor structure, factor loadings, and intercepts are equivalent across groups. Without invariance, group comparisons may be invalid — score differences could reflect measurement artifact rather than true differences.

Why others are wrong:
(A) All empirical tests invariably possess measurable statistical measurement error margins.
(C) Diverse groups frequently achieve differing means; invariance specifies measurement parity, not score parity.
(D) Multiple invariant equivalent test alternate forms can effectively exist logically and empirically.

Subjective clinical rater bias emerging during unstructured observational behavioral data collection
Superficial structural face validity concerning the apparent relevance of presented stimulus materials
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Alternate (parallel) forms: two equivalent versions of the test given to the same group. Controls for practice effects, memory of items, and content sampling. The correlation between forms estimates reliability.

(C) Rater bias → inter-rater reliability measures

reviewQueue.prompt: When interpreting test scores, the standard error of measurement (SEM) indicates:
choices: That the test is fundamentally psychometrically invalid and should be immediately discontinued from use

Why others are wrong:
(A) SEM is present in all tests — it doesn't indicate invalidity.

reviewQueue.prompt: A correlation coefficient of .85 between a predictor and criterion indicates:

reviewQueue.prompt: Hemispatial neglect (unilateral neglect) most commonly results from:

Bilateral occipital damage resulting primarily in complete cortical visual blindness presentations
Isolated cerebellar damage heavily disrupting fundamental automated motor coordination sequencing
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Right parietal (especially inferior parietal lobule/temporoparietal junction) damage → left-sided neglect. The right hemisphere attends to both visual fields; the left hemisphere only attends to the right. So left damage rarely causes right neglect (right hemisphere compensates), but right damage causes left neglect.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Left hemisphere damage rarely produces significant neglect
(C) Occipital damage → visual field cuts (hemianopia), not neglect
(D) Cerebellar damage → ataxia, not neglect

(C) AVOIDING cultural discussion ignores important therapeutic content — cultural dialogue enhances treatment
(D) Knowledge of OTHER cultures is equally essential to self-knowledge
references: Sue, D. W., Arredondo, P., & McDavis, R. J. (1992). Multicultural counseling competencies and standards: A call to the profession. Journal of Counseling & Development, 70(4), 477–486. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1556-6676.1992.tb01642.x

reviewQueue.prompt: Termination in therapy should ideally:
choices: Be abrupt and unexpected
Be a planned, collaborative process discussed well in advance, with addressing remaining concerns and providing referrals if needed
Never happen — therapy should continue indefinitely
Only be initiated by the client
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Ethical termination: planned and collaborative, with adequate notice, review of progress, discussion of relapse prevention, addressing remaining needs, and providing referrals when appropriate. Gradual tapering is often beneficial.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Abrupt termination without planning may constitute abandonment
(C) Indefinite therapy isn't always needed — ethical practice involves knowing when to end treatment
(D) Both therapist and client can initiate termination — it should be a collaborative discussion
references: Norcross, J. C., Zimmerman, B. E., Greenberg, R. P., & Swift, J. K. (2017). Do all therapists do that when saying goodbye? A study of commonalities in termination behaviors. Psychotherapy, 54(1), 66–75. https://doi.org/10.1037/pst0000097

reviewQueue.prompt: Motivational enhancement therapy (MET) is a:
choices: Long-term psychoanalytic approach
Brief, client-centered intervention (typically 4 sessions) designed to mobilize internal motivation for change
Strict behavioral protocol
Medication management approach
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) MET (Miller et al., adapted from Project MATCH): a brief (typically 4 sessions) adaptation of MI that uses assessment feedback and motivational strategies to enhance intrinsic motivation for behavior change.

Why others are wrong:
(A) MET is explicitly brief, not long-term psychoanalytic
(C) MET is collaborative and client-centered, not rigid/prescriptive
(D) MET is a psychosocial intervention, not medication management
references: Miller, W. R., Zweben, A., DiClemente, C. C., & Rychtarik, R. G. (1992). Motivational enhancement therapy manual (Project MATCH Monograph Series, Vol. 2). NIAAA.

reviewQueue.prompt: Shaping in behavioral therapy involves:
choices: Reinforcing only the final target behavior
Reinforcing successive approximations toward the target behavior
Punishing incorrect responses
Ignoring all behavior
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Shaping: reinforcing behaviors that progressively closer approximate the desired final behavior. Each step closer is reinforced; previous levels are no longer reinforced (differential reinforcement of successive approximations).

Why others are wrong:
(A) Reinforcing ONLY the final behavior wouldn't work if the behavior never occurs — shaping builds to the final behavior
(C) Shaping uses positive reinforcement, not punishment
(D) Ignoring all behavior = extinction of all behavior, the opposite of shaping
references: Skinner, B. F. (1953). Science and human behavior. Macmillan.

reviewQueue.prompt: The placebo effect in psychotherapy research demonstrates that:
choices: Placebos never work
Client expectations and hope for improvement can produce genuine therapeutic change
Only medication produces placebo effects
Psychotherapy doesn't work
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Placebo effects: client expectations, hope, and the therapeutic context itself can produce real psychological and physiological improvements. This accounts for a significant portion of therapy outcomes (expectancy factor).

Why others are wrong:
(A) Placebo effects are well-documented and can produce substantial improvements
(C) Placebo effects occur in BOTH medication and psychotherapy research
(D) Psychotherapy works BEYOND placebo — but placebo/expectancy effects contribute to outcomes
references: Kirsch, I. (2019). Placebo effect in the treatment of depression and anxiety. Frontiers in Psychiatry, 10, 407. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyt.2019.00407

reviewQueue.prompt: Prolonged exposure therapy (PE) for PTSD involves:
choices: Brief, surface-level discussion of trauma
Repeated, systematic confrontation with trauma-related memories (imaginal exposure) and avoided situations (in vivo exposure) until habituation occurs
Avoidance of all trauma-related material
Only relaxation training
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Foa's PE: (1) psychoeducation, (2) breathing retraining, (3) in vivo exposure to avoided situations, and (4) imaginal exposure — repeatedly recounting the trauma narrative until emotional processing occurs and SUDS decrease.

Why others are wrong:
(A) PE involves prolonged, detailed engagement WITH trauma memories — not brief/surface-level
(C) Avoidance maintains PTSD — PE specifically counteracts avoidance through systematic exposure
(D) While breathing retraining is included, the core component is repeated exposure
references: Foa, E. B., Hembree, E. A., & Rothbaum, B. O. (2007). Prolonged exposure therapy for PTSD: Emotional processing of traumatic experiences—Therapist guide. Oxford University Press.

reviewQueue.prompt: Harm reduction approaches:
choices: Require complete abstinence before providing services
Meet clients where they are, aiming to reduce negative consequences of substance use without requiring abstinence as a precondition
Are never evidence-based
Promote substance use
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Harm reduction: pragmatic strategies to minimize negative health, social, and economic consequences of substance use. Examples: needle exchange programs, naloxone distribution, managed alcohol programs, medication-assisted treatment.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Requiring abstinence before services = abstinence-based approach; harm reduction removes this barrier
(C) Harm reduction has significant evidence support — needle exchanges reduce HIV, naloxone prevents overdose deaths
(D) Harm reduction aims to REDUCE harm, not promote use — it acknowledges that some use will occur
references: Marlatt, G. A. (Ed.). (1998). Harm reduction: Pragmatic strategies for managing high-risk behaviors. Guilford Press.

reviewQueue.prompt: Behavioral activation (BA) for depression focuses on:
choices: Cognitive restructuring of negative thoughts
Increasing engagement in valued activities and reducing avoidance patterns to improve mood through positive reinforcement
Dream interpretation
Medication adjustment
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) BA (Jacobson, Martell): depression involves withdrawal from rewarding activities → less reinforcement → more depression. BA reverses this cycle by scheduling activities aligned with values, monitoring mood-activity relationships, and reducing avoidance.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Cognitive restructuring = cognitive therapy; BA focuses on behavioral changes (though they complement each other in full CBT)
(C) Dream interpretation = psychoanalytic technique
(D) Medication adjustment = pharmacotherapy, not behavioral activation
references: Martell, C. R., Dimidjian, S., & Herman-Dunn, R. (2010). Behavioral activation for depression: A clinician's guide. Guilford Press.

reviewQueue.prompt: The Premack principle states that:
choices: Punishment is always more effective than reinforcement
A high-probability behavior can serve as a reinforcer for a low-probability behavior ('Eat your vegetables, then you can have dessert')
Only primary reinforcers work
Reinforcement doesn't affect behavior
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Premack (1959): preferred activities reinforce less preferred activities. 'Grandma's rule': First do what you need to do (low-probability), then you can do what you want to do (high-probability).

Why others are wrong:
(A) Premack principle uses reinforcement, not punishment
(C) The Premack principle specifically demonstrates that ACTIVITIES (secondary reinforcers) can reinforce behavior
(D) Reinforcement reliably increases behavior — the Premack principle is one application of this
references: Premack, D. (1959). Toward empirical behavior laws: I. Positive reinforcement. Psychological Review, 66(4), 219–233. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0040891

reviewQueue.prompt: Rational emotive behavior therapy (REBT, Ellis) uses the ABCDE model where:
choices: A=Action, B=Behavior, C=Consequence only
A=Activating event, B=Beliefs (rational/irrational), C=Consequences (emotional/behavioral), D=Disputing irrational beliefs, E=Effective new philosophy
There is no model
Only the therapist uses the model internally
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Ellis's ABCDE: it's not the event (A) that causes emotional disturbance (C), but the irrational BELIEFS (B) about the event. Therapy involves actively DISPUTING (D) irrational beliefs to develop an effective new philosophy (E).

Why others are wrong:
(A) The correct acronym meanings are different from this option
(C) The ABCDE model is central to REBT — it's a core therapeutic framework
(D) Clients actively learn and apply the model — psychoeducation about the ABCDE framework is a key component
references: Ellis, A. (1962). Reason and emotion in psychotherapy. Lyle Stuart.

reviewQueue.prompt: Therapeutic factors unique to GROUP therapy (Yalom) include:
choices: Individual attention and privacy
Universality, group cohesion, interpersonal learning, altruism, and the corrective recapitulation of the primary family group
Complete confidentiality guarantee
Only cognitive restructuring
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Yalom's 11 therapeutic factors: installation of hope, universality, imparting information, altruism, corrective recapitulation of the family, development of socializing techniques, imitative behavior, interpersonal learning, group cohesion, catharsis, existential factors.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Individual attention is typically LESS in groups — groups offer unique social healing factors instead
(C) Group confidentiality cannot be guaranteed because other members' behavior can't be controlled
(D) Group therapy encompasses behavioral, experiential, interpersonal, and existential processes — not just cognitive
references: Yalom, I. D., & Leszcz, M. (2005). The theory and practice of group psychotherapy (5th ed.). Basic Books.

reviewQueue.prompt: Narrative therapy (White & Epston) helps clients:
choices: Only analyze behavior charts
Externalize problems ('the problem is the problem, the person is not the problem'), identify preferred stories, and re-author their life narratives
Only use medication
Only focus on the past
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Narrative therapy: problems are externalized and separated from the person's identity. Therapy helps identify 'unique outcomes' (exceptions to the problem story) and develop preferred, empowering alternative narratives.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Narrative therapy uses conversation and storytelling, not behavior charts
(C) Narrative therapy is a talk therapy approach, not medication-based
(D) Narrative therapy focuses on present meaning-making and future possibilities, not solely the past
references: White, M., & Epston, D. (1990). Narrative means to therapeutic ends. W. W. Norton.

reviewQueue.prompt: Existential therapy focuses on:
choices: Specific behavioral techniques
Universal human concerns: meaning, freedom/responsibility, isolation, and death (mortality)
Only past childhood experiences
Only medication management
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Existential therapy (Yalom, May, Frankl): addresses four ultimate concerns — death (mortality awareness), freedom (choice and responsibility), isolation (fundamental aloneness), and meaninglessness (creating purpose). Therapy explores these themes.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Existential therapy is experiential and philosophical, not technique-driven
(C) Existential therapy is HERE-AND-NOW and future-oriented, not primarily past-focused
(D) Existential therapy is a talk therapy approach, not pharmacological
references: Yalom, I. D. (1980). Existential psychotherapy. Basic Books.

reviewQueue.prompt: Gestalt therapy emphasizes:
choices: Unconscious conflict analysis
Present-moment awareness, personal responsibility, the phenomenological experience, and unfinished business ('here and now')
Only cognitive restructuring
Past-oriented interpretation
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Perls: Gestalt therapy focuses on present experience, awareness (the 'how' of behavior, not 'why'), personal responsibility, contact/withdrawal cycles, and completing unfinished gestalt (unresolved situations). Techniques: empty chair, exaggeration, role reversal.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Unconscious conflict analysis = psychoanalytic focus; Gestalt emphasizes present awareness
(C) Cognitive restructuring = CBT technique; Gestalt is experiential
(D) Gestalt therapy is firmly present-oriented — 'here and now' is the central focus
references: Perls, F. S., Hefferline, R. F., & Goodman, P. (1951). Gestalt therapy: Excitement and growth in the human personality. Julian Press.

reviewQueue.prompt: The therapeutic window for medication refers to:
choices: The window in the therapist's office
The range of drug concentration between the minimum effective dose and the dose that produces unacceptable side effects
Only the first dose
A scheduling concept
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Therapeutic window: the concentration range where a medication produces desired effects without unacceptable toxicity. Too low = ineffective; too high = toxic. Lithium has a notoriously narrow therapeutic window (0.6-1.2 mEq/L).

Why others are wrong:
(A) 'Window' is metaphorical — referring to the effective dosage range, not a physical window
(C) The therapeutic window applies to ongoing dosing, not just the first dose
(D) It's a pharmacological concept about dosage, not a scheduling term
references: Stahl, S. M. (2021). Stahl's essential psychopharmacology (5th ed.). Cambridge University Press.

reviewQueue.prompt: Person-centered therapy (Rogers) considers the therapeutic relationship as:
choices: Unimportant
Both necessary and sufficient for therapeutic change — the relationship IS the treatment
Only one of many tools
A potential obstacle to treatment
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Rogers: the three core conditions (empathy, genuineness/congruence, unconditional positive regard) are necessary AND sufficient for personality change. The relationship itself is the healing agent, not specific techniques.

Why others are wrong:
(A) The therapeutic relationship is the MOST important factor in person-centered therapy
(C) Rogers considered the relationship sufficient by itself — not merely one tool among many
(D) The relationship is the primary therapeutic agent, not an obstacle
references: Rogers, C. R. (1957). The necessary and sufficient conditions of therapeutic personality change. Journal of Consulting Psychology, 21(2), 95–103. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0045357

reviewQueue.prompt: Modeling (Bandura) in therapy involves:
choices: Only fashion modeling
The client learning new behaviors by observing others (therapist, peers, video) perform the desired behavior
Never observing others
Only reading about behavior change
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Bandura's modeling: learning through observation. In therapy, modeling can be live (therapist demonstrates), symbolic (video demonstrations), or participant (client observes then practices with guidance). Based on social learning theory.

Why others are wrong:
(A) 'Modeling' in therapy refers to behavioral demonstration, not fashion
(C) Observational learning is the CORE mechanism of modeling
(D) Modeling is specifically about OBSERVATION, not just reading (though bibliotherapy uses written materials)
references: Bandura, A. (1977). Social learning theory. Prentice-Hall.

reviewQueue.prompt: Decisional balance in motivational interviewing involves:
choices: Making decisions for the client
Helping clients weigh the PROS and CONS of changing versus not changing — exploring ambivalence systematically
Avoiding all discussion of change
Only focusing on negative consequences
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Decisional balance: collaboratively exploring four quadrants — benefits of changing, costs of changing, benefits of staying the same, and costs of staying the same. This clarifies ambivalence and tips motivation toward change.

Why others are wrong:
(A) MI is client-centered — the therapist guides but doesn't make decisions for the client
(C) MI specifically ENCOURAGES discussion of change through exploring ambivalence
(D) Decisional balance examines BOTH positive and negative aspects of change AND the status quo
references: Miller, W. R., & Rollnick, S. (2013). Motivational interviewing: Helping people change (3rd ed.). Guilford Press.

reviewQueue.prompt: Culturally adapted evidence-based treatments:
choices: Are less effective than standard treatments
Modify established treatments to incorporate cultural values, language, and practices — often IMPROVING outcomes for diverse populations
Are never necessary
Ignore cultural differences
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Cultural adaptation: systematically modifying EBTs (CBT, DBT, EMDR) to be congruent with clients' cultural contexts. Research shows adapted treatments often outperform standard versions for culturally diverse populations.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Meta-analyses show cultural adaptations are AT LEAST as effective and often MORE effective
(C) Cultural adaptation IS necessary for ethical, effective service delivery to diverse populations
(D) Cultural adaptation specifically ADDRESSES cultural differences by incorporating them into treatment
references: Griner, D., & Smith, T. B. (2006). Culturally adapted mental health intervention: A meta-analytic review. Psychotherapy: Theory, Research, Practice, Training, 43(4), 531–548. https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-3204.43.4.531

reviewQueue.prompt: The Dodo bird verdict in psychotherapy research suggests:
choices: That therapy doesn't work
That most bona fide psychotherapies produce roughly EQUIVALENT outcomes — 'everyone has won and all must have prizes'
That only CBT works
That only psychoanalysis works
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Rosenzweig (1936), Luborsky et al. (1975): when bona fide treatments are compared, outcome differences are minimal. Common factors (alliance, empathy, expectation) may account for more variance than specific techniques.

Why others are wrong:
(A) The Dodo bird verdict affirms that therapy WORKS — the question is whether specific therapies differ in effectiveness
(C) Multiple therapies show comparable effectiveness, not just CBT
(D) Multiple therapies show comparable effectiveness, not just psychoanalysis
references: Luborsky, L., Singer, B., & Luborsky, L. (1975). Comparative studies of psychotherapies: Is it true that 'everyone has won and all must have prizes'? Archives of General Psychiatry, 32(8), 995–1008. https://doi.org/10.1001/archpsyc.1975.01760260059004

reviewQueue.prompt: Play therapy is particularly appropriate for children because:
choices: Play has no therapeutic value
Play is children's natural medium of expression — it allows them to communicate, process experiences, and work through difficulties
It's easier for the therapist
Children can't benefit from therapy otherwise
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Play is the developmentally appropriate language of children. Through play, children express feelings they can't articulate verbally, process traumatic experiences, practice coping skills, and work through conflicts.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Play is therapeutically valuable — it's the primary medium for child therapy
(C) Play therapy requires specialized training — it's not easier, just developmentally appropriate
(D) Children can benefit from multiple therapy modalities — play therapy is one effective approach
references: Landreth, G. L. (2012). Play therapy: The art of the relationship (3rd ed.). Routledge.

reviewQueue.prompt: Token economy is a behavior modification system that:
choices: Uses real currency
Provides tokens as secondary reinforcers for desired behaviors, which can later be exchanged for preferred items or privileges
Only uses punishment
Has no evidence base
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Token economy (Ayllon & Azrin): tokens are conditioned/secondary reinforcers earned for target behaviors and exchanged for backup reinforcers (privileges, items, activities). Used in psychiatric units, classrooms, and correctional facilities.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Tokens are symbolic reinforcers (points, chips, stickers), not actual currency
(C) Token economies are based on POSITIVE REINFORCEMENT, not punishment
(D) Token economies have extensive research support — one of the most well-validated behavioral interventions
references: Ayllon, T., & Azrin, N. (1968). The token economy: A motivational system for therapy and rehabilitation. Appleton-Century-Crofts.

reviewQueue.prompt: Brief psychodynamic therapy differs from traditional psychoanalysis by:
choices: Being identical in length and technique
Being time-limited (12-40 sessions), focused on a specific dynamic theme, and using a more active/directive therapist role
Having no theoretical basis
Avoiding the therapeutic relationship
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Brief psychodynamic therapy (Sifneos, Davanloo, Strupp, Luborsky): time-limited, focused on a central conflictual relationship theme, therapist is more active/directive, uses interpretation but within a focused framework.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Brief therapy is significantly shorter and more focused than traditional analysis (which may last years)
(C) Brief psychodynamic therapy is rooted in psychoanalytic theory — it's a time-limited adaptation
(D) The therapeutic relationship remains central — alliance and transference are actively used
references: Sifneos, P. E. (1979). Short-term dynamic psychotherapy: Evaluation and technique. Plenum Press.

reviewQueue.prompt: EMDR (Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing) for PTSD involves:
choices: Only eye exercises
Bilateral stimulation (eye movements, tapping, or tones) while processing traumatic memories — based on adaptive information processing theory
Only medication
Only relaxation training
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Shapiro's EMDR: 8-phase protocol using bilateral stimulation during trauma memory processing. AIP theory: trauma memories are stored in isolated, unprocessed neural networks; bilateral stimulation facilitates integration with adaptive networks.

Why others are wrong:
(A) While eye movements are the original bilateral stimulation, the therapy involves comprehensive memory processing, not just eye exercises
(C) EMDR is a psychotherapy approach, not medication
(D) While relaxation skills may be taught, the core mechanism is bilateral stimulation during trauma processing
references: Shapiro, F. (2018). Eye movement desensitization and reprocessing (EMDR) therapy: Basic principles, protocols, and procedures (3rd ed.). Guilford Press.

reviewQueue.prompt: Overcorrection in behavioral therapy involves:
choices: Only positive reinforcement
Having the individual PRACTICE the correct behavior intensively after engaging in the undesired behavior — including restitution and positive practice
Only time-out
Ignoring all behavior
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Overcorrection (Foxx & Azrin): two forms — restitutional (restore environment to better-than-original state) and positive practice (repeatedly practice the CORRECT behavior). Example: a child who throws toys must pick up all toys AND organize the toy shelf.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Overcorrection is a form of punishment/consequence, not positive reinforcement
(C) Time-out removes reinforcement; overcorrection adds effortful correct behavior practice
(D) Overcorrection actively addresses behavior — it doesn't ignore it
references: Foxx, R. M., & Azrin, N. H. (1973). The elimination of autistic self-stimulatory behavior by overcorrection. Journal of Applied Behavior Analysis, 6(1), 1–14. https://doi.org/10.1901/jaba.1973.6-1

reviewQueue.prompt: The transference neurosis in psychoanalysis occurs when:
choices: The therapist projects feelings onto the client
The client recreates patterns from PAST significant relationships within the therapeutic relationship — transferring feelings onto the therapist
Transfer of insurance occurs
The client changes therapists
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Transference: the client unconsciously projects feelings, attitudes, and expectations from past relationships (typically with parents) onto the therapist. Analyzing transference is a primary mechanism of change in psychoanalytic therapy.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Therapist projecting onto the client = countertransference (the therapist's emotional reactions)
(C) Insurance transfer is an administrative matter, not a psychoanalytic concept
(D) Changing therapists is not transference — transference is about projecting past relational patterns
references: Freud, S. (1912). The dynamics of transference. Standard Edition, 12, 97–108.

flags.detail: The correct choice is substantially longer than every distractor.

reviewQueue.prompt: Cognitive defusion in ACT involves:
choices: Merging completely with thoughts
Learning to observe thoughts as mental events rather than literal TRUTHS — creating distance between self and thought content
Eliminating all thoughts
Only positive thinking
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Cognitive defusion (deliteralization): changing one's relationship with thoughts rather than changing their content. Techniques: repeating a word until it loses meaning, prefacing thoughts with 'I notice I'm having the thought that...', singing thoughts.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Merging with thoughts = cognitive FUSION (what defusion targets)
(C) ACT doesn't try to eliminate thoughts — it changes the RELATIONSHIP with thoughts
(D) ACT doesn't promote 'positive thinking' — it promotes acceptance of ALL thoughts while choosing valued action
references: Hayes, S. C., Strosahl, K. D., & Wilson, K. G. (2012). Acceptance and commitment therapy: The process and practice of mindful change (2nd ed.). Guilford Press.

reviewQueue.prompt: Flooding (implosive therapy) involves:
choices: Gradual hierarchical exposure
IMMEDIATE, prolonged exposure to the most feared stimulus until anxiety habituates — without a gradual approach
Only relaxation techniques
Avoiding all feared stimuli
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Flooding (Stampfl): direct, prolonged exposure to the maximum anxiety-provoking stimulus. Based on extinction: sustained exposure without aversive consequence → anxiety habituates. Faster than SD but more distressing.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Gradual hierarchy = systematic desensitization (Wolpe) — flooding bypasses the hierarchy
(C) Flooding involves intense exposure, not relaxation
(D) Avoidance MAINTAINS fear — flooding CONFRONTS it directly
references: Stampfl, T. G., & Levis, D. J. (1967). Essentials of implosive therapy: A learning-theory-based psychodynamic behavioral therapy. Journal of Abnormal Psychology, 72(6), 496–503. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0025238

reviewQueue.prompt: Solution-focused brief therapy (SFBT) assumes:
choices: Problems must be thoroughly analyzed before solutions are explored
Clients have STRENGTHS and RESOURCES to solve problems — focus on solutions and what's working rather than problem analysis
Therapists provide all solutions
Therapy must be long-term
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) de Shazer & Berg: SFBT focuses on what's already WORKING (exceptions to the problem), preferred futures (miracle question), and client strengths. Key tenets: if it works, do more; if it doesn't, try something different.

Why others are wrong:
(A) SFBT intentionally MINIMIZES problem analysis — focusing on solutions instead
(C) CLIENTS generate solutions — the therapist facilitates discovery of existing strengths
(D) SFBT is designed as BRIEF therapy (often 5-8 sessions)
references: de Shazer, S. (1985). Keys to solution in brief therapy. W. W. Norton.

reviewQueue.prompt: Genograms in family therapy:
choices: Are standardized psychological tests
Are multigenerational family maps showing relationships, patterns, medical/mental health history, and recurring family dynamics across 3+ generations
Only show current family members
Are never used in therapy
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Genograms (Bowen, McGoldrick): visual diagrams mapping at least three generations. Include relationship patterns (close, conflictual, cutoff), major events, medical/mental health history, occupations, and family roles. Identify multigenerational patterns.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Genograms are clinical tools/visual representations, not standardized tests with norms
(C) Genograms specifically include MULTIPLE generations (usually 3+) to show patterns
(D) Genograms are widely used in family therapy, medical family therapy, and even individual therapy
references: McGoldrick, M., Gerson, R., & Petry, S. (2008). Genograms: Assessment and intervention (3rd ed.). W. W. Norton.

reviewQueue.prompt: The dose-response relationship in psychotherapy research shows:
choices: More therapy always equals better outcomes
Most improvement occurs in the EARLY sessions, with diminishing returns over time — approximately 50% improve by session 8 and 75% by session 26
All clients need 100+ sessions
Therapy length doesn't matter
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Howard et al. (1986), Lambert: the dose-response curve is negatively accelerating — rapid improvement early, then diminishing returns. This informs session limits and expected treatment trajectories (not everyone follows this pattern).

Why others are wrong:
(A) The relationship is NEGATIVELY ACCELERATING — not linear improvement with more therapy
(C) Most clients show significant improvement well before 100 sessions
(D) Therapy length matters — but with diminishing returns over time
references: Howard, K. I., Kopta, S. M., Krause, M. S., & Orlinsky, D. E. (1986). The dose-effect relationship in psychotherapy. American Psychologist, 41(2), 159–164. https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.41.2.159

reviewQueue.prompt: Which theory of counseling posits that human beings are driven by five basic genetic needs: survival, love and belonging, power, freedom, and fun?

reviewQueue.rationale:
William Glasser's Choice Theory (which underpins Reality Therapy) argues that all our behavior is our best attempt in the moment to satisfy one or more of five basic, genetically encoded needs: survival, love/belonging, power/achievement, freedom/independence, and fun. Reality therapy helps clients make more effective choices to meet these needs responsibly.

Why others are wrong:
• Person-Centered Therapy centers on the actualizing tendency (one core drive to grow) and the necessary/sufficient conditions of empathy, genuineness, and unconditional positive regard.
• REBT posits that emotional distress is caused by irrational, demanding beliefs (the 'musts' and 'shoulds'), not a specific set of 5 genetic needs.
• Existential therapy focuses on four 'ultimate concerns': death, freedom/responsibility, isolation, and meaninglessness.

choices: ANOVA is more powerful than t-tests

ANOVA can only be used with two groups
t-tests cannot compare means
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Running multiple t-tests (e.g., 3 groups = 3 comparisons) inflates familywise alpha. With α=.05 and 3 tests, the actual error rate ≈ .14, not .05. ANOVA controls this by testing all groups simultaneously.

(A) ANOVA isn't inherently more powerful — it controls error rate, which is the primary advantage
(C) ANOVA is specifically designed for 3+ groups; with only 2 groups, ANOVA and t-test give identical results

(D) Quasi-experiments are VERY common in psychology, especially in clinical, educational, and community settings where randomization isn't feasible or ethical

reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Quasi-experiments have an IV manipulation but lack random assignment. Participants are in pre-existing groups (classrooms, hospitals, gender). This limits causal inference due to potential confounds.

Why others are wrong:

(D) Stratification is about REPRESENTATIVENESS, not reducing sample size

reviewQueue.prompt: Construct validity of a study is concerned with:
choices: Whether the sample represents the population
Whether the operationalizations adequately represent the theoretical constructs under study
Whether the study can be replicated
The statistical power of the study
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Construct validity: do the operational definitions (measures, manipulations) truly capture the theoretical constructs they claim to represent? Threats include mono-operation bias, evaluation apprehension, and hypothesis guessing.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Sample representativeness → external validity
(C) Replicability relates to reliability and research practices, not construct validity specifically
(D) Statistical power relates to Type II error probability, not construct representation
references: Cronbach, L. J., & Meehl, P. E. (1955). Construct validity in psychological tests. Psychological Bulletin, 52(4), 281–302. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0040957

reviewQueue.prompt: Retrospective studies differ from prospective studies in that retrospective studies:
choices: Follow participants forward in time
Look BACKWARD at data already collected or events that have already occurred
Always use experimental designs
Have no limitations
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Retrospective studies examine past events (medical records, archived data, participant recall). Prospective studies follow participants forward from the present. Retrospective designs are faster but prone to recall bias.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Following participants forward = prospective (longitudinal) design
(C) Retrospective studies are typically observational/correlational, not experimental
(D) Retrospective studies have significant limitations: recall bias, incomplete records, inability to establish causation
references: Grimes, D. A., & Schulz, K. F. (2002). Cohort studies: Marching towards outcomes. The Lancet, 359(9303), 341–345. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(02)07500-1

reviewQueue.prompt: Social desirability bias occurs when participants:
choices: Give accurate responses
Respond in ways they believe are socially acceptable rather than truthful
Only participate in studies they find interesting
Randomly select responses
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Social desirability bias: participants present themselves favorably (underreporting stigmatized behaviors, overreporting positive ones). Controlled by validity scales (MMPI-2 L and K scales), anonymous administration, or social desirability measures.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Accurate responses would indicate NO social desirability bias
(C) Participating based on interest = volunteer bias/self-selection, a different issue
(D) Random responding = random response style, detectable by validity indicators
references: Paulhus, D. L. (1991). Measurement and control of response bias. In J. P. Robinson, P. R. Shaver, & L. S. Wrightsman (Eds.), Measures of personality and social psychological attitudes (pp. 17–59). Academic Press.

reviewQueue.prompt: Power in statistical testing refers to:
choices: The alpha level
The probability of correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis (finding an effect that truly exists)
Sample bias
The number of variables
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Power = 1 - β (where β = probability of Type II error). Power is the ability to detect a real effect. Influenced by sample size, effect size, alpha level, and test used. Minimum recommended power = .80.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Alpha = probability of Type I error; power is about Type II error (β)
(C) Sample bias threatens validity, not statistical power directly
(D) Number of variables affects design complexity but doesn't define power
references: Cohen, J. (1988). Statistical power analysis for the behavioral sciences (2nd ed.). Erlbaum.

flags.detail: The correct choice is substantially longer than every distractor.

reviewQueue.prompt: Selection bias threatens internal validity because:
choices: Participants are randomly assigned
Pre-existing differences between groups could explain outcome differences rather than the treatment
All participants are identical
The experimenter is unaware of group assignment
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Selection bias: when groups differ systematically before the intervention (not randomly assigned), observed outcomes may be due to pre-existing differences rather than the treatment. Random assignment controls for this.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Random assignment CONTROLS for selection bias — it doesn't create it
(C) Groups are never truly identical — random assignment distributes differences equally
(D) Experimenter unawareness of assignment controls experimenter bias, not selection bias
references: Shadish, W. R., Cook, T. D., & Campbell, D. T. (2002). Experimental and quasi-experimental designs for generalized causal inference. Houghton Mifflin.

flags.detail: The correct choice is substantially longer than every distractor.

reviewQueue.prompt: Chi-square (χ²) tests are used to analyze:
choices: Means of continuous variables
The relationship between CATEGORICAL variables (observed vs. expected frequencies)
Correlations between continuous variables
Regression coefficients
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Chi-square tests compare observed frequencies with expected frequencies for categorical (nominal) data. Goodness-of-fit χ² tests one variable; test of independence χ² tests association between two categorical variables.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Means of continuous variables → t-test or ANOVA
(C) Correlations → Pearson's r (continuous) or Spearman's ρ (ordinal)
(D) Regression coefficients → regression analysis
references: Pearson, K. (1900). On the criterion that a given system of deviations from the probable in the case of a correlated system of variables is such that it can be reasonably supposed to have arisen from random sampling. Philosophical Magazine, 50(302), 157–175.

reviewQueue.prompt: Demand characteristics are:
choices: Requirements for participant consent
Cues in an experiment that communicate the expected behavior to participants, potentially biasing results
Equipment specifications
Sample size requirements
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Demand characteristics (Orne): aspects of the experimental setting that inform participants about expected or desired behavior. Participants may then behave to 'help' the researcher (cooperative subject role) or rebel.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Consent requirements are ethical procedures, not demand characteristics
(C) Equipment specifications are technical matters, not participant-observable experimental cues
(D) Sample size requirements relate to statistical power, not participant behavior influence
references: Orne, M. T. (1962). On the social psychology of the psychological experiment. American Psychologist, 17(11), 776–783. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0043424

reviewQueue.prompt: Effect size describes:
choices: Statistical significance only
The MAGNITUDE of a relationship or difference — how large the effect actually is, regardless of sample size
The p-value
Whether to reject the null hypothesis
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Effect size quantifies the practical significance of findings. Common measures: Cohen's d (mean differences), r (correlations), η² (ANOVA). Effect sizes are sample-size independent, unlike statistical significance.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Statistical significance and effect size are independent — large samples can make trivial effects 'significant'
(C) p-values indicate statistical significance, not effect magnitude
(D) Rejecting the null is about significance, not about HOW MUCH of an effect exists
references: Cohen, J. (1988). Statistical power analysis for the behavioral sciences (2nd ed.). Erlbaum.

reviewQueue.prompt: A factorial design allows researchers to:
choices: Study only one variable
Study TWO or more independent variables SIMULTANEOUSLY and examine their interaction effects
Avoid all confounds automatically
Only use between-subjects comparisons
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Factorial designs: multiple IVs are crossed (e.g., 2x3 design). This reveals main effects of each IV AND interaction effects (whether the effect of one IV depends on the level of another). More informative and efficient than separate experiments.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Factorial designs study MULTIPLE IVs, not just one (that would be a single-factor design)
(C) Factorial designs help control confounds but don't eliminate all threats automatically
(D) Factorial designs can use between-subjects, within-subjects, or mixed approaches
references: Tabachnick, B. G., & Fidell, L. S. (2019). Using multivariate statistics (7th ed.). Pearson.

reviewQueue.prompt: Institutional Review Boards (IRBs) are responsible for:
choices: Funding research
Reviewing and approving research proposals to ensure the protection of human participants' welfare, rights, and privacy
Publishing research articles
Setting academic curriculum
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) IRBs review research proposals before data collection to ensure: informed consent, risk-benefit ratio, privacy protections, equitable participant selection, and special protections for vulnerable populations.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Funding agencies (NIH, NSF) fund research; IRBs review ethical protections
(C) Journal editors and peer reviewers handle publication decisions, not IRBs
(D) Academic curriculum is set by departments and universities, not IRBs
references: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. (2018). Federal policy for the protection of human subjects (Common Rule, 45 CFR 46). https://www.hhs.gov/ohrp/regulations-and-policy/regulations/45-cfr-46/index.html

reviewQueue.prompt: Qualitative research differs from quantitative research primarily in:
choices: Being less rigorous
Using non-numerical data (interviews, observations, text) to understand meaning, experiences, and social processes in depth
Having no systematic methodology
Never being published in journals
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Qualitative research: collects and analyzes non-numerical data (interviews, observation, documents) using methods like thematic analysis, grounded theory, ethnography, and phenomenology. Focuses on understanding MEANING and context.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Qualitative research has its own rigorous standards (trustworthiness, credibility, transferability)
(C) Qualitative research uses systematic methodologies (grounded theory, IPA, discourse analysis)
(D) Qualitative research is widely published in psychology journals
references: Creswell, J. W., & Poth, C. N. (2018). Qualitative inquiry and research design: Choosing among five approaches (4th ed.). SAGE.

reviewQueue.prompt: Construct validity encompasses:
choices: Only face validity
CONVERGENT validity (correlates with related measures) AND DISCRIMINANT validity (does NOT correlate with unrelated measures)
Only criterion-related validity
Only content validity
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Construct validity evidence includes: convergent (high correlation with measures of the SAME construct), discriminant (low correlation with measures of DIFFERENT constructs), factor analysis, and known-groups validity.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Face validity is the weakest form and is a small subset of construct validity evidence
(C) Criterion-related validity (concurrent/predictive) provides evidence FOR construct validity but is a separate concept
(D) Content validity is one TYPE of validity evidence, not the whole of construct validity
references: Campbell, D. T., & Fiske, D. W. (1959). Convergent and discriminant validation by the multitrait-multimethod matrix. Psychological Bulletin, 56(2), 81–105. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0046016

reviewQueue.prompt: A between-subjects design:
choices: Has the same participants in all conditions
Assigns DIFFERENT participants to each condition — each person experiences only ONE level of the independent variable
Cannot use random assignment
Is always inferior to within-subjects
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Between-subjects (independent groups): different participants in each condition. Advantages: no order effects, no practice effects. Disadvantages: individual differences as confounds (controlled by random assignment), requires larger samples.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Same participants in all conditions = within-subjects (repeated measures) design
(C) Random assignment is typically USED in between-subjects designs to control individual differences
(D) Both designs have strengths and weaknesses — neither is inherently superior
references: Shadish, W. R., Cook, T. D., & Campbell, D. T. (2002). Experimental and quasi-experimental designs for generalized causal inference. Houghton Mifflin.

reviewQueue.prompt: Stratified random sampling:
choices: Selects participants without any strategy
Divides the population into relevant SUBGROUPS (strata) and then randomly samples from EACH stratum — ensuring proportional representation
Only uses volunteers
Is the same as convenience sampling
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Stratified sampling: identify important subgroups (gender, race, age, SES), then randomly sample from each stratum in proportion to their population representation. This ensures the sample reflects population diversity.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Stratified sampling is highly STRATEGIC — it systematically represents important subgroups
(C) Volunteer sampling = self-selection bias; stratified sampling uses random selection within strata
(D) Convenience sampling selects whoever is available — stratified sampling systematically represents the population
references: Kish, L. (1965). Survey sampling. Wiley.

reviewQueue.prompt: Type I error occurs when:
choices: The null hypothesis is correctly retained
A TRUE null hypothesis is INCORRECTLY REJECTED — concluding an effect exists when it doesn't (a false positive)
A false null is correctly rejected
Sample size is too large
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Type I error (α error, false positive): rejecting H₀ when it's actually true. The alpha level (.05) is the probability of making this error. Like a false alarm — concluding a treatment works when it doesn't.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Correctly retaining a true null = correct decision (true negative)
(C) Correctly rejecting a false null = correct decision (true positive/power)
(D) Large sample size doesn't define Type I error — though it can increase power and detect trivial effects
references: Neyman, J., & Pearson, E. S. (1933). On the problem of the most efficient tests of statistical hypotheses. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London, Series A, 231, 289–337. https://doi.org/10.1098/rsta.1933.0009

flags.detail: The correct choice is substantially longer than every distractor.

reviewQueue.prompt: Type II error occurs when:
choices: A true null is rejected
A FALSE null hypothesis is INCORRECTLY RETAINED — failing to detect a real effect (a miss/false negative)
Statistical power is very high
The alpha level is too strict
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Type II error (β error, false negative): failing to reject H₀ when it's actually false. Like missing a real disease — concluding no effect when one exists. Power = 1 - β.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Rejecting a true null = Type I error
(C) High power REDUCES Type II error — they're inversely related
(D) A very strict alpha (e.g., .001) increases Type II error risk but doesn't define it
references: Cohen, J. (1988). Statistical power analysis for the behavioral sciences (2nd ed.). Erlbaum.

flags.detail: The correct choice is substantially longer than every distractor.

reviewQueue.prompt: Counterbalancing in within-subjects designs:
choices: Is unnecessary
Controls for ORDER EFFECTS by varying the sequence of conditions across participants
Eliminates all confounds
Only applies to between-subjects designs
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Counterbalancing: varying the order in which conditions are experienced. Complete counterbalancing: all possible orders. Latin square: systematic partial counterbalancing. This distributes practice, fatigue, and carryover effects equally.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Counterbalancing is ESSENTIAL in within-subjects designs to control order effects
(C) Counterbalancing controls ORDER effects specifically — not all possible confounds
(D) Counterbalancing is specifically used in WITHIN-subjects (repeated measures) designs
references: Shadish, W. R., Cook, T. D., & Campbell, D. T. (2002). Experimental and quasi-experimental designs for generalized causal inference. Houghton Mifflin.

reviewQueue.prompt: Matched-pairs design:
choices: Randomly assigns without matching
PAIRS participants on relevant variables (age, IQ, severity) and then randomly assigns ONE member of each pair to each condition
Has no advantages over simple random assignment
Is the same as a within-subjects design
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Matched-pairs: participants matched on potentially confounding variables are paired, then randomly assigned to conditions. Reduces error variance from individual differences while maintaining independent groups.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Matching specifically PRECEDES random assignment to reduce error
(C) Matched-pairs designs REDUCE error variance by controlling for known confounds — an advantage over simple random assignment
(D) Matched pairs use DIFFERENT participants in each condition (between-subjects) — within-subjects uses the SAME participants
references: Shadish, W. R., Cook, T. D., & Campbell, D. T. (2002). Experimental and quasi-experimental designs for generalized causal inference. Houghton Mifflin.

flags.detail: The correct choice is substantially longer than every distractor.

reviewQueue.prompt: Standard deviation is:
choices: The same as the mean
A measure of VARIABILITY — the average distance of scores from the mean in a distribution
A measure of central tendency
Only used in qualitative research
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) SD measures spread/dispersion: larger SD = more variability, smaller SD = less variability. In a normal distribution: ~68% of scores fall within ±1 SD, ~95% within ±2 SD, ~99.7% within ±3 SD of the mean.

Why others are wrong:
(A) The mean is a measure of central tendency; SD is a measure of variability
(C) Central tendency = mean, median, mode; SD is VARIABILITY/dispersion
(D) SD is fundamental to quantitative (not qualitative) research and statistics
references: Field, A. (2017). Discovering statistics using IBM SPSS Statistics (5th ed.). SAGE Publications.

flags.detail: The correct choice is substantially longer than every distractor.

reviewQueue.prompt: A confounding variable:
choices: Is always controlled in research
Is an UNCONTROLLED variable that systematically covaries with the IV and could provide an ALTERNATIVE explanation for results
Never affects research outcomes
Is the same as the dependent variable
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Confound: a variable that varies systematically with the IV, making it impossible to determine whether the IV or the confound caused the DV change. Random assignment, matching, and statistical control help manage confounds.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Confounds are UNCONTROLLED — if controlled, they're no longer confounding
(C) Confounds can SERIOUSLY compromise research conclusions
(D) Confounds are THIRD variables — distinct from both the IV and DV
references: Shadish, W. R., Cook, T. D., & Campbell, D. T. (2002). Experimental and quasi-experimental designs for generalized causal inference. Houghton Mifflin.

reviewQueue.prompt: APA style requires research papers to include:
choices: Only results
Title page, abstract, introduction, method, results, discussion, and references — following a specific formatting structure
No citations
Only a conclusion paragraph
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) APA 7th edition structure: title page, abstract, introduction (literature review + hypotheses), method (participants, measures, procedure), results (statistical analyses), discussion (interpretation, limitations, implications), references.

Why others are wrong:
(A) APA papers include MULTIPLE required sections, not just results
(C) APA style REQUIRES in-text citations and a references list
(D) APA papers have a detailed structure far beyond a single paragraph
references: American Psychological Association. (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association (7th ed.). https://doi.org/10.1037/0000165-000

reviewQueue.prompt: Correlation does NOT equal causation because:
choices: Correlation is never useful
A third variable may cause BOTH correlated variables, or the direction of causation may be reversed — correlation alone cannot establish causal direction
Correlations are always zero
Only experiments can measure relationships
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Correlation limitations: (1) directionality problem (A→B or B→A?), (2) third variable problem (C causes both A and B), (3) correlation provides no evidence for the mechanism of connection between variables.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Correlations ARE useful for prediction, relationship identification, and hypothesis generation
(C) Many variables are significantly correlated — correlations of zero are only one possibility
(D) Correlational designs can identify relationships — only experiments establish CAUSATION
references: Shadish, W. R., Cook, T. D., & Campbell, D. T. (2002). Experimental and quasi-experimental designs for generalized causal inference. Houghton Mifflin.

reviewQueue.prompt: The Pearson r correlation coefficient ranges from:
choices: -1.00 to +1.00 — with -1 and +1 indicating perfect relationships and 0 indicating no linear relationship
1 to 10
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Pearson r: -1.00 (perfect negative), 0 (no relationship), +1.00 (perfect positive). The SIGN indicates DIRECTION; the MAGNITUDE indicates STRENGTH. r = -.80 is stronger than r = +.50.

Why others are wrong:
(A) r is a standardized coefficient, not a percentage
(C) r uses a -1 to +1 scale, not 1 to 10
(D) r is bounded between -1.00 and +1.00
references: Pearson, K. (1895). Notes on regression and inheritance in the case of two parents. Proceedings of the Royal Society of London, 58, 240–242. https://doi.org/10.1098/rspl.1895.0041

reviewQueue.prompt: ANOVA (Analysis of Variance) is used to:
choices: Compare only two groups
Compare means across THREE or more groups while controlling Type I error rate — using F-ratio to test for significant differences
Measure correlation
Only analyze qualitative data
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) ANOVA: tests whether means differ across 3+ groups. Uses F-ratio (between-groups variance / within-groups variance). If significant, post-hoc tests (Tukey, Bonferroni) identify which specific groups differ.

Why others are wrong:
(A) While ANOVA CAN compare two groups, its primary use is 3+ groups (use t-test for two groups)
(C) Correlation is measured by Pearson r or Spearman's rho, not ANOVA
(D) ANOVA analyzes quantitative data (means and variances)
references: Fisher, R. A. (1925). Statistical methods for research workers. Oliver and Boyd.

reviewQueue.prompt: The coefficient of determination (r²) indicates:
choices: The direction of a relationship
The PROPORTION of variance in one variable that is explained or accounted for by the other variable
The sample size needed
The probability of Type I error
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) r² (r-squared): square of the correlation coefficient. r = .60 → r² = .36, meaning 36% of variance in Y is accounted for by X (and 64% is unexplained). This quantifies effect size for correlational relationships.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Direction is indicated by the SIGN of r, not r²
(C) Sample size is determined by power analysis, not r²
(D) Type I error probability = alpha level (p-value), not r²
references: Cohen, J. (1988). Statistical power analysis for the behavioral sciences (2nd ed.). Erlbaum.

reviewQueue.prompt: Demand characteristics in research occur when:
choices: Participants don't understand the study
Participants change their behavior based on CUES about what the researcher EXPECTS or desires — acting to confirm the hypothesis
The researcher demands cooperation
Only in qualitative research
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Orne (1962): demand characteristics — participants interpret situational cues about the study's purpose and modify behavior accordingly. They may try to be 'good subjects' (confirm hypothesis), apprehensive evaluators, or even saboteurs.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Participants may understand (or think they understand) the study's purpose — that's the problem
(C) Demand characteristics come from SUBTLE CUES, not explicit demands
(D) Demand characteristics occur primarily in quantitative experimental research
references: Orne, M. T. (1962). On the social psychology of the psychological experiment: With particular reference to demand characteristics and their implications. American Psychologist, 17(11), 776–783. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0043424

reviewQueue.prompt: Type I error in hypothesis testing refers to:
choices: Failing to reject a false null hypothesis
Rejecting a true null hypothesis
Using the wrong statistical test
Having insufficient sample size
reviewQueue.rationale: Type I error (α) is incorrectly rejecting the null hypothesis when it is actually true — finding a significant effect that doesn't really exist (false positive). The conventional α level of .05 means accepting a 5% risk of Type I error.

reviewQueue.prompt: Which measure of central tendency is most appropriate for skewed distributions?

Median
Mode
Standard deviation
reviewQueue.rationale: The median is most appropriate for skewed distributions because it is not affected by extreme scores (outliers). The mean is pulled in the direction of the skew, making it a less representative measure of central tendency.

Large effect
Negligible effect
reviewQueue.rationale: Cohen's conventions for d: 0.20 = small, 0.50 = medium, 0.80 = large. A d of 0.80 means the two group means differ by 0.80 standard deviations, considered a large and practically significant effect.

reviewQueue.prompt: Which correlation coefficient indicates the strongest relationship?
reviewQueue.rationale: The strength of a correlation is determined by its absolute value, regardless of sign. |-.78| = .78 is the largest, indicating the strongest relationship. The negative sign indicates an inverse relationship, not a weaker one.

Cronbach's alpha
Inter-rater agreement
Alternate forms correlation
reviewQueue.rationale: Cronbach's alpha estimates internal consistency by examining the correlations among all items on a test. It reflects the degree to which items measure the same construct. Alpha ≥ .70 is generally considered acceptable for research.

A tail extending to the right
A symmetrical shape

Effect size
Sample size
Publication year

The effect is clinically significant

reviewQueue.prompt: Which sampling method gives every member of the population an equal chance of being selected?
choices: Convenience sampling
Snowball sampling

reviewQueue.prompt: In psychological research, 'Type I Error' (alpha) occurs when a researcher:
choices: Rejects a true null hypothesis (false positive)
Fails to reject a false null hypothesis (false negative)
Uses an inappropriately small sample size
Calculates a correlation coefficient incorrectly
reviewQueue.rationale:
Type I error (represented by alpha, usually set at .05) occurs when researchers conclude there is a significant effect or difference when in reality, there is none. It is a 'false positive'—rejecting the null hypothesis when the null hypothesis is actually true.

Why others are wrong:
• Failing to reject a false null hypothesis is a Type II error (beta)—a 'false negative' where a real effect is missed.
• Small sample sizes decrease statistical power, strongly increasing the risk of a Type II error, but are not the definition of Type I error.
• Calculation errors are data analysis mistakes, not inherent statistical decision errors.

reviewQueue.prompt: Which statistical test is most appropriate to determine if there is a significant difference in the mean depression scores between three distinct treatment groups (CBT, Medication, Control)?
choices: Independent-samples t-test
Chi-square test of independence
One-way Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
Pearson correlation coefficient
reviewQueue.rationale:
A One-Way ANOVA is used to compare the means of three or more independent groups on a single continuous dependent variable (depression score). It tests the null hypothesis that all group means are equal. If the F-statistic is significant, post-hoc tests are used to find which specific pairs differ.

Why others are wrong:
• An independent-samples t-test can only compare the means of TWO groups.
• A chi-square test is for categorical (nominal) data, comparing observed frequencies to expected frequencies, not for comparing means.
• Pearson correlation measures the degree of linear association between two continuous variables, not differences between group means.

reviewQueue.prompt: A researcher wants to predict a college student's final GPA (continuous dependent variable) based on their SAT score, high school GPA, and number of extracurricular activities. The appropriate statistical technique is:
choices: Multiple Regression
Factor Analysis
Logistic Regression
Multivariate Analysis of Variance (MANOVA)
reviewQueue.rationale:
Multiple regression is used when you have two or more independent (predictor) variables and you want to predict the value of a single, continuous dependent (criterion) variable. It yields an R-squared value indicating how much variance in the DV is explained by all predictors combined.

Why others are wrong:
• Factor analysis reduces a large number of variables into fewer underlying 'factors' or constructs.
• Logistic regression is used when the dependent variable is categorical/binary (e.g., predicting 'Graduated' vs. 'Dropped Out' instead of a continuous GPA).
• MANOVA is used when there are MULTIPLE dependent variables being measured simultaneously, not just one (GPA).

reviewQueue.prompt: In a normal distribution (bell curve), approximately what percentage of scores fall within one standard deviation (+1 and -1) of the mean?
reviewQueue.rationale:
The empirical rule (68-95-99.7 rule) dictates that in a perfectly normal distribution: ~68% of scores fall within ±1 SD of the mean, ~95% within ±2 SD, and ~99.7% within ±3 SD.

Why others are wrong:
• 50% represents the proportion of scores falling strictly above (or below) the mean (median).
• 95% falls within exactly two standard deviations.
• 99.7% falls within three standard deviations.

reviewQueue.prompt: A test's 'construct validity' is best established by demonstrating both:
choices: High face validity and high predictive validity
Convergent validity and discriminant (divergent) validity
High internal consistency and high test-retest reliability
Concurrent validity and criterion-related validity
reviewQueue.rationale:
Construct validity—the extent to which a test measures the theoretical trait it claims to—is established using a multitrait-multimethod approach. It requires convergent validity (scores correlate highly with other tests measuring the SAME construct) AND discriminant validity (scores do not correlate highly with tests measuring unrelated constructs).

Why others are wrong:
• Face validity (looks like it tests the construct) is not empirical validity. Predictive validity applies to criterion validity.
• Internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha) and test-retest are measures of RELIABILITY, a necessary but insufficient condition for validity.
• Concurrent and predictive validity are the two subtypes of criterion-related validity, not the primary pillars of construct validity.

reviewQueue.prompt: A single-subject research design formatted 'A-B-A-B' represents a:
choices: Multiple baseline design
Changing criterion design
Withdrawal or Reversal design
Latin square design
reviewQueue.rationale:
An A-B-A-B design is a withdrawal/reversal design. 'A' represents the baseline phase, and 'B' represents the treatment phase. Baseline is recorded, treatment is applied, treatment is withdrawn to see if behavior reverts (demonstrating experimental control), and then treatment is re-introduced for the subject's final benefit.

Why others are wrong:
• Multiple baseline introduces treatment sequentially across different subjects, behaviors, or settings to avoid withdrawing beneficial treatment.
• Changing criterion applies one treatment but requires the subject to meet successively stricter criteria to earn reinforcement.
• Latin square is a counterbalancing technique used in group repeated-measures designs to control for order effects.

reviewQueue.prompt: The defining feature of a 'true' experimental design compared to a quasi-experimental design is:
choices: The use of a control group
The manipulation of an independent variable
Random assignment of subjects to groups
Collecting data in a laboratory setting
reviewQueue.rationale:
The hallmark of a true experiment is the random assignment of participants to experimental and control conditions. This equalizes pre-existing subject variables (like intelligence, motivation, genetics) across groups, allowing researchers to assert that the independent variable CAUSED changes in the dependent variable.

Why others are wrong:
• Quasi-experiments often have control/comparison groups, but participants are grouped by pre-existing conditions (e.g., gender, class section) rather than random assignment.
• Both designs involve manipulating an independent variable (e.g., introducing a new teaching method).
• 'Laboratory setting' relates to internal vs external validity, not the formal design criteria; true experiments can be done in the field.

reviewQueue.prompt: In an item analysis, an 'Item Difficulty Index' (p-value) of .90 indicates that:
choices: The item is extremely difficult
The item is extremely easy
The item discriminates very well between high and low scorers
90% of the variance is explained
reviewQueue.rationale:
The Item Difficulty Index (p) simply represents the proportion or percentage of examinees who answered the item correctly. A value of .90 means 90% of test-takers got it right, making it a very easy item. (A p-value of .20 would indicate a hard item that only 20% answered correctly).

Why others are wrong:
• A high number means a high percentage got it right, so it's easy, not difficult.
• Item Discrimination Index (D) measures how well the item discriminates high scorers from low scorers. An item where 90% of people get it right has poor discriminative power because it's too easy.
• Explained variance is R-squared.

reviewQueue.prompt: Statistical power is defined as the probability of:
choices: Committing a Type I error
Correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis
Selecting a perfectly representative sample
Finding a large effect size
reviewQueue.rationale:
Power is the sensitivity of a statistical test—the probability of detecting a real effect if one actually exists in the population (i.e., the probability of correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis). It is mathematically defined as 1 - Beta (where Beta is the Type II error rate). Power increases with larger sample sizes, larger effect sizes, and higher alpha levels.

Why others are wrong:
• The probability of a Type I error is alpha (α).
• A representative sample relates to external validity, not statistical power.
• Power is the ability to DETECT an effect size, not the probability of the effect size actually being large.

reviewQueue.prompt: The dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia proposes:

choices: The repetitive compulsive behaviors or mental acts performed in response to intrusive anxiety-provoking thoughts
Recurrent, intrusive, unwanted thoughts, images, or urges that cause marked distress and anxiety
Thoughts that are always immediately and fully acted upon without any resistance or suppression attempts
Exclusively focused on a single theme of contamination without encompassing any other obsessional content
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Obsessions: intrusive, unwanted, repetitive thoughts/images/urges that cause distress. Common themes: contamination, doubting, symmetry, forbidden thoughts, harm.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Compulsions are the repetitive BEHAVIORS performed in response to obsessions.
(C) Many obsessions are ego-dystonic — the person resists acting on them.
(D) Obsessions span many themes beyond contamination.

reviewQueue.prompt: Schizoaffective Disorder requires:
choices: Only mood symptoms without any concurrent psychotic features present during the illness duration
A period of psychotic symptoms WITHOUT mood symptoms plus periods where psychotic and mood symptoms co-occur
Only psychotic symptoms without any mood disturbance present at any point during the illness course
Only anxiety symptoms as the primary clinical feature without psychotic or mood symptom involvement
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Schizoaffective Disorder: major mood episode co-occurring with schizophrenia criterion A symptoms. PLUS ≥2 weeks of delusions/hallucinations WITHOUT mood symptoms. This distinguishes it from Mood Disorders with Psychotic Features.

Why others are wrong:
(A) It requires both mood AND psychotic symptoms.
(C) Mood symptoms must also be present for a substantial portion.
(D) Anxiety is not the primary feature.

Only excessive physical exercise as the sole compensatory method without any other purging strategies
Only psychotherapy sessions as the required intervention without any specific diagnostic behavioral criteria
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) BN: recurrent binge eating + compensatory behaviors (vomiting, laxatives, fasting, exercise) ≥1×/week for 3 months. Self-evaluation unduly influenced by body shape/weight.

(A) Compensatory behaviors are required for BN diagnosis.

(D) Therapy is treatment, not a diagnostic criterion.

Only being present in large dense crowds without any concern about individual social evaluation or scrutiny

Exceptionally high social skills and advanced interpersonal competence relative to same-age peers
Only academic learning difficulties and educational underachievement without any behavioral symptom criteria

reviewQueue.prompt: Dissociative Identity Disorder (DID) involves:
choices: Only recurrent major depressive episodes alternating with hypomanic mood elevation periods
The presence of two or more distinct personality states with gaps in recall for everyday events
Only generalized anxiety symptoms with persistent excessive worry and physiological hyperarousal
Only substance-related cognitive and behavioral impairments resulting from chronic intoxication
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) DID: ≥2 distinct personality states (alters) that recurrently take control. Amnesia for daily events and personal information. Typically associated with severe childhood trauma. Most controversial DSM diagnosis — debated regarding prevalence and etiology.

Why others are wrong:
(A) DID is a dissociative disorder, not a mood disorder.
(C) Anxiety is a common comorbidity but not the defining feature.
(D) Substance use is a separate diagnostic category entirely.

reviewQueue.prompt: Reactive Attachment Disorder (RAD) develops from:
choices: Primarily heritable genetic factors operating independently of any environmental caregiving context
Severely inadequate caregiving including neglect, deprivation, or frequent changes of caregivers
Entirely normal developmental processes unfolding within typical supportive family environments
Only documented physical abuse without any contribution from emotional neglect or deprivation
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) RAD: emotionally withdrawn, inhibited attachment behavior. The child rarely seeks or responds to comfort from caregivers. Develops from a pattern of insufficient care: social neglect, repeated changes of primary caregivers, or rearing in institutions. Must appear before age 5.

Why others are wrong:
(A) While biology contributes, the environmental context of deprivation is specifically required.
(C) RAD is pathological, arising fundamentally from abnormal caregiving.
(D) Neglect and inadequate caregiving (not just physical abuse) are the primary causes.

reviewQueue.prompt: The prodromal phase of schizophrenia refers to:
choices: The active psychotic phase featuring prominent hallucinations, delusions, and disorganized thinking
The period BEFORE full psychotic symptoms emerge, marked by subtle cognitive and social changes
The residual phase following successful pharmacological treatment and symptom stabilization
Complete sustained remission from all positive, negative, and cognitive schizophrenia symptoms
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Prodrome: weeks to years before the first psychotic episode. Subtle changes: social withdrawal, unusual preoccupations, declining functioning, attenuated psychotic symptoms (brief, low-intensity perceptual disturbances or unusual ideas). Identifying the prodrome enables early intervention.

Why others are wrong:
(A) The active phase involves full psychotic symptoms, not the subtle prodromal changes.
(C) The residual phase follows the active phase, not before it.
(D) The prodrome precedes illness onset, not remission.
