reviewQueue.prompt: Substance-Induced Psychotic Disorder requires:
choices: A documented pre-existing primary psychotic disorder diagnosis preceding any substance exposure
Psychotic symptoms developing during or shortly after substance intoxication or withdrawal
Only cannabis use as the exclusive pharmacological trigger substance producing psychotic symptoms
Lifelong chronic psychotic symptoms persisting independently of any ongoing substance intoxication
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Substance-induced psychosis: hallucinations/delusions developing during or soon after intoxication or withdrawal. Must be beyond what's expected for the substance and must cause significant distress. Substances: amphetamines, cannabis, cocaine, hallucinogens, alcohol withdrawal.

Why others are wrong:
(A) If pre-existing psychotic disorder exists, the substance exacerbation may be coded differently.
(C) Multiple substances can cause psychotic symptoms, not exclusively cannabis.
(D) Symptoms typically resolve when the substance clears from the system.

Only middle-aged and elderly adults can receive an ARFID clinical diagnosis currently

A highly specific isolated profound neurodevelopmental deficiency exclusively affecting phonological processing, word recognition, and reading comprehension fluency
A pervasive overarching neurobehavioral pattern defined fundamentally by severe oppositional, defiant, and disruptively aggressive behavioral conduct problems

reviewQueue.prompt: The difference between delirium and dementia is:
choices: Delirium and dementia are essentially identical pathological neurocognitive diagnostic entities distinguished solely by patient age at the initial clinical presentation
Delirium is ACUTE onset with FLUCTUATING consciousness and attention, while dementia is CHRONIC progressive cognitive decline with typically preserved consciousness
Delirium precisely mirrors dementia in all clinical symptomatic presentations with the sole distinguishing factor being the overall comprehensive temporal duration
Delirium represents an entirely distinct pharmacological treatment approach while sharing fundamentally identical underlying neurobiological disease pathogeneses
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Delirium: acute (hours to days), fluctuating, affects consciousness/attention, often reversible (treat underlying cause — infection, medication, metabolic). Dementia (major NCD): chronic (months to years), progressive, consciousness usually clear initially, often irreversible. Delirium can be superimposed on dementia.

Why others are wrong:
(A) They are distinct clinical entities
(C) Onset, course, consciousness, and etiology all differ
(D) Both differ across fundamentally diverse presentations, etiologies, courses, and treatments

reviewQueue.prompt: Neurocognitive disorder due to Lewy body disease features:
choices: An exclusive distinct profound deficit strictly limited entirely to profound accelerating progressive anterograde explicit short-term declarative memory loss
Fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, and REM sleep behavior disorder — with sensitivity to antipsychotic medications
A pervasive persistent mood disturbance characterized exclusively by profound chronic systemic intractable unremitting generalized clinical depressive symptoms
An overwhelming systemic physiological state characterized specifically by relentless excessive uncontrollable continuous generalized sympathetic anxiety arousal

Correct: (B) Lewy Body Dementia: alpha-synuclein protein deposits. Core features: fluctuating attention/cognition, recurrent detailed visual hallucinations, and REM Sleep Behavior Disorder (acting out dreams). Parkinsonism (bradykinesia, rigidity). CRITICAL: extreme sensitivity to antipsychotics (can cause severe neuroleptic malignant syndrome).

(A) Memory loss is present but isn't the distinguishing feature
(C)(D) Psychiatric symptoms occur but aren't the primary diagnostic features

They are fundamentally distinguished exclusively by the precise standardized clinical measurement of exact quantitative somatic symptom severity presentation

reviewQueue.prompt: The difference between Bipolar I and Bipolar II is:
choices: They represent entirely identical neurobiological mood spectra separated arbitrarily strictly through differing specific diagnostic institutional structural categorizations
Bipolar I requires at least one MANIC episode (may have depressive episodes), while Bipolar II requires at least one HYPOMANIC episode AND one major depressive episode
Bipolar II fundamentally systematically represents a consistently significantly more severe profound clinical symptomatic presentation than typical classical Bipolar I
They are actively differentiated explicitly and exclusively based upon their specific specialized long-term maintenance pharmacological medication treatment regimens
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Bipolar I: full manic episodes (≥7 days or hospitalization) — depressive episodes are common but NOT required for diagnosis. Bipolar II: hypomanic episodes (≥4 days, less severe, no hospitalization/psychosis) PLUS ≥1 major depressive episode. Bipolar II is NOT a milder form — depression is often severe.

Why others are wrong:
(A) They are distinct diagnoses
(C) Bipolar II is not necessarily less severe — it has significant depressive burden
(D) They differ in diagnostic criteria, not just treatment

reviewQueue.prompt: Intermittent Explosive Disorder requires:
choices: A distinct systematic singular isolated solitary uncontrollable intense extreme aggressive psychological outburst occurring exactly once throughout the entire lifespan

A persistent continuous structural psychological pattern exclusively utilizing profound intense verbal aggression while completely avoiding all physical manifestations
A highly calculated meticulously strategically planned deeply systematic intentional premeditated pattern featuring orchestrated targeted physical violent aggression
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) IED: recurrent impulsive (not premeditated) aggressive outbursts — verbal (verbal tirades) or physical (property damage, physical assault). Must be grossly disproportionate. Either: ≥2 outbursts involving physical damage in 12 months, OR ≥3 tantrums/tirades weekly for 3 months.

reviewQueue.prompt: The key feature distinguishing Schizophreniform Disorder from Schizophrenia is:
choices: SYMPTOM PRESENTATION — Schizophreniform selectively features prominent predominant negative symptoms while Schizophrenia invariably necessitates active florid positive acute psychotic hallucinations
DURATION AND IMPAIRMENT — Schizophreniform Disorder lasts between 1-6 months without requiring functional decline, while Schizophrenia requires symptoms for ≥6 months with marked impairment

TREATMENT PARADIGMS — Schizophreniform Disorder specifically requires immediate intensive acute hospitalization while Schizophrenia mandates exclusively ongoing outpatient maintenance psychopharmacology

ONSET TIMELINE — Schizophreniform systematically initially emerges exclusively during early early childhood whereas Schizophrenia fundamentally presents strictly throughout late middle adulthood epochs
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Same symptoms as Schizophrenia (≥2 of: delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, disorganized/catatonic behavior, negative symptoms) but total duration ≥1 month and <6 months. If symptoms persist past 6 months, diagnosis changes to Schizophrenia. Functional decline not required.

Why others are wrong:
(A) The symptom criteria are the same
(C) Treatment may be similar but the diagnostic distinction is duration
(D) The key distinction is duration, not age of onset

reviewQueue.prompt: Acute Stress Disorder differs from PTSD primarily in:
choices: Strictly exclusively explicitly differing entirely profoundly based purely upon explicit core symptom types

Strictly exclusively explicitly differing entirely profoundly based purely upon clinical treatment approaches
Strictly exclusively explicitly differing entirely profoundly regarding exactly when children are affected

Correct: (B) ASD: ≥3 days to ≤1 month post-trauma. PTSD: >1 month. ASD includes dissociative symptoms prominently. ~50% of those with ASD develop PTSD. ASD diagnosis validates acute responses and enables early intervention. Symptoms are similar (intrusion, avoidance, arousal, mood).

Why others are wrong:
(A) Similar symptoms apply to both diagnoses

(D) Both occur in all ages

Specifically uniformly explicitly developing strictly severe rigidly distinct persistent profoundly lifelong clinical symptoms
Specifically uniformly explicitly developing strictly severe rigidly distinct symptoms only following catastrophic severe trauma

reviewQueue.prompt: Competency to stand trial (CST) evaluates whether a defendant:
choices: Is innocent or guilty
Has a sufficient present ability to consult with their attorney with a reasonable degree of rational understanding AND has a factual and rational understanding of the proceedings
Was insane at the time of the offense
Needs treatment

Correct: (B) CST (Dusky v. United States, 1960): present-focused. Can the defendant understand the charges, the roles of courtroom personnel, potential consequences, and assist their attorney? Why others are wrong:
(A) CST is about trial fitness, not guilt/innocence
(C) Mental state at time of offense → insanity defense (different evaluation)

reviewQueue.prompt: The M'Naghten rule for insanity requires:
choices: Only mental illness
That at the time of the offense, the defendant had a mental disease or defect AND did not understand the NATURE and quality of their act OR did not know it was WRONG
Any mental health history
Only substance intoxication
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) M'Naghten (1843): cognitive test of insanity. Two prongs: (1) didn't know nature/quality of act ('thought he was squeezing a lemon, not strangling a person'), OR (2) didn't know it was wrong. Most widely used insanity standard. Does NOT include 'irresistible impulse' test.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Mental illness alone doesn't establish insanity — must affect knowledge
(C) History is relevant but the evaluation is about the specific offense time
(D) Voluntary intoxication typically doesn't qualify for insanity defense

reviewQueue.prompt: Risk assessment in forensic psychology uses:
choices: Only clinical judgment
Structured professional judgment (SPJ) tools like the HCR-20 that combine empirical risk factors with clinical expertise to evaluate violence risk
Crystal ball predictions

Why others are wrong:
(A) Unstructured clinical judgment alone has poor predictive validity
(C) Prediction of future behavior always involves uncertainty
(D) SPJ combines actuarial factors WITH clinical judgment — best of both

reviewQueue.prompt: The McNaughten rule (insanity defense) requires proving that:
choices: The defendant was angry during the crime

The defendant planned the crime poorly
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) McNaughten (1843): the defendant, due to a 'disease of the mind,' either (1) did not know the NATURE and QUALITY of the act, or (2) did not know that the act was WRONG. This is a COGNITIVE standard focused on knowledge.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Anger doesn't meet the McNaughten standard — it requires a mental disease affecting knowledge

(D) Poor planning doesn't meet McNaughten — the standard is about knowledge, not planning ability
references: M'Naghten's Case, 10 Cl. & Fin. 200, 8 Eng. Rep. 718 (1843). See also: Melton, G. B., Petrila, J., Poythress, N. G., & Slobogin, C. (2018). Psychological evaluations for the courts (4th ed.). Guilford Press.

reviewQueue.prompt: Social media ethics for psychologists include:
choices: Freely posting about client cases and treatment progress on personal and professional social media accounts
Maintaining appropriate boundaries, avoiding dual relationships, and never disclosing client information online
Accepting all incoming social media friend requests and connection invitations from current therapy clients
Providing psychotherapy services through social media platforms without any established clinical protocols
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Social media: maintain professional boundaries, don't search for client information online, address social media in informed consent, avoid dual relationships (friending clients), and never disclose identifying client information on any platform.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Posting about clients violates confidentiality.
(C) Friending clients creates dual relationships.
(D) Any therapy via technology requires proper procedures and platforms.

reviewQueue.prompt: Psychologists' obligation to 'do no harm' is reflected in which ethical principle?
choices: Justice (Principle D) concerning fairness and equal access to psychological services universally
Beneficence and Nonmaleficence (Principle A) requiring psychologists to benefit and avoid harming
Fidelity and Responsibility (Principle B) emphasizing trust and professional accountability standards
Integrity (Principle C) prioritizing honesty, accuracy, and truthfulness in professional practice
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Principle A (Beneficence and Nonmaleficence): psychologists strive to benefit those they work with and take care to do no harm. They guard against personal, financial, social, organizational, or political factors that might lead to misuse of their influence.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Justice (Principle D) specifically concerns fairness and equitable access to services.
(C) Fidelity and Responsibility (Principle B) emphasizes professional trust and accountability.
(D) Integrity (Principle C) focuses on honesty, accuracy, and truthfulness.

flags.detail: No citation or reference overlay is attached.

reviewQueue.prompt: The ethical principle of nonmaleficence requires psychologists to:
choices: Exclusively provide medically necessary essential psychiatric pharmacological treatment interventions optimizing measurable physiological outcomes
Take care not to cause harm, including through omission, and to minimize unavoidable harm in professional activities
Completely ignore potential hypothetical minor clinical harms prioritizing broader theoretical experimental scientific empirical discoveries
Consistently strictly prioritize publishing comprehensive rigorous experimental academic research findings over individualized client welfare
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Nonmaleficence ('do no harm'): active responsibility to avoid practices, methods, or interventions that cause harm. Includes harm from: biased assessments, inappropriate interventions, dual relationships, breaches of confidentiality, cultural insensitivity, or failure to act.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Nonmaleficence is specifically about avoiding harm
(C) Psychologists must actively work to prevent harm
(D) Client welfare always takes priority in clinical work

reviewQueue.prompt: When treating a minor, confidentiality generally belongs to:
choices: Exclusively fundamentally independently the highly trained individual clinical treating therapist completely dictating all informational access parameters
The parent/guardian has access rights, but the psychologist balances parental rights with the therapeutic needs of the minor
Solely uniquely completely exclusively the individual child patient strictly forbidding any external parental guardian awareness whatsoever
Categorically fundamentally exclusively the child's encompassing educational school organizational academic structural institutional system administration
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Minors: parents generally hold the right to access records and information. However, best practice: negotiate confidentiality agreements at the start — discussing with parents what will/won't be shared. Some jurisdictions grant teens confidentiality for substance abuse, sexual health, or mental health.

Why others are wrong:
(A) The therapist doesn't hold confidentiality rights
(C) Generally, minors don't have full confidentiality from parents (with some exceptions)
(D) Schools have separate FERPA protections

flags.detail: No citation or reference overlay is attached.

reviewQueue.prompt: When a psychologist suspect elder abuse, they must:
choices: Strictly absolutely completely preserve fundamental clinical interrelational confidentiality maintaining absolute therapeutic professional silence
Follow state mandatory reporting laws — most states require reporting suspected elder abuse to Adult Protective Services (APS) or law enforcement
Exclusively confidentially discreetly thoroughly privately discuss these profound concerns solely among specific trusted close professional colleagues
Wait patiently conservatively continuously until obtaining incontrovertible definitive unassailable explicit objective physical forensic proof
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Most states include psychologists as mandated reporters for elder abuse (physical, sexual, emotional, financial, neglect). Reporting is based on reasonable suspicion, not certainty. The reporter is typically protected from civil liability for good-faith reports.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Mandatory reporting overrides confidentiality
(C) Colleague consultation may inform the report but doesn't replace it
(D) Waiting for proof may endanger the elder — suspicion suffices

flags.detail: No citation or reference overlay is attached.

reviewQueue.prompt: Psychologists' use of social media requires awareness of:
choices: Absolutely nothing exceptionally unusual exceptionally difficult deeply complex structurally novel surprisingly complicated or profoundly special
Maintaining strong professional boundaries, potential dual relationships, core client privacy, and the impact of online self-disclosure
The explicit established formal objective reality that contemporary global social media remains completely safely entirely fully irrelevant
Exclusively distinctly explicitly firmly strictly purely focusing essentially primarily upon specific formal systemic advertising regulations
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Social media ethics: don't 'friend' or follow clients. Be aware that clients may view your profiles. Don't acknowledge the therapeutic relationship online. Consider how self-disclosure reflects on the profession. Maintain separate personal/professional accounts. Privacy settings. Online testimonials.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Social media presents significant ethical considerations
(C) Social media is highly relevant to modern professional ethics
(D) Issues extend far beyond advertising

reviewQueue.prompt: Record retention guidelines generally recommend keeping client records for:
choices: A specifically limited formally defined strictly established exceptionally remarkably brief highly truncated standardized precisely 1 year
A minimum of 7 full years after the last date of service for valid adults, although specific individual state regulations clearly vary
Exclusively structurally systematically distinct temporal periods occurring strictly precisely uniquely completely during active treatment
An essentially permanently preserved profoundly rigorously safeguarded consistently strictly fundamentally completely permanent archival term
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) APA Record Keeping Guidelines (2007): full record for ≥7 years after last service date (adults). Minors: ≥3 years past age of majority. State laws may require longer. Must maintain records in a way that allows transfer to another provider. Secure destruction when appropriate.

Why others are wrong:
(A) 1 year is insufficient
(C) Records must be maintained well beyond active treatment
(D) Indefinite retention isn't required (and creates its own issues)

flags.detail: No citation or reference overlay is attached.

reviewQueue.prompt: In clinical supervision, parallel process refers to:
choices: Only administrative supervision
The phenomenon where the dynamics between the supervisee and client are mirrored (replayed) in the supervisory relationship
Only billing issues
Random therapeutic events
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Parallel process (Searles): unconscious reenactment in supervision of the therapeutic relationship dynamics. Example: if a client is resistant, the supervisee may become resistant in supervision. Recognizing this provides insight into the therapy. Bidirectional: can also flow from supervision to therapy.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Parallel process is a clinical supervision concept, not administrative
(C) It's about relational dynamics, not billing
(D) It's a systematic, recognized phenomenon in supervision theory

flags.detail: No citation or reference overlay is attached.
The correct choice is substantially longer than every distractor.

reviewQueue.prompt: The Discrimination Model of supervision (Bernard) identifies three supervisor roles:
choices: Only mentor
Teacher, counselor, and consultant — applied across three focus areas: intervention, conceptualization, and personalization
Only evaluator
Only administrator
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Bernard's model: 3 × 3 matrix. Roles: Teacher (didactic instruction), Counselor (exploring supervisee's personal reactions), Consultant (collaborative, peer-like). Focus areas: Intervention (skills), Conceptualization (understanding), Personalization (self-awareness). Role shifts based on supervisee need.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Mentor isn't one of Bernard's three roles
(C) Evaluator is a function of supervision but not one of Bernard's three roles
(D) Administrator is an organizational function, not a supervision role

flags.detail: No citation or reference overlay is attached.
The correct choice is substantially longer than every distractor.

reviewQueue.prompt: Multicultural supervision competencies include:
choices: Ignoring cultural differences
The supervisor's self-awareness of cultural biases, knowledge of culturally diverse worldviews, and ability to develop culturally responsive interventions and supervisory relationships
Only focusing on one culture
Avoiding cultural topics
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Multicultural supervision (Ancis & Ladany): supervisors must examine their own cultural identity and biases, create safe spaces for discussion, address cultural dynamics in the supervisory relationship, and help supervisees develop cultural competence. Cultural considerations in case conceptualization.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Ignoring differences leads to cultural blindness
(C) Competence involves understanding multiple cultural contexts
(D) Cultural topics must be actively addressed in supervision

flags.detail: No citation or reference overlay is attached.
The correct choice is substantially longer than every distractor.

reviewQueue.prompt: Supervisee developmental models (e.g., IDM, Stoltenberg & Delworth) propose:
choices: All supervisees are the same
Supervisees progress through predictable stages from anxious/dependent (beginner) to autonomous/confident (advanced), requiring different supervision approaches at each stage
Only experienced therapists need supervision
Development is random
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) IDM (Integrated Developmental Model): Level 1: high motivation, limited skills, needs structure (teacher role). Level 2: fluctuating confidence, growing awareness (counselor role). Level 3: stable, autonomous, seeks consultation. Level 3i: integrated across domains. Supervision adapts to level.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Developmental models emphasize individual differences across stages
(C) All levels of experience benefit from appropriate supervision
(D) Development follows discernible patterns

The correct choice is substantially longer than every distractor.

reviewQueue.prompt: In forensic settings, who is typically the 'client' that a psychologist serves?
choices: The individual being evaluated
The court, attorney, or referring agency
The victim of the crime
The individual's family
reviewQueue.rationale: In forensic evaluations, the client is usually the retaining party (e.g., the court or attorney), not the examinee. The examinee must be informed of the limits of confidentiality and the purpose of the evaluation.

reviewQueue.prompt: Regarding the retention of patient records, APA guidelines generally recommend retaining full records for at least:
choices: 3 years after last contact
5 years after last contact
7 years after last contact for adults
Records must never be destroyed
reviewQueue.rationale: APA Record Keeping Guidelines stipulate holding full records for at least 7 years for adults, and for minors, 3 years after they reach the age of majority (but not less than 7 years total).

reviewQueue.prompt: A patient with damage to the ventromedial prefrontal cortex would MOST likely show:
choices: Inability to form new memories
Poor decision-making and impaired social conduct
Loss of vision in the left visual field
Inability to understand spoken language
reviewQueue.rationale:
The vmPFC is critical for decision-making, emotional regulation, and social behavior. Damage (as in Phineas Gage) leads to impulsivity, poor judgment, and personality changes.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Inability to form new memories → hippocampus damage (anterograde amnesia)
(C) Loss of vision in left visual field → right occipital lobe or optic pathway damage
(D) Inability to understand spoken language → Wernicke's area (left temporal lobe) damage
references: Damasio, A. R. (1994). Descartes' error: Emotion, reason, and the human brain. Putnam. See also: Bechara, A., Damasio, H., Tranel, D., & Damasio, A. R. (1997). Deciding advantageously before knowing the advantageous strategy. Science, 275(5304), 1293–1295. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.275.5304.1293

reviewQueue.prompt: A patient presents with intention tremor, ataxia, and difficulty with rapid alternating movements. The MOST likely site of damage is:
choices: Basal ganglia
Cerebellum
Hippocampus
Thalamus
reviewQueue.rationale:
The cerebellum coordinates voluntary movement, balance, and motor learning. Cerebellar damage produces intention tremor, ataxia, and dysmetria — distinct from basal ganglia's resting tremor.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Basal ganglia → resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia (Parkinson's-type symptoms), not intention tremor
(C) Hippocampus → memory formation, not motor coordination
(D) Thalamus → sensory relay, not motor coordination (though thalamic lesions can cause tremor)
references: Kolb, B., & Whishaw, I. Q. (2015). Fundamentals of human neuropsychology (7th ed.). Worth Publishers.

reviewQueue.prompt: Which of the following is TRUE about long-term potentiation (LTP)?
choices: It weakens synaptic connections
It primarily involves the frontal lobe
It is dependent on NMDA receptor activation
It is unrelated to learning
reviewQueue.rationale:
LTP requires activation of NMDA glutamate receptors, which allow calcium influx that triggers molecular cascades strengthening synaptic connections — the cellular basis of learning.

Why others are wrong:
(A) LTP STRENGTHENS synaptic connections — weakening would be long-term depression (LTD)
(B) LTP is most studied in the hippocampus, not primarily the frontal lobe
(D) LTP is the primary cellular mechanism underlying learning and memory formation
references: Bliss, T. V. P., & Collingridge, G. L. (1993). A synaptic model of memory: Long-term potentiation in the hippocampus. Nature, 361(6407), 31–39. https://doi.org/10.1038/361031a0

reviewQueue.prompt: Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome is caused by deficiency of:
choices: Vitamin B12
Thiamine (Vitamin B1)
Folic acid
Vitamin D
reviewQueue.rationale:
Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome results from thiamine (B1) deficiency, most commonly due to chronic alcoholism. Features confabulation, anterograde amnesia, and ataxia.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Vitamin B12 deficiency → pernicious anemia, peripheral neuropathy, and cognitive changes, not WKS
(C) Folic acid deficiency → megaloblastic anemia and neural tube defects in pregnancy
(D) Vitamin D deficiency → rickets (children), osteomalacia (adults), not neuropsychiatric syndrome
references: Arts, N. J. M., Walvoort, S. J. W., & Kessels, R. P. C. (2017). Korsakoff's syndrome: A critical review. Neuropsychiatric Disease and Treatment, 13, 2875–2890. https://doi.org/10.2147/NDT.S130078

reviewQueue.prompt: A patient cannot recognize familiar faces despite intact vision. This condition is called:
choices: Agnosia
Prosopagnosia
Aphasia
Apraxia
reviewQueue.rationale:
Prosopagnosia (face blindness) involves inability to recognize faces, typically from damage to the fusiform face area in the temporal lobe. Visual acuity is preserved.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Agnosia is a broader term for recognition failure — prosopagnosia is a specific type of visual agnosia
(C) Aphasia → language impairment, not face recognition
(D) Apraxia → inability to perform learned movements, not recognition failure
references: Kanwisher, N., & Yovel, G. (2006). The fusiform face area: A cortical region specialized for the perception of faces. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B, 361(1476), 2109–2128. https://doi.org/10.1098/rstb.2006.1934

reviewQueue.prompt: Second-generation (atypical) antipsychotics differ from first-generation primarily because they:
choices: Are more potent dopamine blockers
Block both dopamine and serotonin receptors
Have higher risk of tardive dyskinesia
Are only available in injectable form
reviewQueue.rationale:
Atypical antipsychotics (e.g., clozapine, risperidone, olanzapine) block both D2 dopamine and 5-HT2A serotonin receptors, reducing EPS risk while addressing both positive and negative symptoms.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Atypicals are generally LESS potent dopamine blockers, not more — their efficacy comes from combined D2/5-HT2A blockade
(C) Atypicals have LOWER risk of tardive dyskinesia than first-generation antipsychotics
(D) Atypicals are available in multiple forms (oral, injectable, LAI) — not only injectable
references: Stahl, S. M. (2021). Stahl's essential psychopharmacology: Neuroscientific basis and practical applications (5th ed.). Cambridge University Press.

reviewQueue.prompt: A patient with left neglect syndrome most likely has damage to the:
choices: Left parietal lobe
Right parietal lobe
Left frontal lobe
Occipital lobe bilaterally
reviewQueue.rationale:
Left hemispatial neglect typically results from right parietal lobe damage. Patients ignore stimuli in the left visual field despite intact visual pathways.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Left parietal damage would cause RIGHT neglect (contralateral to the lesion)
(C) Left frontal lobe damage → motor/executive deficits, not hemispatial neglect
(D) Bilateral occipital damage → cortical blindness, not neglect (patients are unaware of visual loss but don't 'neglect' one side)
references: Corbetta, M., & Shulman, G. L. (2011). Spatial neglect and attention networks. Annual Review of Neuroscience, 34, 569–599. https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-neuro-061010-113731

reviewQueue.prompt: Which brain imaging technique provides the BEST temporal resolution?
choices: fMRI
PET scan
EEG
CT scan
reviewQueue.rationale:
EEG (electroencephalography) measures electrical activity in real-time (millisecond resolution), giving superior temporal resolution. fMRI has better spatial resolution but poorer temporal resolution.

Why others are wrong:
(A) fMRI has temporal resolution of seconds (hemodynamic lag), not milliseconds
(B) PET has poor temporal resolution (minutes) and requires radioactive tracers
(D) CT scan provides structural images, not real-time brain activity measurement
references: Luck, S. J. (2014). An introduction to the event-related potential technique (2nd ed.). MIT Press.

reviewQueue.prompt: The adrenal glands release cortisol in response to stress via the:
choices: Sympathetic nervous system directly
HPA axis
Parasympathetic nervous system
Somatic nervous system
reviewQueue.rationale:
The HPA (Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Adrenal) axis: hypothalamus releases CRH → pituitary releases ACTH → adrenal cortex releases cortisol. Chronic activation is linked to depression and immune suppression.

Why others are wrong:
(A) The sympathetic NS releases epinephrine/norepinephrine (fast response), not the slower cortisol pathway
(C) The parasympathetic NS promotes rest/digest, opposing stress responses
(D) The somatic NS controls voluntary skeletal muscles, not hormonal stress responses
references: Herman, J. P., McKlveen, J. M., Ghosal, S., Kopp, B., Wulsin, A., Makinson, R., ... & Myers, B. (2016). Regulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenocortical stress response. Comprehensive Physiology, 6(2), 603–621. https://doi.org/10.1002/cphy.c150015

reviewQueue.prompt: The fight-or-flight response is mediated by the:
choices: Parasympathetic nervous system
Sympathetic nervous system
Somatic nervous system
Enteric nervous system
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) The sympathetic nervous system activates fight-or-flight: increased heart rate, blood pressure, pupil dilation, bronchial dilation, and glucose release. Mediated by norepinephrine and epinephrine from the adrenal medulla.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Parasympathetic = rest-and-digest (slows heart rate, promotes digestion) — the opposite response
(C) Somatic nervous system controls voluntary skeletal muscles, not autonomic fight-or-flight
(D) Enteric nervous system governs the gastrointestinal tract specifically, not the whole-body stress response
references: Cannon, W. B. (1932). The wisdom of the body. W. W. Norton. See also: Selye, H. (1956). The stress of life. McGraw-Hill.

reviewQueue.prompt: Wernicke's aphasia is characterized by:
choices: Non-fluent speech with good comprehension
Fluent but meaningless speech with poor comprehension
Inability to write
Loss of motor function only
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Wernicke's aphasia (receptive/sensory): speech is fluent and grammatically correct but lacks meaningful content (word salad, neologisms, paraphasias). Comprehension is severely impaired. Caused by left superior temporal gyrus damage.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Non-fluent with good comprehension = Broca's aphasia
(C) Inability to write = agraphia, which can be isolated or part of a larger syndrome
(D) Motor function loss = hemiplegia/paresis from motor cortex or corticospinal tract damage, not aphasia
references: Wernicke, C. (1874). Der aphasische Symptomenkomplex [The aphasia symptom complex]. Cohn & Weigert.

reviewQueue.prompt: The ventral tegmental area (VTA) is a key structure in:
choices: Primary visual processing occurring in the occipital lobe striate and extrastriate cortical areas
The brain's reward and motivation circuitry projecting dopaminergic pathways to nucleus accumbens
Primary auditory processing occurring in temporal lobe Heschl's gyrus and surrounding cortex
Cerebellar motor coordination and procedural learning involving Purkinje cell circuit computations
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) The VTA is the origin of the mesolimbic dopamine pathway (VTA → nucleus accumbens), central to reward, motivation, reinforcement learning, and addiction. Also projects to the prefrontal cortex (mesocortical pathway).

Why others are wrong:
(A) Visual processing → occipital lobe (primary visual cortex, V1-V5).
(C) Auditory processing → temporal lobe (primary auditory cortex, Heschl's gyrus).
(D) Motor coordination → cerebellum and basal ganglia.
references: Wise, R. A. (2004). Dopamine, learning and motivation. Nature Reviews Neuroscience, 5(6), 483–494. https://doi.org/10.1038/nrn1406

reviewQueue.prompt: The insula cortex is involved in:
choices: Only primary motor control of voluntary skeletal movements through corticospinal tract projections
Interoception, emotional awareness, empathy, disgust perception, and pain processing functions
Only primary visual processing of spatial orientation and object recognition in the visual field
Only expressive language production through coordination of articulatory motor speech programs
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) The insula processes interoceptive signals (internal body states), subjective emotional experience, empathy, disgust, pain, and risk assessment. It bridges bodily sensations with emotional awareness.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Motor control primarily involves the motor cortex, basal ganglia, and cerebellum.
(C) Visual processing → occipital cortex.
(D) Language production → Broca's area (left frontal lobe).
references: Craig, A. D. (2009). How do you feel — now? The anterior insula and human awareness. Nature Reviews Neuroscience, 10(1), 59–70. https://doi.org/10.1038/nrn2555

reviewQueue.prompt: Broca's area is located in the:
choices: Right temporal lobe processing music perception and prosodic speech contour recognition
Left inferior frontal gyrus controlling speech production, grammar, and language output
Occipital lobe processing primary visual information from the lateral geniculate nucleus
Cerebellum coordinating motor timing, procedural learning, and postural balance control
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Broca's area (Brodmann areas 44/45) is in the left inferior frontal gyrus. It controls speech production, grammar, and language output. Damage produces non-fluent (expressive) aphasia.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Right temporal lobe → involved in music processing and non-verbal abilities.
(C) Occipital lobe → visual processing.
(D) Cerebellum → motor coordination, balance, and procedural learning.
references: Broca, P. (1861). Remarques sur le siège de la faculté du langage articulé. Bulletins de la Société Anatomique de Paris, 6, 330–357.

reviewQueue.prompt: Tardive dyskinesia is MOST associated with long-term use of:
choices: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors prescribed for depressive and anxiety spectrum disorders
Benzodiazepine anxiolytic medications that enhance GABAergic inhibitory neurotransmission systemically
Typical first-generation antipsychotics that block dopamine D2 receptors causing receptor supersensitivity
Psychostimulant medications that increase catecholamine availability in prefrontal synaptic clefts
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (C) Tardive dyskinesia (TD) — involuntary, repetitive orofacial movements — develops after prolonged use of dopamine D2 receptor-blocking agents, especially typical antipsychotics (haloperidol, chlorpromazine). Due to dopamine receptor supersensitivity.

Why others are wrong:
(A) SSRIs don't block dopamine receptors and rarely cause movement disorders.
(B) Benzodiazepines enhance GABA — they don't cause TD.
(D) Stimulants increase dopamine rather than blocking it — they cause different side effects.
references: Correll, C. U., Kane, J. M., & Citrome, L. L. (2017). Epidemiology, prevention, and assessment of tardive dyskinesia and advances in treatment. Journal of Clinical Psychiatry, 78(8), 1136–1147. https://doi.org/10.4088/JCP.tv17016ah4c

reviewQueue.prompt: Phenylketonuria (PKU) illustrates:
choices: A purely environmental specific formalized targeted external pathological condition with explicit absolute strictly zero genetic bases
Gene-environment interaction: a genetic condition whose effects are prevented by environmental modification (dietary restriction)
A specifically pervasive irreversible explicit formal structural absolute clinical condition with completely zero established treatments
A formal explicitly localized unique developmental strict functional specific central condition solely via early prenatal alcohol exposure
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) PKU: an autosomal recessive genetic disorder where phenylalanine cannot be metabolized. Without dietary restriction, it causes intellectual disability. With early dietary modification, normal development occurs — a classic gene-environment interaction.

Why others are wrong:
(A) PKU has a clear genetic basis (PAH gene mutation) — it's not purely environmental
(C) PKU IS treatable through phenylalanine-restricted diet — early detection via newborn screening is critical
(D) Prenatal alcohol exposure causes Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorders (FASD), a different condition
references: National Institutes of Health. (2000). Phenylketonuria: Screening and management (NIH Consensus Statement, Vol. 17, No. 3). https://consensus.nih.gov/2000/2000phenylketonuria113html.htm

reviewQueue.prompt: Neurotransmitter deactivation occurs through all of the following EXCEPT:
choices: Reuptake into the presynaptic neuron
Enzymatic degradation in the synapse
Diffusion away from the synapse
Myelination of axons
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (D) Myelination insulates axons to speed signal conduction — it has nothing to do with neurotransmitter deactivation. Deactivation occurs through reuptake, enzymatic breakdown, and diffusion.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Reuptake IS a major deactivation mechanism — transporters pull neurotransmitter back into the presynaptic terminal
(B) Enzymatic degradation IS a deactivation mechanism (e.g., MAO breaks down monoamines, AChE breaks down acetylcholine)
(C) Diffusion IS a deactivation mechanism — neurotransmitter drifts away from receptors
references: Stahl, S. M. (2021). Stahl's essential psychopharmacology: Neuroscientific basis and practical applications (5th ed.). Cambridge University Press.

reviewQueue.prompt: The limbic system includes all EXCEPT:
choices: Amygdala
Hippocampus
Hypothalamus
Primary motor cortex
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (D) The primary motor cortex (precentral gyrus, frontal lobe) controls voluntary movement and is NOT part of the limbic system. The limbic system includes the amygdala, hippocampus, hypothalamus, cingulate gyrus, and other structures.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Amygdala IS a limbic structure — emotional processing, especially fear
(B) Hippocampus IS a limbic structure — memory formation
(C) Hypothalamus IS a limbic structure — homeostasis and motivation
references: Purves, D., Augustine, G. J., Fitzpatrick, D., Hall, W. C., LaMantia, A.-S., & White, L. E. (2012). Neuroscience (5th ed.). Sinauer Associates.

reviewQueue.prompt: The cerebellum contains approximately what percentage of the brain's neurons?
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (D) Despite being only ~10% of brain volume, the cerebellum contains approximately 80% of the brain's neurons (~69 billion of ~86 billion total). Its granule cells are extremely numerous and densely packed.

Why others are wrong:
(A) 5% dramatically underestimates the cerebellum's neuronal density
(B) 20% still significantly underestimates
(C) 50% underestimates — the actual proportion is much higher
references: Herculano-Houzel, S. (2009). The human brain in numbers: A linearly scaled-up primate brain. Frontiers in Human Neuroscience, 3, 31. https://doi.org/10.3389/neuro.09.031.2009

reviewQueue.prompt: Executive functions are primarily associated with the:
choices: Occipital lobe
Temporal lobe
Prefrontal cortex
Cerebellum
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (C) Executive functions (planning, inhibition, working memory, cognitive flexibility, decision-making, abstract reasoning) are primarily mediated by the prefrontal cortex and its connections.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Occipital lobe → visual processing
(B) Temporal lobe → auditory processing, language comprehension, memory
(D) Cerebellum → motor coordination, timing, procedural learning
references: Miyake, A., Friedman, N. P., Emerson, M. J., Witzki, A. H., Howerter, A., & Wager, T. D. (2000). The unity and diversity of executive functions. Cognitive Psychology, 41(1), 49–100. https://doi.org/10.1006/cogp.1999.0734

reviewQueue.prompt: Norepinephrine is involved in all EXCEPT:
choices: Alertness and arousal
Attention and vigilance
Fight-or-flight response
Myelin production
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (D) Myelin is produced by oligodendrocytes (CNS) and Schwann cells (PNS). Norepinephrine is a neurotransmitter involved in arousal, attention, and stress responses — not myelin production.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Norepinephrine IS crucial for alertness and arousal (locus coeruleus projections)
(B) Norepinephrine IS important for attention and vigilance (implicated in ADHD)
(C) Norepinephrine IS a primary mediator of the sympathetic fight-or-flight response
references: Sara, S. J. (2009). The locus coeruleus and noradrenergic modulation of cognition. Nature Reviews Neuroscience, 10(3), 211–223. https://doi.org/10.1038/nrn2573

reviewQueue.prompt: Glia cells include all EXCEPT:
choices: Astrocytes
Oligodendrocytes
Microglia
Pyramidal cells
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (D) Pyramidal cells are NEURONS (excitatory, found in cortex and hippocampus), not glial cells. Glial cells include astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, microglia, and Schwann cells — they support, protect, and nourish neurons.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Astrocytes ARE glial cells — they provide structural support, maintain the BBB, and regulate neurotransmitters
(B) Oligodendrocytes ARE glial cells — they produce myelin in the CNS
(C) Microglia ARE glial cells — they serve as the brain's immune cells
references: Allen, N. J., & Barres, B. A. (2009). Glia — more than just brain glue. Nature, 457(7230), 675–677. https://doi.org/10.1038/457675a

reviewQueue.prompt: Hemispheric lateralization research shows that the LEFT hemisphere (in most right-handed people) is specialized for:
choices: Spatial processing and face recognition
Language, logic, and sequential processing
Emotional processing of negative stimuli
Holistic pattern recognition
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Left hemisphere specialization: language (Broca's and Wernicke's areas), logical/analytical reasoning, math, sequential/temporal processing, and fine motor control (right hand).

Why others are wrong:
(A) Spatial processing and face recognition → right hemisphere specialization
(C) Negative emotion processing → mixed evidence, but right hemisphere shows stronger association
(D) Holistic/gestalt pattern recognition → right hemisphere specialization
references: Gazzaniga, M. S. (2005). Forty-five years of split-brain research and still going strong. Nature Reviews Neuroscience, 6(8), 653–659. https://doi.org/10.1038/nrn1723

reviewQueue.prompt: Phantom limb pain after amputation is best explained by:
choices: The explicit structural physical objective biological functional limb remains partially objectively present
Cortical reorganization — the brain's somatosensory map remaps the missing limb's territory to adjacent areas
A specifically entirely complex deeply rooted unconscious psychological systemic denial of the amputation
An exclusively localized profoundly severe explicit objective structural infection at the amputation site
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Ramachandran's research: after amputation, cortical areas mapped to the missing limb are 'invaded' by adjacent cortical representations. Touching the face may evoke sensation in the 'phantom' hand because face and hand areas are adjacent on the somatosensory cortex.

Why others are wrong:
(A) The limb is completely absent — phantom sensations originate in the brain's cortical maps
(C) Phantom limb is a neurological phenomenon, not psychological denial
(D) Infection would cause local pain at the stump, not phantom sensations in the missing limb
references: Ramachandran, V. S., & Rogers-Ramachandran, D. (2000). Phantom limbs and neural plasticity. Archives of Neurology, 57(3), 317–320. https://doi.org/10.1001/archneur.57.3.317

reviewQueue.prompt: The substantia nigra is critical for:
choices: Specifically regulating complex explicit advanced linguistic grammar and language comprehension
Dopamine production and voluntary movement — its degeneration causes Parkinson's disease
Specifically regulating explicit advanced complex primary fundamental holistic visual processing
Specifically regulating explicit advanced complex primary long-term memory trace consolidation
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) The substantia nigra (midbrain) produces dopamine via the nigrostriatal pathway to the basal ganglia, facilitating voluntary movement. Degeneration of substantia nigra dopaminergic neurons → Parkinson's disease (bradykinesia, rigidity, resting tremor).

Why others are wrong:
(A) Language comprehension → Wernicke's area (left temporal lobe)
(C) Visual processing → occipital lobe
(D) Memory consolidation → hippocampus
references: Dauer, W., & Przedborski, S. (2003). Parkinson's disease: Mechanisms and models. Neuron, 39(6), 889–909. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0896-6273(03)00568-3

reviewQueue.prompt: The action potential follows the:
choices: The explicitly broad highly specific fundamentally continuous proportional graded potential principle
All-or-none law — once threshold is reached, the neuron fires at full strength regardless of stimulus intensity
The explicitly broad highly specific fundamentally continuous proportional inverse square physical law
The explicitly broad highly specific fundamentally continuous proportional law of diminishing returns
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Action potentials are all-or-none: once the membrane potential reaches threshold (~-55mV), a full action potential occurs. Stimulus intensity is coded by FIRING RATE and NUMBER of neurons firing, not action potential magnitude.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Graded potentials (EPSPs/IPSPs) vary in magnitude — action potentials do not (they're all-or-none)
(C) The inverse square law applies to physics (light, gravity), not neuronal firing
(D) Law of diminishing returns is an economics principle, not a neuroscience concept
references: Bear, M. F., Connors, B. W., & Paradiso, M. A. (2016). Neuroscience: Exploring the brain (4th ed.). Wolters Kluwer.

reviewQueue.prompt: The ventricles of the brain contain:
choices: Circulating arterial blood
Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)
Densely packed neurons
Myelinated white matter
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) The four ventricles (two lateral, third, fourth) contain CSF, which cushions the brain, removes waste, delivers nutrients, and maintains intracranial pressure. CSF is produced by the choroid plexus.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Blood flows through arteries, veins, and capillaries — not through the ventricles
(C) Neurons are located in cortical and subcortical gray matter, not in the ventricles
(D) White matter tracts run through brain parenchyma, not ventricles
references: Purves, D., Augustine, G. J., Fitzpatrick, D., Hall, W. C., LaMantia, A.-S., & White, L. E. (2012). Neuroscience (5th ed.). Sinauer Associates.

reviewQueue.prompt: Acetylcholine is important for:
choices: Exclusively distinctly directly driving only rigorous skeletal muscle contraction
Memory, learning, muscle contraction, and parasympathetic nervous system function
Exclusively distinctly directly driving only rigorous circadian sleep regulation
Exclusively distinctly directly driving only rigorous generalized pain perception
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Acetylcholine (ACh) has diverse roles: neuromuscular junction (muscle contraction), parasympathetic NS (rest/digest), basal forebrain → cortex (attention, memory, learning). ACh depletion in Alzheimer's disease contributes to cognitive decline.

Why others are wrong:
(A) ACh has CNS functions (memory, learning) in addition to peripheral neuromuscular roles
(C) While ACh modulates sleep-wake cycles, it has many other functions
(D) ACh is not primarily a pain-processing neurotransmitter
references: Hasselmo, M. E. (2006). The role of acetylcholine in learning and memory. Current Opinion in Neurobiology, 16(6), 710–715. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.conb.2006.09.002

reviewQueue.prompt: Functional connectivity in neuroimaging refers to:
choices: Direct observable explicitly continuous primary physical white matter anatomical tract connections
Statistical correlations in brain activity between regions that may not be directly anatomically connected
Strictly exclusively explicitly objectively purely mathematically exclusively measuring blood flow
Strictly exclusively explicitly objectively purely mathematically isolating specific electrical activity
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Functional connectivity identifies brain regions whose activity patterns are temporally correlated (co-activate together). This reveals neural networks without requiring direct anatomical connections. Used extensively in resting-state fMRI research.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Physical white matter connections = structural/anatomical connectivity (measured with DTI), not functional
(C) Functional connectivity can be measured using fMRI (blood flow), EEG (electrical), or other modalities
(D) Multiple imaging modalities can assess functional connectivity, not just EEG
references: Friston, K. J. (2011). Functional and effective connectivity: A review. Brain Connectivity, 1(1), 13–36. https://doi.org/10.1089/brain.2011.0008

reviewQueue.prompt: Sensitization is a form of non-associative learning in which:
choices: A highly specific repeated consistent exposure strictly decreases any response
A single strong stimulus leads to an INCREASED response to subsequent stimuli
Two highly distinct specific biological stimuli are definitively paired together
A highly distinct specific biological behavior is definitively fully reinforced
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Sensitization: after an intense or noxious stimulus, subsequent responses to even mild stimuli are amplified. Example: after a loud bang, you startle more easily to minor sounds. Opposite of habituation.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Decreased response to repeated exposure = habituation (the opposite)
(C) Pairing stimuli = associative learning (classical conditioning), not sensitization
(D) Reinforcement = operant conditioning (associative), not non-associative sensitization
references: Kandel, E. R. (2001). The molecular biology of memory storage: A dialogue between genes and synapses. Science, 294(5544), 1030–1038. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1067020

reviewQueue.prompt: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) have a therapeutic lag of approximately:
choices: 1-2 hours
2-6 weeks
6 months
There is no lag — effects are immediate
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) SSRIs require approximately 2-6 weeks for full therapeutic effect. This lag is thought to involve downstream neuroplastic changes (neurogenesis, receptor sensitivity changes) rather than acute serotonin increase alone.

Why others are wrong:
(A) While serotonin reuptake blockade begins within hours, therapeutic antidepressant effects take weeks
(C) Full response may continue to develop but the primary therapeutic lag is 2-6 weeks, not 6 months
(D) If effects were immediate, the mechanism would be purely serotonin reuptake — the lag suggests additional neuroplastic mechanisms
references: Stahl, S. M. (2021). Stahl's essential psychopharmacology (5th ed.). Cambridge University Press.

reviewQueue.prompt: The sympathetic nervous system's fight-or-flight response includes:
choices: Systematically decreased resting heart rate and highly constricted visual pupils
Increased heart rate, dilated pupils, bronchodilation, and blood flow to muscles
Significantly increased active gastrointestinal systemic metabolic digestion
Significantly persistently decreased total structural systemic blood pressure
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Sympathetic activation prepares for emergency: increased heart rate, dilated pupils, bronchodilation (more air), blood diverted to skeletal muscles, glycogen → glucose release, adrenal epinephrine secretion.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Decreased heart rate and constricted pupils = parasympathetic ('rest and digest') responses
(C) Increased digestion = parasympathetic activity — sympathetic activation INHIBITS digestion
(D) Sympathetic activation INCREASES blood pressure to support emergency response
references: Cannon, W. B. (1932). The wisdom of the body. W. W. Norton.

reviewQueue.prompt: Melatonin, produced by the pineal gland, is important for:
choices: Systematic physiological fight-or-flight stress response
Circadian rhythm regulation and sleep-wake cycle timing
Voluntary procedural coordinated physical muscle contraction
Conscious subjective structural psychological pain perception
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Melatonin: produced by the pineal gland in response to darkness. It signals the biological clock (suprachiasmatic nucleus) to promote sleepiness. Suppressed by light exposure, especially blue light.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Stress response → cortisol (HPA axis) and epinephrine/norepinephrine (sympathetic NS)
(C) Muscle contraction → acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction
(D) Pain perception → substance P, glutamate, endorphins — not melatonin
references: Pandi-Perumal, S. R., Trakht, I., Srinivasan, V., Spence, D. W., Maestroni, G. J. M., Zisapel, N., & Cardinali, D. P. (2008). Physiological effects of melatonin. Progress in Neurobiology, 85(3), 335–353. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pneurobio.2008.04.001

reviewQueue.prompt: The superior colliculus is responsible for:
choices: Basic foundational temporal auditory processing
Visual reflexes and eye movement coordination
Complex semantic expressive language production
Systematic episodic declarative memory consolidation
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Superior colliculus (midbrain tectum): coordinates visual reflexes (orienting toward visual stimuli), saccadic eye movements, and integration of visual, auditory, and somatosensory information for head/eye orientation.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Auditory processing → inferior colliculus (midbrain) and auditory cortex (temporal lobe)
(C) Language production → Broca's area (left frontal lobe)
(D) Memory consolidation → hippocampus
references: Wurtz, R. H., & Albano, J. E. (1980). Visual-motor function of the primate superior colliculus. Annual Review of Neuroscience, 3, 189–226. https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev.ne.03.030180.001201

reviewQueue.prompt: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is caused by:
choices: Pathological systemic massive overproduction and explicit dopamine excess
Autoimmune demyelination — the immune system attacks myelin sheaths in the CNS
Severe chronic pervasive structural specific cortical serotonin deficiency
Aggressive fast-acting pervasive biological bacterial infection of the brain
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) MS: the immune system attacks oligodendrocyte-produced myelin in the CNS, creating lesions (plaques) that disrupt signal transmission. Symptoms: vision problems, motor weakness, fatigue, sensory disturbances; relapsing-remitting course common.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Dopamine excess is associated with psychotic symptoms, not MS
(C) Serotonin deficiency is linked to depression, not MS
(D) MS is autoimmune, not caused by bacterial infection (though infections may trigger flare-ups)
references: Compston, A., & Coles, A. (2008). Multiple sclerosis. The Lancet, 372(9648), 1502–1517. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(08)61620-7

reviewQueue.prompt: The prefrontal cortex undergoes significant development through:
choices: Exclusively during early infancy, strictly restricted from birth to age two only
Adulthood — particularly through adolescence, with myelination continuing into mid-20s
It is considered entirely completely physically structurally developed precisely at birth
Exclusively strictly restricted to the highly sensitive early prenatal fetal development
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) The PFC is one of the LAST brain regions to fully mature. Synaptic pruning, myelination, and connectivity refinement continue through adolescence into the mid-20s, explaining adolescent risk-taking and impulsivity.

Why others are wrong:
(A) PFC development extends FAR beyond age 2
(C) The PFC is among the LEAST mature brain regions at birth
(D) PFC development extends well beyond fetal development through adolescence
references: Casey, B. J., Giedd, J. N., & Thomas, K. M. (2000). Structural and functional brain development and its relation to cognitive development. Biological Psychology, 54(1–3), 241–257. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0301-0511(00)00058-2

reviewQueue.prompt: The insula is involved in:
choices: Exclusively strictly uniquely restricted to deliberate physical motor control
Interoception, emotional awareness, empathy, disgust, and pain processing
Exclusively entirely strictly restricted to primary chemical sensory olfaction
Exclusively uniquely localized specifically solely for primary peripheral vision
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) The insula processes interoceptive signals (body state awareness), subjective feeling states, empathy, disgust, pain, taste, and risk/uncertainty evaluation. It bridges bodily sensation with emotional experience.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Motor control → motor cortex, basal ganglia, cerebellum
(C) Olfaction → piriform cortex and orbitofrontal cortex (though the insula does process taste)
(D) Vision → occipital lobe
references: Craig, A. D. (2009). How do you feel — now? The anterior insula and human awareness. Nature Reviews Neuroscience, 10(1), 59–70. https://doi.org/10.1038/nrn2555

reviewQueue.prompt: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) work by:
choices: Non-selectively blocking the reuptake of all major monoamine neurotransmitters at the synaptic cleft
Selectively blocking serotonin reuptake at the presynaptic neuron, increasing synaptic availability
Directly activating postsynaptic dopamine D1 and D2 receptors to enhance motivational drive
Irreversibly inhibiting monoamine oxidase enzymes responsible for metabolizing catecholamines
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) SSRIs (fluoxetine/Prozac, sertraline/Zoloft, etc.): selectively block the serotonin transporter (SERT), preventing reuptake of 5-HT into the presynaptic neuron → more serotonin available in the synaptic cleft. First-line for depression, anxiety disorders.

Why others are wrong:
(A) SSRIs are selective for serotonin; SNRIs and TCAs are broader.
(C) Direct dopamine receptor activation characterizes dopamine agonists.
(D) MAO enzyme inhibition defines MAOIs, a different antidepressant class.
references: Stahl, S. M. (2021). Stahl's essential psychopharmacology: Neuroscientific basis and practical applications (5th ed.). Cambridge University Press.

reviewQueue.prompt: A researcher conditions a dog to salivate to a tone, then pairs the tone with a light. Eventually, the light alone elicits salivation. This is:
choices: Stimulus generalization
Higher-order conditioning
Spontaneous recovery
Sensory preconditioning
reviewQueue.rationale:
Higher-order (second-order) conditioning: a new CS (light) is paired with an established CS (tone) rather than with the original UCS, acquiring the ability to elicit a CR.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Stimulus generalization = responding to similar stimuli (e.g., similar tones), not pairing with a new stimulus
(C) Spontaneous recovery = reappearance of an extinguished CR after time passes
(D) Sensory preconditioning = pairing two neutral stimuli BEFORE any conditioning with a UCS
references: Pavlov, I. P. (1927). Conditioned reflexes: An investigation of the physiological activity of the cerebral cortex (G. V. Anrep, Trans.). Oxford University Press.

reviewQueue.prompt: According to dual-process theory, System 1 thinking is BEST characterized as:
choices: Slow, deliberate, and analytical
Fast, automatic, and intuitive
Only used for complex problems
Entirely conscious and controlled
reviewQueue.rationale:
Kahneman's System 1 is fast, automatic, and intuitive (heuristic-based). System 2 is slow, deliberate, and analytical. Most thinking relies on System 1, leading to predictable biases.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Slow/deliberate/analytical = System 2, not System 1
(C) System 1 is used for ALL types of problems by default — not only complex ones
(D) System 1 is largely UNCONSCIOUS and automatic, not conscious and controlled
references: Kahneman, D. (2011). Thinking, fast and slow. Farrar, Straus and Giroux.

reviewQueue.prompt: Token economies are based primarily on principles of:
choices: Classical conditioning
Operant conditioning
Observational learning
Cognitive restructuring
reviewQueue.rationale:
Token economies use operant conditioning — tokens serve as secondary/conditioned reinforcers that can be exchanged for backup reinforcers (rewards). Based on positive reinforcement principles.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Classical conditioning involves involuntary responses to paired stimuli — tokens involve voluntary behavior for earned reinforcement
(C) Observational learning (Bandura) involves modeling, not earning tokens
(D) Cognitive restructuring changes thought patterns — token economies change behavior via reinforcement contingencies
references: Ayllon, T., & Azrin, N. (1968). The token economy: A motivational system for therapy and rehabilitation. Appleton-Century-Crofts.

reviewQueue.prompt: A child is rewarded for drawing. After the reward is removed, the child draws LESS than before rewards were introduced. This illustrates:
choices: Extinction
The overjustification effect
Negative punishment
Habituation
reviewQueue.rationale:
The overjustification effect: providing extrinsic rewards for intrinsically motivated behavior undermines intrinsic motivation when rewards are removed.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Extinction = stopping a previously reinforced behavior — but the behavior drops BELOW baseline, not just to zero
(C) Negative punishment = removing something pleasant to decrease behavior — here no punishment was applied
(D) Habituation = decreased response to repeated stimulation, a different process from motivational change
references: Deci, E. L., Koestner, R., & Ryan, R. M. (1999). A meta-analytic review of experiments examining the effects of extrinsic rewards on intrinsic motivation. Psychological Bulletin, 125(6), 627–668. https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.125.6.627

reviewQueue.prompt: Which memory system allows you to remember what you had for breakfast?
choices: Semantic memory
Procedural memory
Episodic memory
Implicit memory
reviewQueue.rationale:
Episodic memory (a type of explicit/declarative memory) stores personally experienced events in their temporal-spatial context — your breakfast is a personal event.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Semantic memory stores general facts and knowledge (e.g., 'breakfast is the first meal of the day'), not personal events
(B) Procedural memory stores skills and habits (e.g., how to use a fork), not specific events
(D) Implicit memory is unconscious — recalling breakfast requires conscious, explicit retrieval
references: Tulving, E. (1972). Episodic and semantic memory. In E. Tulving & W. Donaldson (Eds.), Organization of memory (pp. 381–403). Academic Press.

reviewQueue.prompt: The serial position effect demonstrates that items at the _____ and _____ of a list are best remembered.
choices: Middle and end
Beginning and middle
Beginning and end
Random positions
reviewQueue.rationale:
Serial position effect: primacy (beginning items — transferred to LTM) and recency (end items — still in STM). Middle items are recalled poorest.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Middle items are recalled WORST, not best — the serial position curve is U-shaped
(B) Beginning items are recalled well (primacy) but middle items are not
(D) The serial position effect shows a SYSTEMATIC pattern, not random recall
references: Murdock, B. B. (1962). The serial position effect of free recall. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 64(5), 482–488. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0045106

reviewQueue.prompt: According to Lazarus's transactional model of stress, the MOST critical factor determining the stress response is:
choices: The objective severity of the stressor
The individual's cognitive appraisal of the situation
The person's physiological arousal level
The presence of social support
reviewQueue.rationale:
Lazarus argued cognitive appraisal is central: primary appraisal (Is this threatening?) and secondary appraisal (Can I cope?) determine the stress response, not objective threat level.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Objective severity matters less than PERCEIVED threat — the same event can be appraised differently
(C) Physiological arousal is a CONSEQUENCE of appraisal, not the primary determining factor
(D) Social support is a coping resource that affects secondary appraisal, but appraisal itself is the critical factor
references: Lazarus, R. S., & Folkman, S. (1984). Stress, appraisal, and coping. Springer.

reviewQueue.prompt: In operant conditioning, a variable-interval schedule would produce:
choices: High, steady response rates
Moderate, steady response rate
Post-reinforcement pauses
Rapid bursts then stops
reviewQueue.rationale:
Variable-interval schedules produce moderate, steady response rates (e.g., checking email — reinforcement available at unpredictable times). No post-reinforcement pause because timing is unpredictable.

Why others are wrong:
(A) High, steady rates are more characteristic of variable-ratio schedules (e.g., slot machines)
(C) Post-reinforcement pauses are characteristic of fixed-ratio schedules
(D) Rapid bursts then stops describe fixed-ratio patterns, not variable-interval
references: Ferster, C. B., & Skinner, B. F. (1957). Schedules of reinforcement. Appleton-Century-Crofts.

reviewQueue.prompt: Tolman's research on latent learning demonstrated that:
choices: All learning requires reinforcement
Learning can occur without observable behavioral change
Classical conditioning explains all learning
Punishment is more effective than reinforcement
reviewQueue.rationale:
Tolman showed rats learned maze layouts (cognitive maps) without reinforcement, demonstrating learning when there was no motivation to perform — challenging strict behaviorism.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Tolman's research specifically DISPROVED this — learning occurred WITHOUT reinforcement
(C) Tolman's cognitive approach was a challenge TO classical conditioning explanations, not support for them
(D) Tolman's work did not address punishment vs. reinforcement — it was about whether reinforcement is necessary for learning at all
references: Tolman, E. C., & Honzik, C. H. (1930). Introduction and removal of reward, and maze performance in rats. University of California Publications in Psychology, 4, 257–275.

reviewQueue.prompt: Garcia and Koelling's research on taste aversion demonstrated that:
choices: All stimuli are equally associable
Biological preparedness constrains conditioning
Extinction is permanent
Higher-order conditioning is impossible
reviewQueue.rationale:
Garcia showed rats readily associated taste (not light/sound) with illness — demonstrating biological preparedness/selective association. Animals are predisposed to make certain CS-UCS pairings.

Why others are wrong:
(A) The key finding was that NOT all stimuli are equally associable — taste pairs with illness, not audiovisual cues
(C) The study was about acquisition constraints, not extinction permanence
(D) Higher-order conditioning was not the topic — the study was about biological constraints on CS-UCS associations
references: Garcia, J., & Koelling, R. A. (1966). Relation of cue to consequence in avoidance learning. Psychonomic Science, 4(1), 123–124. https://doi.org/10.3758/BF03342209

reviewQueue.prompt: A child who can sort objects by color OR shape, but not both simultaneously, is likely in Piaget's:
choices: Sensorimotor stage
Preoperational stage
Concrete operational stage
Formal operational stage
reviewQueue.rationale:
Centration in the preoperational stage: children can focus on only one dimension at a time. Multi-dimensional classification emerges in concrete operations.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Sensorimotor stage (0-2) children wouldn't be sorting at all — they're developing object permanence
(C) Concrete operational children CAN classify by multiple dimensions simultaneously
(D) Formal operational thinkers handle abstract multi-dimensional reasoning easily
references: Piaget, J. (1952). The origins of intelligence in children (M. Cook, Trans.). International Universities Press.

reviewQueue.prompt: The peak-end rule (Kahneman) states that:
choices: People judge experiences by their peak intensity and how they ended, not by the average
People always remember the beginning of an experience most clearly
Emotional experiences are always remembered accurately
The most intense moment of an experience determines overall satisfaction
reviewQueue.rationale: Kahneman's peak-end rule demonstrates that people evaluate past experiences based on: (1) the peak moment (most intense point) and (2) the ending, rather than the duration or average experience. This has implications for clinical work — ending therapy sessions on a positive note and addressing peak distress moments can shape how clients remember treatment.
references: Kahneman, D., Fredrickson, B. L., Schreiber, C. A., & Redelmeier, D. A. (1993). When more pain is preferred to less: Adding a better end. Psychological Science, 4(6), 401–405. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9280.1993.tb00589.x

reviewQueue.prompt: Cognitive load theory distinguishes between:
choices: Only short-term and long-term memory storage systems within the modal memory architecture model
Intrinsic load (task complexity), extraneous load (poor design), and germane load (schema building)
Only explicit declarative memory and implicit nondeclarative memory taxonomic classification systems
Only sensory registration processing and subsequent motor output execution response pathways
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Sweller's cognitive load theory: intrinsic load (inherent task complexity), extraneous load (poor instructional design), and germane load (effort devoted to schema construction). Effective instruction minimizes extraneous load.

Why others are wrong:
(A) STM/LTM distinction is part of Atkinson-Shiffrin's model, not cognitive load theory specifically.
(C) Explicit/implicit memory is Squire's taxonomy, not related to cognitive load.
(D) Sensory/motor processing relates to perception and action, not instructional load management.
references: Sweller, J. (1988). Cognitive load during problem solving: Effects on learning. Cognitive Science, 12(2), 257–285. https://doi.org/10.1207/s15516709cog1202_4

reviewQueue.prompt: Amygdala hijack (Goleman) refers to:
choices: A neurosurgical procedure for removing the amygdala to treat refractory seizure disorders
An immediate emotional response that bypasses rational cortical processing through subcortical pathways
A hippocampal-dependent memory encoding process for consolidating emotional episodic events
A type of acquired traumatic brain injury resulting from focal damage to medial temporal structures
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Goleman popularized this term: the amygdala can trigger rapid emotional responses (especially fear/anger) via the thalamo-amygdala pathway BEFORE cortical areas fully process the information, producing impulsive emotional reactions.

Why others are wrong:
(A) It's a neuropsychological concept, not a surgical procedure.
(C) Memory encoding involves hippocampal processes — amygdala hijack is about immediate emotional reactivity.
(D) It describes normal brain functioning under emotional stress, not pathological brain injury.
references: Goleman, D. (1995). Emotional intelligence. Bantam Books. See also: LeDoux, J. E. (1996). The emotional brain. Simon & Schuster.

reviewQueue.prompt: Cognitive dissonance theory (Festinger) predicts that people who receive MINIMAL justification for counter-attitudinal behavior will:
choices: Maintain their original attitudes without any measurable change in beliefs or cognitive orientation
Show the MOST attitude change because insufficient external justification drives internal attribution
Show substantially less attitude change compared to those who received large external justification
Become increasingly more committed to strengthening and defending their original pre-existing attitude
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Insufficient justification effect: when external justification is minimal, people must internally justify their behavior by changing their attitudes. More justification = less dissonance = less attitude change.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Dissonance produces attitude change — people don't simply maintain conflicting cognitions.
(C) LARGE justification reduces dissonance externally, producing LESS attitude change (the opposite).
(D) Counter-attitudinal behavior with insufficient justification weakens the original attitude.
references: Festinger, L., & Carlsmith, J. M. (1959). Cognitive consequences of forced compliance. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 58(2), 203–210. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0041593

reviewQueue.prompt: The negativity bias refers to:
choices: A personality trait of chronic pessimism characterized by always thinking negatively about everything
The tendency for negative information to have greater psychological impact than equivalent positive information
A specific clinical diagnostic symptom exclusively associated with major depressive disorder presentations
A cognitive distortion identified within cognitive behavioral therapy such as catastrophizing or filtering
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Negativity bias: negative events, information, and emotions are processed more deeply, remembered better, and weighted more heavily in decision-making than equivalent positive information. This is an evolved adaptive mechanism.

Why others are wrong:
(A) It's not a personality trait of pessimism — it's a universal cognitive tendency.
(C) While depression amplifies negativity, the negativity bias is a normal phenomenon present in everyone.
(D) CBT identifies cognitive distortions — the negativity bias is a broader cognitive science finding.
references: Rozin, P., & Royzman, E. B. (2001). Negativity bias, negativity dominance, and contagion. Personality and Social Psychology Review, 5(4), 296–320. https://doi.org/10.1207/S15327957PSPR0504_2

reviewQueue.prompt: Working memory capacity is approximately:
choices: Essentially unlimited in storage capacity with no meaningful constraints on information maintenance
Approximately 4±1 chunks of information according to Cowan's updated capacity estimate research
At least 50 discrete items maintained simultaneously within the working memory buffer system
Only a single item at a time with absolutely no capacity for maintaining multiple representations
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Cowan's updated estimate: working memory holds approximately 4±1 chunks (revising Miller's classic 7±2). Chunking and rehearsal strategies can effectively increase functional capacity.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Working memory is severely capacity-limited — that's its defining feature.
(C) 50 items far exceeds working memory capacity.
(D) While attention may focus on 1 item, working memory can maintain ~4 items simultaneously.
references: Cowan, N. (2001). The magical number 4 in short-term memory: A reconsideration of mental storage capacity. Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 24(1), 87–114. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0140525X01003922

reviewQueue.prompt: Prototype theory of categorization proposes that:
choices: Categories have strict boundaries with necessary and sufficient features
People categorize items based on similarity to a typical example (prototype) of the category
All members of a category are equally representative
Categories are innate and unchangeable
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Rosch's prototype theory: categories are organized around the most representative/typical member (prototype). Category membership is graded — some members are more typical than others (robin is more 'bird' than penguin).

Why others are wrong:
