(A) Strict boundaries = classical/definitional view of categories, which prototype theory replaced
(C) Category members vary in typicality — prototypical members are more representative
(D) Categories are learned and culturally influenced, not entirely innate
references: Rosch, E. (1975). Cognitive representations of semantic categories. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 104(3), 192–233. https://doi.org/10.1037/0096-3445.104.3.192

reviewQueue.prompt: Schemas (Bartlett) influence memory by:
choices: Specifically guaranteeing explicitly perfect structural consistent accurate profoundly formal reliable objective memory recall
Guiding encoding and retrieval, leading to both efficient processing and systematic distortions that fit existing knowledge structures
Demonstrating absolutely minimal measurable observable tangible practical direct functional effect upon general memory recall
Exclusively specifically selectively influencing only deeply established formally rigid active procedural motor memory systems
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Bartlett (Remembering, 1932): schemas help us process and organize information efficiently but also cause distortions — we fill in gaps with schema-consistent information and distort memories to match expectations.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Schemas cause systematic distortions — they don't ensure perfect recall
(C) Schemas profoundly affect what we attend to, encode, and retrieve
(D) Schemas primarily affect DECLARATIVE memory (semantic and episodic), not just procedural
references: Bartlett, F. C. (1932). Remembering: A study in experimental and social psychology. Cambridge University Press.

reviewQueue.prompt: Learned helplessness (Seligman) occurs when:
choices: Organisms consistently successfully explicitly learn to actively deliberately rapidly escape all severe aversive situations
Organisms exposed to uncontrollable aversive events learn their actions are futile and stop trying despite possible escape
Organisms paradoxically consistently systematically become significantly profoundly more motivated following distinct failure
The expressed pervasive deep psychological helplessness is always strictly inherently purely fundamentally innately biological
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Seligman & Maier: dogs exposed to inescapable shocks later failed to escape when escape was possible. Extended to human depression: belief that outcomes are uncontrollable leads to motivational, cognitive, and emotional deficits.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Active escape = normal learning; learned helplessness is the FAILURE to escape
(C) Learned helplessness produces DECREASED motivation, not increased motivation after failure
(D) Learned helplessness is LEARNED through experience with uncontrollable events, not innate
references: Seligman, M. E. P. (1975). Helplessness: On depression, development, and death. W. H. Freeman.

reviewQueue.prompt: Intrinsic motivation (Deci & Ryan) is enhanced by satisfaction of:
choices: Strictly fundamental absolute monetary needs
Autonomy, competence, and relatedness needs
Strictly intense absolute competitive needs
Strictly specific basic external approval
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Self-determination theory (SDT): intrinsic motivation flourishes when three basic psychological needs are met — autonomy (sense of choice/control), competence (feeling effective), and relatedness (connection to others).

Why others are wrong:
(A) Monetary rewards are EXTRINSIC and can actually UNDERMINE intrinsic motivation (overjustification effect)
(C) Competition can UNDERMINE intrinsic motivation if it reduces autonomy and competence perceptions
(D) External approval is an extrinsic motivator — SDT emphasizes internal satisfaction of basic needs
references: Deci, E. L., & Ryan, R. M. (2000). The 'what' and 'why' of goal pursuits: Human needs and the self-determination of behavior. Psychological Inquiry, 11(4), 227–268. https://doi.org/10.1207/S15327965PLI1104_01

reviewQueue.prompt: Dunning-Kruger effect describes:
choices: Highly proficient specialized trained experts dramatically systematically overestimating their own cognitive abilities
Low-ability individuals overestimating their competence, while high-ability individuals slightly underestimate theirs
Everyone uniformly consistently accurately assessing their own explicit precise specific actual cognitive abilities
A unique distinct psychological heuristic explicitly practically applying exclusively isolated to academic settings
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Dunning-Kruger: people with limited knowledge/skill lack the metacognitive ability to recognize their incompetence, leading to inflated self-assessments. Experts, conversely, assume others share their knowledge level and slightly underestimate their relative standing.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Experts tend to slightly UNDERESTIMATE their relative abilities, not overestimate
(C) The effect specifically demonstrates systematic INACCURACY in self-assessment
(D) The effect applies across domains (driving, grammar, logic, medicine, etc.), not just academics
references: Kruger, J., & Dunning, D. (1999). Unskilled and unaware of it: How difficulties in recognizing one's own incompetence lead to inflated self-assessments. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 77(6), 1121–1134. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.77.6.1121

reviewQueue.prompt: Mood-congruent memory refers to:
choices: Specific powerful memories robustly explicitly altering an individual's immediate active mood
The distinct tendency to constantly recall memories that match one's current emotional state
Exclusively distinctly reliably remembering solely objective profoundly positive historic events
Specific explicit objective autobiographical memories that are universally consistently accurate
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Mood-congruent memory: current mood facilitates retrieval of memories with matching emotional valence. When sad, negative memories are more accessible; when happy, positive memories are more accessible. Contributes to depression maintenance.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Mood-congruent memory is about mood FACILITATING recall of matching memories, not memories changing mood
(C) Any mood state (positive, negative, neutral) can facilitate mood-congruent recall
(D) Mood-congruent recall doesn't guarantee accuracy — it's about emotional matching, not truth
references: Bower, G. H. (1981). Mood and memory. American Psychologist, 36(2), 129–148. https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.36.2.129

reviewQueue.prompt: Baddeley's model of working memory includes:
choices: Only a single undifferentiated temporary short-term informational capacity storage buffer
The phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, central executive, and episodic buffer
An entirely completely unlimited expansive capacity for simultaneous cognitive processing
Only fully consolidated stable permanent structural long-term semantic memory components
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Baddeley & Hitch (1974, updated 2000): working memory has four components — phonological loop (verbal), visuospatial sketchpad (visual/spatial), central executive (attention controller), and episodic buffer (integrates information from multiple sources).

Why others are wrong:
(A) Baddeley proposed MULTIPLE subsystems, not a single buffer
(C) Working memory has LIMITED capacity (7 ± 2 items, or about 4 chunks)
(D) Working memory is distinct from long-term memory — it temporarily maintains and manipulates information
references: Baddeley, A. D. (2000). The episodic buffer: A new component of working memory? Trends in Cognitive Sciences, 4(11), 417–423. https://doi.org/10.1016/S1364-6613(00)01538-2

reviewQueue.prompt: Peak-end rule (Kahneman) states that:
choices: People systematically evaluate experiences equally across every single temporal moment
People evaluate experiences based primarily on the INTENSE peak and the ultimate ENDING
Endings are fundamentally completely clinically irrelevant to ultimate experience evaluation
Only explicitly intense positive peaks are consciously remembered after the experience ends
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Kahneman: retrospective evaluation of experiences is disproportionately influenced by two moments — the peak intensity (best or worst moment) and the end. Duration plays a surprisingly small role (duration neglect).

Why others are wrong:
(A) Moment-by-moment evaluation is how the 'experiencing self' works, but the 'remembering self' uses peak-end
(C) Endings are CRUCIAL — a good ending can improve evaluation of an otherwise unpleasant experience
(D) Both positive and negative peaks influence evaluation
references: Kahneman, D., Fredrickson, B. L., Schreiber, C. A., & Redelmeier, D. A. (1993). When more pain is preferred to less: Adding a better end. Psychological Science, 4(6), 401–405. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9280.1993.tb00589.x

reviewQueue.prompt: Semantic memory refers to:
choices: Autobiographical episodic memory strictly for highly specific personal life history events
General knowledge about the world, facts, concepts, and language independent of personal context
Implicit procedural nondeclarative motor skill memory developed over repeated active practice
Temporary transient sensory iconic and echoic memory trace duration lasting mere milliseconds
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Semantic memory (Tulving): organized knowledge about the world — facts, concepts, word meanings, and general knowledge. It's decontextualized (you know Paris is the capital of France without remembering WHEN you learned it).

Why others are wrong:
(A) Memory for personal events = episodic memory (autobiographical, contextualized)
(C) Motor skill memory = procedural memory (implicit/non-declarative)
(D) Millisecond sensory memory = sensory register (iconic for visual, echoic for auditory)
references: Tulving, E. (1972). Episodic and semantic memory. In E. Tulving & W. Donaldson (Eds.), Organization of memory (pp. 381–402). Academic Press.

reviewQueue.prompt: The weapons focus effect in eyewitness testimony refers to:
choices: Systematically improved overall memory capacity for all sensory details during threatening events
Eyewitnesses intensely focusing on a weapon, which IMPAIRS memory for other peripheral details
Witnesses universally always flawlessly and accurately identifying the specific correct weapon
The highly unusually low frequency of actual visible weapons appearing within true crime scenes
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Weapons focus (Loftus): the presence of a weapon narrows attention to the threat object, reducing encoding of peripheral details like the perpetrator's appearance. This leads to WORSE facial identification.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Weapon focus IMPAIRS overall detail memory by narrowing attention
(C) Witnesses may accurately recall the weapon but POORLY recall the perpetrator
(D) The effect is about the IMPACT of weapons on attention and memory, not their frequency
references: Loftus, E. F., Loftus, G. R., & Messo, J. (1987). Some facts about 'weapon focus.' Law and Human Behavior, 11(1), 55–62. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01044839

reviewQueue.prompt: The representativeness heuristic leads to errors when:
choices: People systematically correctly universally apply appropriate base rates across all situations
People erroneously judge probability based on similarity to a prototype rather than base rates
People systematically exclusively apply formal rigid algorithmic logic for all daily decisions
People completely fully actively deliberately entirely avoid utilizing any cognitive shortcuts
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Representativeness heuristic (Kahneman & Tversky): judging probability by resemblance to a category prototype. This ignores base rates, sample size, and regression to the mean (e.g., the 'Linda problem' — conjunction fallacy).

Why others are wrong:
(A) The error specifically occurs because people IGNORE base rates
(C) Heuristics ARE shortcuts that replace algorithms — the representativeness heuristic is a cognitive shortcut
(D) People commonly use heuristics — avoiding all shortcuts is rare and impractical
references: Tversky, A., & Kahneman, D. (1974). Judgment under uncertainty: Heuristics and biases. Science, 185(4157), 1124–1131. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.185.4157.1124

reviewQueue.prompt: The representativeness heuristic leads to:
choices: Always correct and accurate probability judgments in every decision-making context and situation
Judging probability by similarity to a prototype which can lead to base rate neglect and conjunction fallacy
Perfect statistical reasoning that consistently produces optimal Bayesian probability estimates and updates
Successfully avoiding all cognitive heuristics entirely and relying only on formal logical analysis methods
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Representativeness heuristic (Tversky & Kahneman): judging probability by similarity to a mental prototype. Errors: ignoring base rates, conjunction fallacy.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Heuristics often lead to systematic errors.
(C) Heuristics are mental shortcuts that bypass statistical reasoning.
(D) Everyone uses heuristics — they can't be entirely avoided.
references: Tversky, A., & Kahneman, D. (1974). Judgment under uncertainty: Heuristics and biases. Science, 185(4157), 1124–1131. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.185.4157.1124

reviewQueue.prompt: Zimbardo's Stanford Prison Experiment primarily demonstrated:
choices: The stability of personality traits across situations
The power of social roles and situational forces on behavior
That obedience to authority is genetic
The effectiveness of punishment
reviewQueue.rationale:
Zimbardo's SPE showed how rapidly assigned social roles (guard/prisoner) shaped behavior, demonstrating the power of situational forces over individual personality traits.

Why others are wrong:
(A) The SPE showed the INSTABILITY of behavior across situations — personality traits were overridden by roles
(C) Obedience to authority relates to Milgram's study — Zimbardo focused on ROLE behavior, not obedience to a specific authority
(D) The SPE wasn't about punishment effectiveness — it was about how social roles and situations control behavior
references: Zimbardo, P. G. (2007). The Lucifer effect: Understanding how good people turn evil. Random House. See also: Haney, C., Banks, W. C., & Zimbardo, P. G. (1973). Interpersonal dynamics in a simulated prison. International Journal of Criminology and Penology, 1, 69–97.

reviewQueue.prompt: In Sherif's Robbers Cave experiment, intergroup conflict was BEST reduced by:
choices: Separating the groups
Introducing superordinate goals
Punishing aggressive behavior
Individual therapy sessions
reviewQueue.rationale:
Sherif found that superordinate goals (objectives requiring cooperation between groups) were most effective at reducing intergroup conflict — not mere contact or separation.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Separating the groups maintained hostility — physical distance didn't reduce prejudice
(C) Punishing aggression addresses symptoms, not the underlying intergroup dynamics
(D) Individual therapy wasn't used and wouldn't address the group-level dynamics driving the conflict
references: Sherif, M., Harvey, O. J., White, B. J., Hood, W. R., & Sherif, C. W. (1961). Intergroup conflict and cooperation: The Robbers Cave experiment. University of Oklahoma Book Exchange.

reviewQueue.prompt: Self-serving bias is MOST likely when:
choices: People experience failure
People experience success in public
People are in collectivist cultures
People are clinically depressed
reviewQueue.rationale:
Self-serving bias (attributing success internally, failure externally) is strongest in public success situations. It's less prominent in collectivist cultures and often reversed in depression.

Why others are wrong:
(A) During failure, self-serving bias attributes externally — it's strongest during SUCCESS
(C) Collectivist cultures show LESS self-serving bias due to emphasis on modesty and group harmony
(D) Depression is associated with REVERSED self-serving bias — depressed individuals often blame themselves
references: Miller, D. T., & Ross, M. (1975). Self-serving biases in the attribution of causality: Fact or fiction? Psychological Bulletin, 82(2), 213–225. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0076486

reviewQueue.prompt: A person publicly agrees with a group but privately disagrees. This is an example of:
choices: Internalization
Compliance
Identification
Conversion
reviewQueue.rationale:
Compliance (Kelman): public conformity without private acceptance. The person goes along to avoid conflict or gain reward but doesn't truly change their beliefs.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Internalization = private acceptance with genuine belief change — the opposite of compliance
(C) Identification = conforming based on desire to be like the group — involves some private acceptance
(D) Conversion = genuine attitude change (usually from minority influence), not superficial public agreement
references: Kelman, H. C. (1958). Compliance, identification, and internalization: Three processes of attitude change. Journal of Conflict Resolution, 2(1), 51–60. https://doi.org/10.1177/002200275800200106

reviewQueue.prompt: An African American student performs worse on a test described as measuring intelligence than on the same test described as a problem-solving exercise. This BEST illustrates:
choices: Test bias
Stereotype threat
Low motivation
Inadequate education
reviewQueue.rationale:
Steele & Aronson: framing the test as diagnostic of intelligence activates stereotype threat, causing anxiety that impairs performance. Same test without that framing shows no decrement.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Test bias involves differential prediction across groups — here the SAME test produced different results based on framing
(C) Low motivation doesn't explain why performance changed based on how the test was described
(D) Inadequate education would affect performance equally regardless of how the test was framed
references: Steele, C. M., & Aronson, J. (1995). Stereotype threat and the intellectual test performance of African Americans. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 69(5), 797–811. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.69.5.797

reviewQueue.prompt: Collectivist cultures are MOST likely to emphasize:
choices: Individual achievement and self-reliance
Group harmony and interdependence
Competition between family members
Personal autonomy above all
reviewQueue.rationale:
Collectivist cultures (common in East Asia, Latin America) prioritize group harmony, interdependence, familial obligations, and fitting in over individual achievement.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Individual achievement and self-reliance = individualistic culture values (US, Western Europe)
(C) Competition between family members is discouraged in collectivist cultures
(D) Personal autonomy above all = individualistic priority, not collectivistic
references: Triandis, H. C. (1995). Individualism and collectivism. Westview Press.

reviewQueue.prompt: Implicit bias is BEST measured by:
choices: Self-report questionnaires
The Implicit Association Test (IAT)
Direct behavioral observation only
Clinical interview
reviewQueue.rationale:
The IAT measures reaction time differences in pairing concepts (e.g., race + evaluative words), revealing automatic associations not captured by explicit self-report measures.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Self-report measures capture EXPLICIT attitudes — people may not be aware of or willing to report implicit biases
(C) Behavioral observation can reveal bias but isn't the most controlled/standardized measurement method
(D) Clinical interviews capture conscious self-report, not implicit/automatic associations
references: Greenwald, A. G., McGhee, D. E., & Schwartz, J. L. K. (1998). Measuring individual differences in implicit cognition: The Implicit Association Test. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 74(6), 1464–1480. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.74.6.1464

reviewQueue.prompt: The foot-in-the-door technique is based on:
choices: Scarcity principle
Commitment and consistency
Authority
Reciprocity
reviewQueue.rationale:
Foot-in-the-door: start with small request, then escalate. Based on commitment/consistency (Cialdini) — once people comply with a small request, they see themselves as cooperative and agree to larger ones.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Scarcity principle = increased value of limited items, not sequential request compliance
(C) Authority = compliance based on perceived expertise/power, not self-consistency
(D) Reciprocity = returning favors, which underlies door-in-the-face, not foot-in-the-door
references: Freedman, J. L., & Fraser, S. C. (1966). Compliance without pressure: The foot-in-the-door technique. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 4(2), 195–202. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0023552

reviewQueue.prompt: Deindividuation is MOST likely to occur when:
choices: People are alone
People are identifiable
People are in large groups with anonymity
People are in leadership roles
reviewQueue.rationale:
Deindividuation occurs in large groups with anonymity and arousal, reducing self-awareness and increasing impulsive, uninhibited behavior (e.g., mobs, online anonymity).

Why others are wrong:
(A) People alone maintain self-awareness — deindividuation requires group anonymity
(B) Being identifiable PREVENTS deindividuation — identification increases accountability
(D) Leaders are typically MORE identifiable and self-aware, reducing deindividuation
references: Zimbardo, P. G. (1969). The human choice: Individuation, reason, and order vs. deindividuation, impulse, and chaos. Nebraska Symposium on Motivation, 17, 237–307.

reviewQueue.prompt: Bystander apathy (bystander effect) is MOST influenced by:
choices: The objective physical severity of the emergency situation witnessed by the observing bystanders
Diffusion of responsibility among witnesses and pluralistic ignorance about the situation's urgency
The biological sex or gender presentation of the victim requiring emergency assistance in public
The specific geographic time of day when the emergency event occurs in the bystanders' vicinity
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Darley & Latané: bystanders are less likely to help as group size increases due to diffusion of responsibility (someone else will help) and pluralistic ignorance (everyone looks calm, so it must not be serious).

Why others are wrong:
(A) Even severe emergencies show bystander effects — severity alone doesn't override the social dynamics.
(C) Victim gender may play a minor role but isn't the primary mechanism driving the bystander effect.
(D) Time of day can affect presence of bystanders but isn't the psychological mechanism.
references: Darley, J. M., & Latané, B. (1968). Bystander intervention in emergencies: Diffusion of responsibility. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 8(4), 377–383. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0025589

reviewQueue.prompt: The fundamental attribution error is the tendency to:
choices: Attribute other people's behavior primarily to situational and environmental contextual factors
Overattribute others' behavior to dispositional factors while underestimating situational influences
Always blame oneself for all negative outcomes regardless of external contributing circumstances
Make perfectly accurate and unbiased causal inferences about the determinants of behavior
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) FAE (correspondence bias): when explaining OTHERS' behavior, people overweight personality/character and underweight situational constraints. Less common in collectivist cultures.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Attributing to situational factors = the OPPOSITE tendency (actor-observer bias).
(C) Always blaming oneself = depressive attributional style, not the FAE.
(D) The FAE is specifically an attribution ERROR — it produces systematic inaccuracy.
references: Ross, L. (1977). The intuitive psychologist and his shortcomings. In L. Berkowitz (Ed.), Advances in experimental social psychology (Vol. 10, pp. 173–220). Academic Press.

reviewQueue.prompt: Stereotype threat affects performance by:
choices: Increasing intrinsic motivation and enhancing task engagement through heightened arousal activation
Consuming working memory resources through anxiety, rumination, and excessive self-monitoring processes
Improving test-taking skills through increased vigilance and enhanced strategic cognitive processing
Having no demonstrable measurable effect on cognitive performance in any well-controlled study
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Stereotype threat impairs performance through multiple mechanisms: increased anxiety, rumination, self-monitoring, and working memory depletion — all of which divert cognitive resources from the task.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Stereotype threat typically DECREASES effective motivation by creating debilitating anxiety.
(C) It IMPAIRS test performance, not improves test-taking skills.
(D) Meta-analyses confirm significant, measurable effects on performance across many studies.
references: Steele, C. M. (1997). A threat in the air: How stereotypes shape intellectual identity and performance. American Psychologist, 52(6), 613–629. https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.52.6.613

reviewQueue.prompt: Milgram's obedience studies found that approximately what percentage of participants administered the maximum shock?
choices: Approximately 10% of participants administered the maximum voltage in the baseline condition
Approximately 35% of participants administered the maximum voltage in the baseline condition
Approximately 65% of participants administered the maximum voltage in the baseline condition
Approximately 95% of participants administered the maximum voltage in the baseline condition
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (C) In Milgram's baseline condition, approximately 65% of participants administered the maximum 450-volt shock when instructed by the authority figure — far exceeding initial predictions by psychiatrists (~1%).

Why others are wrong:
(A) 10% dramatically underestimates — this was the expert prediction, not the actual result.
(B) 35% underestimates the actual compliance rate.
(D) 95% overestimates — about 35% DID refuse at some point.
references: Milgram, S. (1963). Behavioral study of obedience. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 67(4), 371–378. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0040525

reviewQueue.prompt: In-group bias (in-group favoritism) occurs even in:
choices: Only real-world political and economic intergroup conflict situations involving scarce resource competition
Only between established racial and ethnic groups with long historical intergroup contact histories
Minimal group paradigm conditions based on entirely arbitrary and meaningless categorization criteria
Only structured therapeutic group settings supervised by a trained mental health professional
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (C) Tajfel's minimal group paradigm: even when groups are formed on trivial/random criteria (e.g., coin flip, art preference), members favor their in-group — demonstrating that mere categorization is sufficient for bias.

Why others are wrong:
(A) In-group bias occurs even without any conflict or competition.
(B) In-group bias extends far beyond ethnic groups — any social categorization can trigger it.
(D) In-group bias is a general social phenomenon, not limited to therapy contexts.
references: Tajfel, H., Billig, M. G., Bundy, R. P., & Flament, C. (1971). Social categorization and intergroup behaviour. European Journal of Social Psychology, 1(2), 149–178. https://doi.org/10.1002/ejsp.2420010202

reviewQueue.prompt: Scapegoat theory proposes that prejudice increases when:
choices: People are highly well-educated and possess sophisticated critical thinking analytical abilities
Frustrated individuals displace aggression onto vulnerable outgroups who serve as convenient targets
Economic conditions substantially improve and material prosperity increases for all population groups
People possess high self-esteem and strong positive self-concept reducing social comparison needs
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Scapegoat theory (based on frustration-aggression hypothesis): when people experience frustration (economic hardship, stress), they displace aggression onto vulnerable, less powerful groups who become scapegoats.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Education can REDUCE prejudice, not increase it.
(C) Improving economic conditions would REDUCE frustration and scapegoating.
(D) Low self-esteem (not high) is associated with greater need for outgroup derogation.
references: Dollard, J., Miller, N. E., Doob, L. W., Mowrer, O. H., & Sears, R. R. (1939). Frustration and aggression. Yale University Press.

reviewQueue.prompt: Cognitive dissonance increases with:
choices: Greater structure objective formal external justification for the target behaviors
Greater perceived choice and personal responsibility for the counter-attitudinal behavior
Fundamentally significantly noticeably lower core importance of the specific key issue
Specifically whenever the targeted clinical behavioral manifestation is strictly forced
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Dissonance is maximized when people feel they FREELY CHOSE the counter-attitudinal behavior with minimal external justification. High choice + low justification = maximum dissonance = maximum attitude change.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Greater external justification REDUCES dissonance (the person has a ready explanation for the behavior)
(C) Greater importance of the issue INCREASES dissonance, not decreases it
(D) Forced behavior provides external justification, REDUCING dissonance
references: Festinger, L. (1957). A theory of cognitive dissonance. Stanford University Press.

reviewQueue.prompt: Acculturation strategies (Berry) include all EXCEPT:
choices: Integration
Assimilation
Marginalization
Differentiation
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (D) Berry's four acculturation strategies are: Integration (maintaining heritage culture + adopting host), Assimilation (adopting host, abandoning heritage), Separation (maintaining heritage, rejecting host), and Marginalization (neither). 'Differentiation' is not one of Berry's categories.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Integration IS one of Berry's strategies — maintaining both cultures
(B) Assimilation IS one of Berry's strategies — adopting the dominant culture
(C) Marginalization IS one of Berry's strategies — rejecting both cultures
references: Berry, J. W. (1997). Immigration, acculturation, and adaptation. Applied Psychology, 46(1), 5–34. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1464-0597.1997.tb01087.x

reviewQueue.prompt: The actor-observer bias states that:
choices: Independent active actors and formal independent observers correctly reliably consistently exactly agree upon targeted specific identified exact causal attributions
Actors tend to attribute their OWN behavior to situations, while observers attribute the same behavior to the actor's disposition
Basic human psychological subjects consistently flawlessly definitively explicitly functionally seamlessly avoid making any formal clinical valid attributional errors
Targeted specific active actors objectively seamlessly carefully essentially dependably perfectly completely efficiently accurately identify their exact clinical dispositions
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Actor-observer asymmetry: we attribute our OWN behavior to external/situational factors but attribute OTHERS' behavior to internal/dispositional factors. The information available differs for actors vs. observers.

Why others are wrong:
(A) The bias exists precisely because actors and observers DISAGREE on attributions
(C) The bias IS an attributional 'error' — a systematic asymmetry in causal attribution
(D) This bias is universal across people, not limited to psychologists
references: Jones, E. E., & Nisbett, R. E. (1971). The actor and the observer: Divergent perceptions of the causes of behavior. General Learning Press.

reviewQueue.prompt: Asch's conformity studies found that conformity INCREASED with:
choices: Significantly rigorously dramatically systematically completely effectively decreased optimal formal core central clinical overall structural target group size elements
Unanimous group disagreement with the participant
Precisely whenever active explicitly formally targeted psychological specific experimental test clinical participant research components successfully strictly responded absolutely privately directly

Explicitly whenever the targeted formal given operational specific experimental evaluation assessment diagnostic functional targeted test core analytical operational behavioral evaluation test trial task was extremely simple clearly essentially overtly explicitly easy structurally
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Asch found conformity highest when the confederate group was unanimous. Even ONE dissenter dramatically reduced conformity. Group size increased conformity up to about 3-5 members.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Conformity INCREASED with group size (up to about 3-5 members), not decreased
(C) Private responding DECREASED conformity — public responses increased it
(D) Easy tasks with obvious answers DECREASED conformity (Asch used line-length tasks where the correct answer was clear)
references: Asch, S. E. (1956). Studies of independence and conformity: I. A minority of one against a unanimous majority. Psychological Monographs, 70(9), 1–70. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0093718

reviewQueue.prompt: Prosocial behavior is MOST likely when:
choices: The specific potential active helper is currently in a severe hurry
The targeted specific social situational context is highly ambiguous
The potential helper perceives similarity with the person in need
There are many other additional specific passive bystanders present
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (C) Perceived similarity (in-group membership, shared identity) increases empathy and willingness to help. Other factors: clear emergency, sole witness, mood, personal norms, and cost-benefit analysis.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Being in a hurry DECREASES helping (Darley & Batson's Good Samaritan study)
(B) Ambiguity DECREASES helping through pluralistic ignorance
(D) Many bystanders DECREASE helping through diffusion of responsibility (bystander effect)
references: Batson, C. D. (2011). Altruism in humans. Oxford University Press.

reviewQueue.prompt: The self-fulfilling prophecy occurs when:
choices: Specific targeted structural behavioral early objective predictions are effectively systematically wrong
A false expectation leads to behaviors that cause the expectation to safely, reliably, and consistently come true
Individuals completely accurately explicitly and functionally formally specifically predict the exact literal future
Exclusively pure targeted explicit strict robust specific behavioral positive psychological expectations come fully true
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Merton (1948): a self-fulfilling prophecy begins with a false definition of a situation that evokes new behavior which makes the original false conception come true. Examples: Rosenthal's teacher expectancy effect, bank runs.

Why others are wrong:
(A) The prediction becomes TRUE because behavior changes to confirm it
(C) The key is that the prediction was initially FALSE but becomes true through behavioral changes
(D) Both positive (Pygmalion effect) and negative (Golem effect) expectations can be self-fulfilling
references: Merton, R. K. (1948). The self-fulfilling prophecy. The Antioch Review, 8(2), 193–210.

reviewQueue.prompt: System justification theory proposes that:
choices: Targeted active demographic human populations firmly strictly strongly consistently strictly prefer successfully reliably smoothly cleanly specifically completely actively strongly actively comprehensively actively completely exactly structurally actively to structurally deeply gracefully thoroughly nicely properly alter the base actual explicit valid existing central formal system
People are motivated to defend and justify existing social, economic, and political arrangements, even when they are personally disadvantaged

Specifically entirely robust explicitly exclusively rigorously solely targeted explicit successfully fully identified strictly isolated privileged formal explicit demographic groups purely effectively efficiently squarely support the explicit defined structural distinct systemic pure explicit direct baseline status quo entirely seamlessly

Fundamental central discrete formal explicit recognized targeted independent strictly pure clinical external identified formal strict institutionalized target specific societal structured frameworks reliably correctly appropriately successfully firmly essentially securely cleanly dependably smoothly practically securely actively fully represent completely purely formal just optimal organizations
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Jost & Banaji: system justification is a psychological need to perceive existing systems as fair, legitimate, and desirable. Even disadvantaged group members may rationalize inequality to maintain a sense of predictability and control.

Why others are wrong:
(A) System justification theory specifically predicts RESISTANCE to change, not desire for it
(C) Both privileged AND disadvantaged groups engage in system justification — that's a key finding
(D) The theory is about PERCEIVING systems as just, not claiming they actually are
references: Jost, J. T., & Banaji, M. R. (1994). The role of stereotyping in system-justification and the production of false consciousness. British Journal of Social Psychology, 33(1), 1–27. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.2044-8309.1994.tb01008.x

reviewQueue.prompt: Social loafing is MOST likely when:
choices: Individual contributions can be identified
Group tasks make individual efforts identifiable
Individual contributions are pooled and anonymous
Group size is very small
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (C) Social loafing (Latané et al.): people exert less effort on collective tasks when their individual contribution cannot be identified. Reduced accountability leads to reduced effort ('free riding').

Why others are wrong:
(A) When individual contributions ARE identifiable, social loafing DECREASES (evaluation apprehension)
(B) Making efforts identifiable REDUCES social loafing — that's a mitigation strategy
(D) Very small groups (2-3) show less loafing because individual contributions are more visible
references: Latané, B., Williams, K., & Harkins, S. (1979). Many hands make light the work: The causes and consequences of social loafing. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 37(6), 822–832. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.37.6.822

reviewQueue.prompt: The elaboration likelihood model (ELM, Petty & Cacioppo) proposes:
choices: Only one single exclusive route to achieving profound lasting cognitive persuasion
Two routes: central (careful evaluation) and peripheral (superficial cue reliance)
Authentic long-term cognitive persuasion is fundamentally completely impossible
Logical structured arguments never matter during authentic interpersonal persuasion
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) ELM: central route — high motivation/ability → careful, thoughtful evaluation of argument quality → durable attitude change. Peripheral route — low motivation/ability → reliance on superficial cues → temporary change.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Two routes exist, not one — and which is used depends on motivation and ability
(C) Persuasion is well-documented and predictable under the right conditions
(D) Arguments matter greatly in the CENTRAL route — when people are motivated to scrutinize
references: Petty, R. E., & Cacioppo, J. T. (1986). The elaboration likelihood model of persuasion. In L. Berkowitz (Ed.), Advances in experimental social psychology (Vol. 19, pp. 123–205). Academic Press.

reviewQueue.prompt: Relative deprivation theory proposes that social unrest results from:
choices: Strictly measured absolute quantifiable poverty levels documented within the population
People's PERCEPTION that they are worse off compared to others, not objective conditions
Complete absolute psychological satisfaction with one's personal physical circumstances
Exclusively intense overwhelming historically driven macro-level external political forces
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Relative deprivation (Stouffer, Runciman): dissatisfaction arises from perceived discrepancy between what one HAS and what one EXPECTS to have (comparing to reference groups). Revolutions often occur when conditions are improving but expectations rise faster.

Why others are wrong:
(A) ABSOLUTE poverty doesn't always predict unrest — PERCEIVED relative disadvantage does
(C) Satisfaction would reduce social unrest, not create it
(D) While politics matter, relative deprivation is a psychological/perceptual process within individuals
references: Runciman, W. G. (1966). Relative deprivation and social justice. Routledge & Kegan Paul.

reviewQueue.prompt: Social facilitation occurs when the presence of others:
choices: Consistently unequivocally universally impairs overall baseline task performance
ENHANCES performance on simple/well-learned tasks but IMPAIRS complex/novel tasks
Consistently demonstrates absolutely zero empirical measurable effect on performance
Exclusively strictly applies only to highly competitive organized team physical sports
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Zajonc (1965): others' presence increases arousal, which facilitates dominant responses. For simple/practiced tasks, the dominant response is correct → enhanced performance. For complex/new tasks, errors are dominant → impaired performance.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Others' presence ENHANCES performance on simple tasks — it doesn't always impair
(C) Social facilitation demonstrates significant effects on performance
(D) Social facilitation has been documented across many settings (work, education, athletics, even cockroaches)
references: Zajonc, R. B. (1965). Social facilitation. Science, 149(3681), 269–274. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.149.3681.269

reviewQueue.prompt: Intergroup anxiety refers to:
choices: Intense pervasive clinical anxiety focused exclusively about one's own specific ingroup
Anxiety and threat experienced when anticipating interactions with outgroup members
A highly severe formal diagnosed clinical anxiety disorder requiring immediate treatment
Intense specific situational performance anxiety occurring during standardized group tests
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Intergroup anxiety (Stephan & Stephan): apprehension about cross-group interactions — fear of being embarrassed, rejected, or misunderstood. It can lead to avoidance of intergroup contact and increased prejudice.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Intergroup anxiety is about interactions WITH outgroup members, not anxiety about one's own group
(C) It's a normal social-psychological phenomenon, not a clinical disorder
(D) Test anxiety is a separate construct related to evaluation apprehension
references: Stephan, W. G., & Stephan, C. W. (1985). Intergroup anxiety. Journal of Social Issues, 41(3), 157–175. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-4560.1985.tb01134.x

reviewQueue.prompt: Attribution theory (Heider, Weiner) examines how people:
choices: Superficially assign distinct physical sensory attributes systematically to daily objects
Explain the causes of behavior—attributing events to internal or external situational factors
Consistently inherently successfully reliably make perfectly accurate causal social judgments
Exclusively rigidly uniquely apply formal advanced statistical reasoning to social phenomena
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Attribution theory: how people explain causality. Heider distinguished internal (person) vs. external (situation). Weiner added dimensions: stability (stable/unstable), controllability, and locus — creating a 3-dimensional model of causal attribution.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Attribution theory is about CAUSAL explanations for behavior, not physical attributes of objects
(C) Attribution processes involve systematic BIASES (FAE, self-serving bias), not just accurate judgments
(D) People use heuristics and biases, not exclusively statistical reasoning, in making attributions
references: Weiner, B. (1985). An attributional theory of achievement motivation and emotion. Psychological Review, 92(4), 548–573. https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.92.4.548

reviewQueue.prompt: Conformity is REDUCED by:
choices: Systematically continuously actively increasing the total group size indefinitely
Having at least one ally or dissenter who explicitly definitively breaks unanimity
Deliberately structurally actively making the correct desired answer more ambiguous
Significantly directly aggressively increasing the overall prestige of the majority
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Asch: even ONE dissenter dramatically reduces conformity (from ~37% to ~5%). The ally need not give the correct answer — merely breaking unanimity empowers the participant to disagree.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Conformity increases with group size but plateaus around 3-5 members
(C) Increased ambiguity INCREASES reliance on others, which INCREASES conformity
(D) Higher prestige of the majority INCREASES conformity (greater informational influence)
references: Asch, S. E. (1956). Studies of independence and conformity: I. A minority of one against a unanimous majority. Psychological Monographs, 70(9), 1–70.

reviewQueue.prompt: Cultural dimensions theory (Hofstede) includes:
choices: Only one single primary foundational dimension explaining global societal behavior
Multiple dimensions including individualism, power distance, and uncertainty avoidance
Strictly explicitly exclusively focused purely entirely upon standard Western cultural values
Universal behavioral developmental dimensions that are entirely biologically determined
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Hofstede's original four dimensions (later expanded to six): individualism-collectivism, power distance, uncertainty avoidance, masculinity-femininity, long-term orientation, and indulgence-restraint. Used to compare national cultures.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Hofstede identified multiple dimensions, not just one
(C) Hofstede studied cultures worldwide (originally 40+ countries with IBM employees)
(D) Cultural dimensions are socially constructed and historically developed, not biologically determined
references: Hofstede, G. (2001). Culture's consequences: Comparing values, behaviors, institutions, and organizations across nations (2nd ed.). Sage Publications.

reviewQueue.prompt: The sleeper effect in persuasion occurs when:
choices: Overall message persuasion is fundamentally phenomenally strongest strictly immediately after the message
A message from a LOW-credibility source becomes MORE persuasive over time as the source is forgotten
Verbal cognitive persuasion fundamentally functionally never works durably over extended temporal periods
Exclusively strictly highly credible recognized expert sources produce any lasting durable attitude change
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Sleeper effect: initially discounted messages (from non-credible sources) gain persuasive power over time because the source-message association decays faster than the message content itself.

Why others are wrong:
(A) The sleeper effect specifically describes persuasion that INCREASES over time, not strongest immediately
(C) The sleeper effect demonstrates persuasion CAN work (and increase) over time
(D) The sleeper effect shows that even low-credibility sources can produce lasting attitude change
references: Kumkale, G. T., & Albarracín, D. (2004). The sleeper effect in persuasion: A meta-analytic review. Psychological Bulletin, 130(1), 143–172. https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.130.1.143

reviewQueue.prompt: Group polarization refers to:
choices: Groups becoming significantly more moderate and compromised through structural discussion
Groups making more extreme decisions than individual members would initially make alone
Groups always fundamentally disagreeing and fracturing during complex decision processes
Perfectly equal opinion distribution emerging organically within cohesive team structures
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Group polarization: group discussion causes members to adopt more extreme positions in the direction they were already leaning. If individuals lean cautious → group becomes more cautious. If individuals lean risky → 'risky shift.' Mechanisms: persuasive arguments and social comparison.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Groups become MORE extreme, not more moderate
(C) Polarization occurs within like-minded groups, not through disagreement
(D) Opinions converge toward a more extreme average, not distribute equally
references: Stoner, J. A. F. (1968). Risky and cautious shifts in group decisions: The influence of widely held values. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 4(4), 442–459. See also: Moscovici, S., & Zavalloni, M. (1969). The group as a polarizer of attitudes. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 12(2), 125–135.

reviewQueue.prompt: Kohlberg's postconventional level includes:
choices: Punishment and obedience orientation
Good boy/good girl orientation
Social contract and universal ethical principles
Law and order orientation
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (C) Postconventional morality: Stage 5 = Social Contract (laws serve the greater good but can be changed through democratic process) and Stage 6 = Universal Ethical Principles (internalized principles of justice that may override laws).

Why others are wrong:
(A) Punishment/obedience = Stage 1 (preconventional level)
(B) Good boy/good girl = Stage 3 (conventional level)
(D) Law and order = Stage 4 (conventional level)
references: Kohlberg, L. (1981). Essays on moral development: Vol. 1. The philosophy of moral development. Harper & Row.

reviewQueue.prompt: Scaffolding in Vygotsky's theory refers to:
choices: Peer-only learning without any involvement from adults or more knowledgeable individuals
Temporary support from a more knowledgeable other that is gradually removed as competence grows
Innate predetermined learning abilities that unfold through biological maturational processes alone
Punishment-based instructional approaches that suppress incorrect responses through aversive consequences
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Scaffolding (Wood, Bruner, & Ross, building on Vygotsky): the MKO provides just enough support within the ZPD, gradually withdrawing it ('fading') as the child masters the skill independently.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Scaffolding involves a MORE KNOWLEDGEABLE other, not peer-only learning.
(C) Vygotsky emphasized SOCIAL learning, not innate abilities.
(D) Scaffolding is supportive and collaborative, not punishment-based.
references: Wood, D., Bruner, J. S., & Ross, G. (1976). The role of tutoring in problem solving. Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, 17(2), 89–100. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1469-7610.1976.tb00381.x

reviewQueue.prompt: Gilligan's critique of Kohlberg argued that:
choices: Women are fundamentally morally inferior to men across all stages of moral development
Kohlberg's model was biased toward justice orientation and neglected care orientation reasoning
Moral development simply doesn't exist as a meaningful psychological construct or process
Young children are completely incapable of engaging in any form of moral reasoning whatsoever
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Gilligan (In a Different Voice, 1982): Kohlberg's stages prioritized abstract justice principles (more common in male socialization) over care/relationship orientation (more common in female socialization), creating systematic bias.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Gilligan argued the opposite — women use a DIFFERENT but equally valid moral framework.
(C) Gilligan affirmed moral development exists but argued it takes different forms.
(D) This wasn't about children's capacity — it was about gender bias in the model.
references: Gilligan, C. (1982). In a different voice: Psychological theory and women's development. Harvard University Press.

reviewQueue.prompt: Resilience in child development is BEST predicted by:
choices: The complete absence of all adversity, stress, and challenging life circumstances throughout childhood
At least one stable, supportive relationship with a caring and consistently responsive adult
High socioeconomic status alone without consideration of interpersonal relationship quality factors
Exclusively genetic temperamental factors without any environmental or relational protective contributions
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Research consistently identifies a stable, nurturing relationship with at least one adult (parent, grandparent, teacher, mentor) as the single most important factor promoting resilience in adverse circumstances.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Resilience is defined as positive adaptation DESPITE adversity — absence of adversity doesn't demonstrate it.
(C) SES contributes but isn't sufficient — children can lack resilience without supportive relationships.
(D) Genetics contribute to temperamental resilience but aren't the sole or primary predictor.
references: Masten, A. S. (2014). Ordinary magic: Resilience in development. Guilford Press.

reviewQueue.prompt: The Strange Situation (Ainsworth) assesses:
choices: General cognitive developmental milestones using standardized Piagetian conservation tasks
Infant-caregiver attachment quality through structured separation and reunion observation
Exclusively inborn temperamental characteristics independent of any relational caregiver factors
Intellectual quotient potential as measured by standardized infant cognitive assessment batteries
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) The Strange Situation is a structured observational procedure assessing attachment through observed reactions to separations from and reunions with the caregiver, plus behavior with a stranger.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Cognitive development is assessed by Piagetian tasks, Bayley Scales, etc.
(C) While temperament influences behavior, the procedure measures the attachment RELATIONSHIP.
(D) IQ potential is assessed by cognitive intelligence tests, not attachment procedures.
references: Ainsworth, M. D. S., Blehar, M. C., Waters, E., & Wall, S. (1978). Patterns of attachment: A psychological study of the strange situation. Erlbaum.

reviewQueue.prompt: Emerging adulthood (Arnett) spans approximately:
choices: Ages 10-15 corresponding to early adolescent pubertal developmental transition period
Ages 18-25 characterized by identity exploration, instability, self-focus, and possibilities
Ages 30-40 corresponding to the early middle adulthood career consolidation period
Ages 55-65 corresponding to late middle adulthood pre-retirement planning transition period
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Arnett proposed emerging adulthood (ages 18-25) as a distinct developmental period characterized by identity exploration, instability, self-focus, feeling in-between, and a sense of possibilities.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Ages 10-15 = early adolescence.
(C) Ages 30-40 = early middle adulthood.
(D) Ages 55-65 = late middle adulthood approaching retirement.
references: Arnett, J. J. (2000). Emerging adulthood: A theory of development from the late teens through the twenties. American Psychologist, 55(5), 469–480. https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.55.5.469

reviewQueue.prompt: Object permanence is fully achieved by approximately:
choices: 4 months when infants begin tracking moving objects but don't yet search for hidden ones
8 months when partial object permanence emerges but A-not-B errors still commonly occur
18-24 months when invisible displacement understanding completes the sensorimotor achievement
Age 5 when preoperational thought enables symbolic representation of absent physical objects
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (C) Object permanence develops throughout the sensorimotor stage. Full object permanence (including invisible displacements — Stage 6) is achieved around 18-24 months. Partial object permanence begins around 8 months.

Why others are wrong:
(A) At 4 months, infants don't yet search for hidden objects.
(B) At 8 months, the A-not-B error shows incomplete object permanence.
(D) By age 5, object permanence is long established — it's a sensorimotor achievement.
references: Piaget, J. (1954). The construction of reality in the child (M. Cook, Trans.). Basic Books.

reviewQueue.prompt: The 'personal fable' (Elkind) refers to adolescents' belief that:
choices: They are completely ordinary and unremarkable compared to every other person around them
Their experiences and feelings are unique, special, and incomprehensible to anyone else
They have absolutely no audience observing or paying attention to their behavior at all
They are fundamentally invulnerable to all natural laws including physical mortality risks
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) The personal fable: adolescents believe their experiences are unique, special, and unlike anyone else's ('No one understands me'). Related to feelings of invulnerability ('It won't happen to ME').

Why others are wrong:
(A) The personal fable is about feeling EXTRAORDINARY, not ordinary.
(C) Having no audience is the opposite of the imaginary audience concept (Elkind).
(D) Invulnerability is a component of the personal fable but the fable is broader.
references: Elkind, D. (1967). Egocentrism in adolescence. Child Development, 38(4), 1025–1034. https://doi.org/10.2307/1127100

reviewQueue.prompt: Parallel play is typical of children around age:
choices: 6 months when infants primarily engage in solitary sensorimotor exploratory play activities
2-3 years when toddlers play alongside peers with similar materials but without direct interaction
6-7 years when children engage in cooperative rule-governed games with organized team structures
10-12 years when children participate in highly social organized competitive team sport activities
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Parallel play (Parten): children around 2-3 years play alongside other children with similar materials but without direct interaction or coordination. A transitional stage between solitary and cooperative play.

Why others are wrong:
(A) At 6 months, infants engage in solitary/onlooker play, not parallel play.
(C) By 6-7, children engage in cooperative and organized play.
(D) By 10-12, play is highly social, rule-governed, and organized.
references: Parten, M. B. (1932). Social participation among preschool children. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 27(3), 243–269. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0074524

reviewQueue.prompt: Gender identity is typically established by age:
choices: 1 year
3 years
10 years
18 years
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Most children develop a stable sense of gender identity (internal sense of being male, female, or another gender) by approximately age 3. Gender constancy (understanding gender doesn't change) develops by ages 6-7 (Kohlberg).

Why others are wrong:
(A) At 1 year, children don't yet have the cognitive development for stable gender identity
(C) Gender identity is established WELL before age 10
(D) Age 18 is far too late — gender identity is established in early childhood
references: Kohlberg, L. (1966). A cognitive-developmental analysis of children's sex-role concepts and attitudes. In E. E. Maccoby (Ed.), The development of sex differences (pp. 82–173). Stanford University Press.

reviewQueue.prompt: Kohlberg's conventional level of moral reasoning includes:
choices: Stage 1 (obedience/punishment orientation, emphasizing rigid compliance)
Stages 3 and 4 (interpersonal conformity and maintaining social order)
Stage 5 (social contract orientation, emphasizing relative broad rights)
Stage 6 (universal ethical principles, emphasizing internalized justice)
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Conventional level: Stage 3 (good boy/nice girl — maintaining relationships and approval) and Stage 4 (law and order — maintaining social systems and rules). Most adolescents and adults reason at this level.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Stage 1 = preconventional level (morality based on punishment avoidance)
(C) Stage 5 = postconventional level (social contract and individual rights)
(D) Stage 6 = postconventional level (universal ethical principles — very rare)
references: Kohlberg, L. (1981). The philosophy of moral development: Moral stages and the idea of justice. Harper & Row.

reviewQueue.prompt: The 'still face' paradigm (Tronick) demonstrates:
choices: Infants fundamentally lack the developmental cognitive active capacity to reliably notice subtle complex underlying caregiver emotions
Infants are highly sensitive to caregiver emotions — becoming distressed and trying to re-engage when caregivers show a still face
Infants consistently systematically demonstrate a fundamentally profound distinct preference for unfamiliar novel adult strangers
Infants definitively intrinsically lack any biological structural capability to independently regulate internal affective emotions
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Tronick's still face: when caregivers suddenly become emotionally unresponsive (blank face), infants initially try to re-engage (smiling, vocalizing), then become distressed (crying, gaze aversion). Demonstrates infants' sensitivity to social reciprocity.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Infants CLEARLY notice and are disturbed by caregiver emotional unavailability
(C) Infants show strong preference for their caregiver — distress at caregiver unresponsiveness proves this
(D) Infants DO attempt to regulate — they try to re-engage before becoming overwhelmed
references: Tronick, E., Als, H., Adamson, L., Wise, S., & Brazelton, T. B. (1978). The infant's response to entrapment between contradictory messages in face-to-face interaction. Journal of the American Academy of Child Psychiatry, 17(1), 1–13. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0002-7138(09)62273-1

reviewQueue.prompt: Fluid intelligence (Gf) typically:
choices: Consistently increases throughout the entire lifespan
Peaks in early adulthood and gradually declines with age
Demonstrates absolutely no relation to cognitive skills
Always comprehensively remains perfectly globally stable
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Cattell/Horn: fluid intelligence (novel reasoning, abstract problem-solving, pattern recognition) peaks around ages 20-30 and gradually declines. This is related to processing speed and working memory decline.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Crystallized intelligence increases throughout life — fluid intelligence declines
(C) Gf is strongly related to cognitive performance, especially on novel tasks
(D) Gf is one of the cognitive abilities MOST affected by aging — it doesn't remain stable
references: Horn, J. L., & Cattell, R. B. (1967). Age differences in fluid and crystallized intelligence. Acta Psychologica, 26, 107–129. https://doi.org/10.1016/0001-6918(67)90011-X

reviewQueue.prompt: Conservation tasks (Piaget) assess whether children understand that:
choices: Precious natural global resources should be actively preserved
Quantity remains the same despite changes in appearance/shape
Complex factual information should be fully stored permanently
Biological physical energy cannot be fully created or destroyed
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Piaget's conservation: understanding that quantity (number, mass, volume, liquid) is unchanged by superficial transformations (pouring into different-shaped containers, rearranging objects). Achieved in concrete operational stage (~7).

Why others are wrong:
(A) Environmental conservation is a different meaning of the word — Piaget's concept is about cognitive understanding
(C) Information storage = memory concepts, not Piagetian conservation
(D) Energy conservation is a physics law, not a developmental psychology concept
references: Piaget, J. (1965). The child's conception of number (C. Gattegno & F. M. Hodgson, Trans.). W. W. Norton.

reviewQueue.prompt: Preterm birth is defined as delivery before:
choices: 34 weeks gestation
37 weeks gestation
40 weeks gestation
42 weeks gestation
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Preterm birth: delivery before 37 completed weeks of gestation. Full-term = 39-40 weeks. Risk factors: maternal stress, infection, multiple gestation, substance use. Outcomes depend on gestational age and birth weight.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Before 34 weeks is 'late preterm' — preterm is defined from 37 weeks
(C) 40 weeks = average full-term pregnancy duration
(D) 42 weeks = post-term, which carries its own risks
references: World Health Organization. (2018). Preterm birth fact sheet. https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/preterm-birth

reviewQueue.prompt: The socioemotional selectivity theory (Carstensen) proposes that:
choices: Aging older adults systematically demonstrate significantly reduced fundamental care regarding intimate interpersonal relationships
As time perspective shortens with age, people prioritize emotionally meaningful relationships and goals over information-seeking
Aging older adults systematically explicitly prioritize establishing completely novel distinct superficial social acquaintances
Chronological biological age continually exerts absolutely zero distinct measurable impact upon overall social preferences
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Carstensen: when people perceive time as limited (not just in old age — also terminal illness, relocating), they prioritize emotional meaning over novelty or information acquisition. This explains older adults' smaller but more satisfying social networks.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Older adults care DEEPLY about relationships — they're more selective, not less caring
(C) Older adults tend to prefer familiar, emotionally close relationships over new acquaintances
(D) Age significantly affects social goals and partner preferences
references: Carstensen, L. L. (1992). Social and emotional patterns in adulthood: Support for socioemotional selectivity theory. Psychology and Aging, 7(3), 331–338. https://doi.org/10.1037/0882-7974.7.3.331

reviewQueue.prompt: Transitive inference (Piaget) is achieved during:
choices: Primary sensorimotor stage
Early preoperational stage
Concrete operational stage
Innate presence from birth
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (C) Transitive inference (if A > B and B > C, then A > C) requires logical-relational reasoning achieved in the concrete operational stage (~7-11). Preoperational children cannot perform this systematic comparison.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Sensorimotor infants haven't developed logical operations
(B) Preoperational children lack the logical reasoning for transitive inference
(D) Transitive inference develops through cognitive maturation — it's not present at birth
references: Piaget, J. (1952). The origins of intelligence in children (M. Cook, Trans.). International Universities Press.

reviewQueue.prompt: Goodness of fit (Thomas & Chess) refers to:
choices: Strictly uniquely defining exactly how well a developing child physically formally dresses
The match between a child's temperament and the demands/expectations of the environment
Exclusively explicitly focusing solely upon perfect rigid structural genetic compatibility
Strictly an abstract theoretical empirical statistical mathematical conceptual model only
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Thomas & Chess: developmental outcomes depend on how well the child's temperament matches environmental demands. A 'slow-to-warm-up' child does well with patient parents but may struggle with demanding, inflexible ones.

Why others are wrong:
(A) 'Fit' refers to temperament-environment match, not clothing
(C) Goodness of fit considers the interaction between temperament and environment, not just genetics
(D) While used in statistics, in developmental psychology it's specifically about temperament-environment match
references: Thomas, A., & Chess, S. (1977). Temperament and development. Brunner/Mazel.

reviewQueue.prompt: Marcia's identity status of foreclosure involves:
choices: Successfully explicitly exploring diverse broad options and thoroughly making a commitment
Making a commitment WITHOUT having explored alternatives, adopting values without questioning
Demonstrating absolutely no commitment alongside vigorous intense active identity exploration
Demonstrating absolutely complete total lack of both final commitment and active exploration
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Foreclosure: commitment without exploration. The adolescent has 'foreclosed' on identity by accepting predetermined roles, values, or beliefs (often parental) without personally exploring alternatives.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Exploration + commitment = identity achievement
(C) No commitment + active exploration = moratorium
(D) No commitment + no exploration = identity diffusion
references: Marcia, J. E. (1966). Development and validation of ego-identity status. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 3(5), 551–558. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0023281

reviewQueue.prompt: Resiliency research has identified protective factors including:
choices: Strictly exclusively focusing solely upon inherited biological hereditary immutable genetic advantages
Supportive relationships, internal locus of control, problem-solving skills, and community resources
Solely uniquely completely depending upon possessing an exceptionally statistically high baseline IQ score
The fundamental complete sustained absolute objective total permanent absence of any clear risk factors
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Resilience protective factors operate at multiple levels: individual (temperament, intelligence, self-efficacy), family (warm/supportive caregiver, stable environment), and community (school connection, prosocial peers, mentors).

Why others are wrong:
(A) Resilience involves environmental AND individual factors — not just genetics
(C) High IQ helps but is just one of many protective factors
(D) Resilience is specifically about POSITIVE outcomes DESPITE risk exposure — not the absence of risk
references: Werner, E. E. (1995). Resilience in development. Current Directions in Psychological Science, 4(3), 81–85. https://doi.org/10.1111/1467-8721.ep10772327

reviewQueue.prompt: Selective optimization with compensation (SOC, Baltes) proposes that successful aging involves:
choices: Optimistically actively systematically consciously striving to maintain all abilities at peak maximum levels
SELECTING essential goals, OPTIMIZING resources for those goals, and COMPENSATING for losses via strategy
Significantly progressively entirely globally passively withdrawing from all meaningful social activities
Actively aggressively constantly denying and entirely thoroughly completely ignoring any cognitive decline
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Baltes & Baltes: older adults adapt by selecting fewer but important goals, optimizing skills/resources for those goals, and compensating for losses (e.g., Rubinstein playing fewer piano pieces, practicing them more, using contrast techniques to compensate for speed loss).

Why others are wrong:
(A) SOC acknowledges that maintaining ALL abilities at peak is unrealistic — it's about strategic resource management
(C) SOC involves ACTIVE selection and optimization, not complete withdrawal
(D) SOC explicitly addresses adaptation TO decline, not ignoring it
references: Baltes, P. B., & Baltes, M. M. (1990). Psychological perspectives on successful aging: The model of selective optimization with compensation. In P. B. Baltes & M. M. Baltes (Eds.), Successful aging (pp. 1–34). Cambridge University Press.

reviewQueue.prompt: Separation anxiety typically appears around:
choices: Birth
8-10 months, peaking around 14-18 months
6 years
Only in adults with anxiety disorders
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Separation anxiety: distress when separated from the primary attachment figure, emerging ~8-10 months, peaking ~14-18 months. Requires object permanence (knowing the caregiver still exists when out of sight).

Why others are wrong:
(A) Newborns lack the cognitive development for separation anxiety
(C) By age 6, normal separation anxiety has typically resolved (clinical separation anxiety disorder is different)
(D) Separation anxiety is a normal developmental phase in infants/toddlers — distinct from the clinical disorder
references: Bowlby, J. (1969). Attachment and loss: Vol. 1. Attachment. Basic Books.

reviewQueue.prompt: Stranger anxiety typically emerges around:
choices: Birth to 1 month
6 to 8 months
Around 2 years
Around 5 years
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Stranger anxiety peaks around 6-8 months, coinciding with the development of object permanence and specific attachment. The infant can now distinguish familiar from unfamiliar faces and shows wariness toward strangers.

Why others are wrong:
(A) 1 month — too early; social smile just emerging
(C) 2 years — stranger anxiety has typically diminished
(D) 5 years — well past the typical period
references: Sroufe, L. A. (1977). Wariness of strangers and the study of infant development. Child Development, 48(3), 731–746. https://doi.org/10.2307/1128322

reviewQueue.prompt: Standard error of measurement (SEM) indicates:
choices: The strictly formal continuous calculated average baseline test score output parameter limits
The precision of individual test scores
The thoroughly tested structural valid clinical effectiveness confirming exactly all distinct validity components
The specifically explicitly assigned absolute strict psychometric distinct numeric internal item target difficulty
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) SEM estimates the amount of error in an individual's observed score. It creates a confidence interval: observed score ± 1 SEM = 68% confidence, ± 2 SEM = 95% confidence.

Why others are wrong:
(A) The average score is the mean, not SEM
(C) SEM relates to RELIABILITY (measurement precision), not validity
(D) Item difficulty is expressed as p-values (proportion answering correctly), not SEM
references: Anastasi, A., & Urbina, S. (1997). Psychological testing (7th ed.). Prentice Hall.

reviewQueue.prompt: A T-score of 70 on a clinical scale corresponds to:
choices: The mean of the T-score distribution which is set at 50 with a standard deviation of 10
One standard deviation above the mean which would correspond to a T-score of exactly 60
Two standard deviations above the mean which is often considered the clinical significance threshold
Three standard deviations above the mean which would correspond to a T-score of exactly 80
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (C) T-scores: M = 50, SD = 10. A T-score of 70 = 50 + 2(10) = 2 SDs above the mean. On the MMPI-2, T ≥ 65 is typically considered clinically significant.

Why others are wrong:
(A) The mean T-score = 50, not 70.
(B) 1 SD above the mean = T-score of 60 (50 + 10).
(D) 3 SDs above the mean = T-score of 80 (50 + 30).
references: Butcher, J. N. (2011). A beginner's guide to the MMPI-2 (3rd ed.). American Psychological Association.

reviewQueue.prompt: Differential item functioning (DIF) analysis examines whether:
choices: Individual test items are simply too easy for all examinees regardless of their demographic characteristics
Test items function differently across demographic groups after controlling for overall ability levels
The overall test length is excessive and contributes to fatigue effects that diminish performance
The test's internal consistency reliability coefficient meets acceptable psychometric standards
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) DIF analysis identifies test items that function differently across groups (e.g., gender, ethnicity) AFTER controlling for overall ability level. Items with DIF may indicate bias and may need revision or removal.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Item difficulty is assessed by item difficulty indices (p-values), not DIF analysis.
(C) Test length considerations relate to test design, not DIF.
(D) Reliability adequacy is assessed by Cronbach's alpha, test-retest, etc.
references: Holland, P. W., & Wainer, H. (Eds.). (1993). Differential item functioning. Erlbaum.

reviewQueue.prompt: A confidence interval around a test score represents:
choices: The single precisely verified exact accurate unvarying flawless calculated mathematical true score
A range within which the true score is likely to fall, based on the standard error of measurement
The explicit formal quantitative definitive representation of the broad core validity coefficient
The exactly standardized unvarying central population expectation representing the normative mean
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Confidence intervals (CI): using the SEM, we construct a range around the observed score within which the true score likely falls. A 95% CI = observed score ± 1.96 × SEM. This communicates measurement precision.

Why others are wrong:
(A) No single score gives the EXACT true score — all observed scores contain error
(C) Validity coefficients indicate how well the test predicts criteria, not score precision
(D) The normative mean is the group average, not a confidence interval around an individual score
references: Anastasi, A., & Urbina, S. (1997). Psychological testing (7th ed.). Prentice Hall.

reviewQueue.prompt: The Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales assess:
choices: General cognitive intelligence exclusively isolated from target applied functional domains
Adaptive functioning across communication, daily living, socialization, and motor skills
Formal standardized educational developmental achievement regarding broad academic topics
Categorical pathological psychological diagnostic states signifying specific personality
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Vineland-3: a semi-structured interview measuring adaptive behavior across four domains — Communication, Daily Living Skills, Socialization, and Motor Skills. Essential for intellectual disability diagnosis and support planning.

Why others are wrong:
(A) The Vineland measures ADAPTIVE BEHAVIOR, not intelligence (though they're related)
(C) Academic achievement → WJ-IV, WIAT, etc.
(D) Personality disorders → MMPI-2, PAI, MCMI-IV
references: Sparrow, S. S., Cicchetti, D. V., & Saulnier, C. A. (2016). Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales, Third Edition (Vineland-3). Pearson.

reviewQueue.prompt: In factor analysis, eigenvalues represent:
choices: The strict formal temporal test-retest clinical reliability
The amount of variance in the data explained by each factor
The absolute discrete quantitative number of assigned items
The raw quantitative distinct specifically individual scores
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Eigenvalues quantify how much total variance each factor accounts for. Factors with eigenvalues > 1.0 (Kaiser criterion) are typically retained. Larger eigenvalues = more variance explained by that factor.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Reliability is measured by Cronbach's alpha, test-retest correlation, etc.
(C) Number of items is a test design parameter, not what eigenvalues represent
(D) Individual scores are raw data — eigenvalues describe the factor structure underlying the data
references: Tabachnick, B. G., & Fidell, L. S. (2019). Using multivariate statistics (7th ed.). Pearson.

reviewQueue.prompt: The Stanford-Binet Intelligence Scales use the deviation IQ with a mean of:
choices: 50 and SD of 10
100 and SD of 15
100 and SD of 16
500 and SD of 100
reviewQueue.rationale:
