Correct: (C) The Stanford-Binet 5 (SB5) uses a mean of 100 and SD of 16 for composite IQ (note: SUBTESTS use mean 10, SD 3). This differs slightly from the WAIS/WISC which use SD = 15.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Mean 50, SD 10 = T-score distribution, not Stanford-Binet IQ
(B) Mean 100, SD 15 = Wechsler scales (WAIS, WISC), not Stanford-Binet
(D) Mean 500, SD 100 = GRE or SAT scoring, not IQ
references: Roid, G. H. (2003). Stanford-Binet Intelligence Scales, Fifth Edition: Technical manual. Riverside Publishing.

reviewQueue.prompt: Percentile rank of 84 means:
choices: The individual only correctly answered precisely 84 explicit specific test items
The person scored equal to or better than 84% of the normative sample
The examinee performed abysmally entirely failing the standardized assessment
The raw standard score exactly inherently perfectly corresponds to an IQ of 84
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) A percentile rank of 84 means the individual scored at or above 84% of the comparison group. It describes RELATIVE standing, not percentage correct. Note: 84th percentile ≈ 1 SD above the mean in a normal distribution.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Percentile rank ≠ percentage correct or raw score
(C) 84th percentile is above average — it doesn't indicate failure
(D) An IQ of 84 corresponds to approximately the 14th percentile (1 SD below mean), not the 84th percentile
references: Anastasi, A., & Urbina, S. (1997). Psychological testing (7th ed.). Prentice Hall.

reviewQueue.prompt: Inter-rater reliability is assessed by:
choices: Comparing explicitly standard distinct clinical scores from two administrations over time
Having two or more raters independently score the same responses and comparing their agreement
Dividing a single composite test specifically sequentially exactly into two equal halves
Statistically significantly continually correlating against an explicit external criterion
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Inter-rater (inter-scorer) reliability: the degree of agreement between independent raters scoring the same responses. Measured using Cohen's kappa (categorical) or intraclass correlation (continuous). Critical for subjective scoring (essays, behavioral observations).

Why others are wrong:
(A) Two administrations over time = test-retest reliability
(C) Two halves = split-half reliability
(D) External criterion correlation = criterion-related validity
references: Shrout, P. E., & Fleiss, J. L. (1979). Intraclass correlations: Uses in assessing rater reliability. Psychological Bulletin, 86(2), 420–428. https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.86.2.420

reviewQueue.prompt: A stanine score of 5 indicates:
choices: Clearly significantly strictly profoundly below highly standard expected average performance
Average performance (the middle stanine)
Clearly explicitly routinely reliably achieving remarkably above standard average performance
Demonstrating obtaining specifically achieving the absolute explicitly highest possible score
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Stanines (standard nines): 1-9 scale, M = 5, SD ≈ 2. Stanine 5 = average/middle band (40th-60th percentile). Stanines 1-3 = below average; 4-6 = average; 7-9 = above average.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Below average = stanines 1-3
(C) Above average = stanines 7-9
(D) The highest stanine = 9, not 5
references: Anastasi, A., & Urbina, S. (1997). Psychological testing (7th ed.). Prentice Hall.

reviewQueue.prompt: The Rorschach Performance Assessment System (R-PAS) is:
choices: An entirely structured highly specific objective diagnostic clinical self-report questionnaire
A standardized administration and empirical scoring system for the Rorschach inkblot method
A highly formalized specialized comprehensive developmental cognitive intelligence assessment
A fundamental incredibly simple basic primitive introductory behavioral observation checklist
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) R-PAS (Meyer et al., 2011): an empirically-based system for administering and scoring the Rorschach, addressing criticisms of earlier systems. It standardizes administration (optimized number of responses) and emphasizes variables with demonstrated validity.

Why others are wrong:
(A) The Rorschach is a PERFORMANCE-based (behavioral) measure, not self-report
(C) The Rorschach assesses personality, perception, and thought processes, not intelligence
(D) R-PAS involves complex coding of responses, not a simple checklist
references: Meyer, G. J., Viglione, D. J., Mihura, J. L., Erard, R. E., & Erdberg, P. (2011). Rorschach Performance Assessment System: Administration, coding, interpretation, and technical manual. https://r-pas.org

reviewQueue.prompt: Ceiling and floor effects in testing:
choices: Systematically consistently universally drastically improve overall psychometric test sensitivity
REDUCE the test's ability to discriminate between extreme levels of high or low examinee ability
Are universally inherently fundamentally structurally and reliably fully systematically desirable
Exclusively strictly uniquely specifically reliably occur only within formalized computerized tests
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Ceiling effect: too many examinees at the maximum score (test too easy for the group). Floor effect: too many at the minimum (test too hard). Both compress score variance and reduce discriminative ability.

Why others are wrong:
(A) These effects REDUCE sensitivity by compressing scores at extremes
(C) Ceiling/floor effects are UNDESIRABLE — they limit measurement precision
(D) These effects can occur with any test format — paper/pencil, computerized, or performance-based
references: Anastasi, A., & Urbina, S. (1997). Psychological testing (7th ed.). Prentice Hall.

reviewQueue.prompt: The WISC-V (Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children) is designed for ages:
choices: Individuals chronologically aged exactly 2 years and 6 months through 7 years and 7 months
Individuals chronologically aged exactly 6 years and 0 months through 16 years and 11 months
Individuals chronologically aged exactly 16 years and 0 months through 90 years and 11 months
Individuals chronologically aged exactly 0 years and 1 month through 3 years and 11 months
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) WISC-V: ages 6:0-16:11. Provides FSIQ and five primary index scores: Verbal Comprehension, Visual Spatial, Fluid Reasoning, Working Memory, and Processing Speed.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Ages 2:6-7:7 = WPPSI-IV (Wechsler Preschool and Primary Scale of Intelligence)
(C) Ages 16-90 = WAIS-IV/V (Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale)
(D) Ages 0-3 = Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development
references: Wechsler, D. (2014). Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children—Fifth Edition (WISC-V). Pearson.

reviewQueue.prompt: Incremental validity asks whether:
choices: A specific test instrument is fundamentally structurally internally and temporally highly reliable
A new predictor adds MEANINGFUL predictive value BEYOND what existing measures already provide
The clinical testing instrument is structurally exceptionally efficiently and easily administered
The specific clinical testing instrument is highly extraordinarily predictably notably inexpensive
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Incremental validity: does adding this measure improve prediction BEYOND what's already obtained? If a new test doesn't add predictive power beyond existing measures, its clinical utility is limited despite having validity.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Reliability is a separate psychometric property from incremental validity
(C) Ease of administration relates to practical utility, not incremental validity
(D) Cost is an administrative concern, not a validity question
references: Hunsley, J., & Meyer, G. J. (2003). The incremental validity of psychological testing and assessment. Psychological Assessment, 15(4), 446–455. https://doi.org/10.1037/1040-3590.15.4.446

reviewQueue.prompt: A T-score of 70 on the MMPI-2 indicates:
choices: Perfectly normal standard healthy typical strictly universally established average functioning
A clinically significant elevation (two standard deviations substantially far above the mean)
Significantly distinctly dramatically highly markedly abnormally poor below average functioning
The strictly explicit objective precisely measured absolute diagnostic basic raw score equals 70
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) T-scores have M = 50, SD = 10. T = 70 = 2 SDs above the mean, which on the MMPI-2 is the typical threshold for clinical significance (suggesting the scale content is being endorsed at a clinically meaningful level).

Why others are wrong:
(A) Average = T-score of 50 (± 10)
(C) Below average would be T < 40 (more than 1 SD below mean)
(D) T-scores are standardized scores derived FROM raw scores — they're not the same as raw scores
references: Butcher, J. N. (2011). A beginner's guide to the MMPI-2 (3rd ed.). American Psychological Association.

reviewQueue.prompt: Ecological validity in assessment refers to:
choices: Testing conducted exclusively within naturalistic environmental settings rather than standardized laboratories
The extent to which assessment results predict real-world functioning and behavior outside testing
Only assessment conducted using advanced computer-based platforms rather than paper-and-pencil formats
The environmental sustainability and carbon footprint of psychological assessment material production
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Ecological validity: do test results generalize to everyday functioning? A neuropsych test might show memory deficits, but does that predict real-world problems (forgetting appointments, getting lost)? Ecological validity is a type of external validity applied to assessment.

Why others are wrong:
(A) It's about generalizability of predictions to real-world behavior, not testing location.
(C) Computer-based testing is merely a delivery method, not a validity type.
(D) Ecological validity in psychology refers to real-world behavioral generalizability.
references: Chaytor, N., & Schmitter-Edgecombe, M. (2003). The ecological validity of neuropsychological tests: A review of the literature on everyday cognitive skills. Neuropsychology Review, 13(4), 181–197. https://doi.org/10.1023/B:NERV.0000009483.91468.fb

reviewQueue.prompt: The therapeutic alliance is BEST defined as:
choices: The therapist's specific theoretical orientation and preferred treatment modality or clinical framework
The collaborative relationship between therapist and client characterized by bond, goals, and task agreement
The client's perfect compliance with all assigned between-session homework exercises and activities
Insurance company preauthorization and administrative approval required before initiating treatment services
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Bordin's working alliance model: three components — bond (mutual trust, liking, respect), goals (agreement on treatment goals), and tasks (agreement on therapeutic activities). Strongest predictor of therapy outcomes.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Theoretical orientation is the therapist's framework — the alliance is the RELATIONSHIP quality.
(C) Homework compliance may reflect the alliance but doesn't define it.
(D) Insurance authorization is an administrative matter, not a therapeutic relationship concept.
references: Bordin, E. S. (1979). The generalizability of the psychoanalytic concept of the working alliance. Psychotherapy: Theory, Research & Practice, 16(3), 252–260. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0085885

reviewQueue.prompt: Prolonged exposure therapy (Foa) for PTSD involves:
choices: Systematically avoiding all trauma reminders to prevent retraumatization and emotional destabilization
Repeated systematic revisiting of trauma memories through imaginal and in vivo exposure techniques
Only progressive muscle relaxation training without any direct confrontation of traumatic material
Exclusively psychopharmacological medication management without any psychotherapeutic interventions at all
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Foa's PE: imaginal exposure (recounting the trauma narrative repeatedly until habituation occurs) + in vivo exposure (gradually approaching avoided trauma-related situations). Emotional processing theory underlies the approach.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Avoidance MAINTAINS PTSD — PE specifically targets avoidance through exposure.
(C) Relaxation is sometimes used as a coping tool but is NOT the active ingredient in PE.
(D) PE is a psychotherapy — it may be combined with medication but isn't medication management.
references: Foa, E. B., Hembree, E. A., & Rothbaum, B. O. (2007). Prolonged exposure therapy for PTSD: Emotional processing of traumatic experiences—Therapist guide. Oxford University Press.

reviewQueue.prompt: Functional analysis in behavioral therapy identifies:
choices: Unconscious intrapsychic conflicts originating in early childhood developmental psychosexual stages
The antecedents, behaviors, and consequences (ABC) that maintain a specific problem behavior
Latent dream symbolism requiring psychoanalytic interpretation of manifest dream content material
Core maladaptive cognitive beliefs and automatic thoughts underlying negative emotional reactions
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Functional analysis (ABC model): identifies what triggers behavior (Antecedents), describes the specific Behavior, and examines what reinforces it (Consequences). This guides behavioral intervention design.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Unconscious conflicts = psychoanalytic focus, not behavioral analysis.
(C) Dream symbolism = psychoanalytic technique (dream analysis).
(D) Core beliefs = cognitive therapy (Beck), not functional behavioral analysis.
references: Cooper, J. O., Heron, T. E., & Heward, W. L. (2020). Applied behavior analysis (3rd ed.). Pearson.

reviewQueue.prompt: Harm reduction approaches to substance use differ from abstinence-only by:
choices: Requiring immediate complete sobriety as an absolute precondition before any treatment can begin
Accepting that some substance use may occur while systematically working to minimize negative consequences
Actively encouraging increased substance use as a therapeutic paradoxical intervention strategy approach
Completely ignoring substance use entirely and focusing exclusively on unrelated mental health concerns
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Harm reduction: pragmatic, non-judgmental approach that reduces dangerous consequences of substance use without requiring abstinence as a precondition. Examples: needle exchanges, methadone maintenance, controlled drinking.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Harm reduction specifically does NOT require immediate sobriety — that's the abstinence-only approach.
(C) Harm reduction aims to REDUCE harm, not increase use.
(D) Harm reduction actively addresses substance use — it just doesn't require abstinence as the only goal.
references: Marlatt, G. A. (Ed.). (1998). Harm reduction: Pragmatic strategies for managing high-risk behaviors. Guilford Press.

reviewQueue.prompt: Narrative therapy (White & Epston) involves helping clients:
choices: Only focusing intensively on problems while analyzing their root causes and maintaining factors
Externalize problems and re-author their life stories using preferred alternative narrative identities
Follow strict manualized behavioral protocols with predetermined session-by-session treatment structure
Analyze unconscious motivations through free association and transference interpretation techniques
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Narrative therapy: problems are externalized ('the problem is the problem, not the person'), and clients re-author their narratives by identifying 'unique outcomes' — exceptions to the problem story that support a preferred identity.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Narrative therapy actively moves AWAY from problem-saturated stories toward alternative narratives.
(C) It's a collaborative, non-prescriptive approach — not strict behavioral protocols.
(D) Unconscious analysis = psychoanalytic approach, not narrative therapy.
references: White, M., & Epston, D. (1990). Narrative means to therapeutic ends. W. W. Norton.

reviewQueue.prompt: The token economy is MOST appropriate for use in:
choices: Complex unstructured individual specific psychoanalysis addressing explicit early development
Structured settings with clearly defined target behaviors (inpatient units, classrooms, group homes)
Short-term targeted brief outpatient cognitive therapy addressing mild acute specific stressors
Collaborative unstructured interpersonal couples counseling addressing recurrent relationship issues
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Token economies work best in controlled environments where staff can consistently observe target behaviors, deliver tokens, and manage the exchange system. Used in psychiatric units, schools, correctional settings, and developmental disability programs.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Psychoanalysis uses free association, interpretation, and transference analysis — not behavioral tokens
(C) Brief outpatient therapy lacks the consistent environmental control needed for token economies
(D) Couples counseling addresses relational dynamics, not individual behavior modification via tokens
references: Ayllon, T., & Azrin, N. (1968). The token economy: A motivational system for therapy and rehabilitation. Appleton-Century-Crofts.

reviewQueue.prompt: Reality therapy (Glasser) focuses on:
choices: Profoundly repressed structural unconscious psychological drives stemming from strict early development
Present choices and taking responsibility for meeting one's basic needs (love, power, freedom, fun, survival)
Continuous unstructured verbal free association expressing exact repressed foundational core conflicts
Systematic formal diagnostic dream interpretation revealing explicit latent unconscious symbolic meaning
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Glasser's choice theory/reality therapy: people choose their behaviors. Therapy focuses on present actions, evaluating current behavior effectiveness, and making plans to meet five basic needs responsibly.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Unconscious drives = psychoanalytic focus; reality therapy is explicitly present-focused
(C) Free association = psychoanalytic technique
(D) Dream interpretation = psychoanalytic technique
references: Glasser, W. (1998). Choice theory: A new psychology of personal freedom. HarperCollins.

reviewQueue.prompt: Flooding (implosive therapy) differs from systematic desensitization in that flooding:
choices: Explicitly employs systematically gradual clinical exposure combined seamlessly with relaxation
Involves immediate, intense exposure to the feared stimulus without a hierarchy or relaxation
Is fundamentally and consistently practically always executed directly within in vivo contexts
Is fundamentally formalized completely as a strictly distinct cognitive restructuring protocol
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Flooding: immediate, prolonged exposure to the maximum-anxiety stimulus without relaxation pairing. Based on extinction — maintaining exposure until the anxiety response diminishes (habituation).

Why others are wrong:
(A) Gradual exposure + relaxation = systematic desensitization (Wolpe), not flooding
(C) Flooding can be done both in vivo (real-life) and in vitro/imaginal (in imagination)
(D) Flooding is a behavioral technique based on classical conditioning principles, not a cognitive technique
references: Stampfl, T. G., & Levis, D. J. (1967). Essentials of implosive therapy. Journal of Abnormal Psychology, 72(6), 496–503. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0025238

reviewQueue.prompt: Strategic family therapy (Haley) uses:
choices: Exclusively gentle emotionally unstructured reflective active listening applied during family sessions
Directives, paradoxical interventions, and tasks designed to change dysfunctional interaction patterns
Profound extensive psychodynamic unconscious psychoanalytic interpretations of early childhood trauma
Strictly isolated exclusive individual therapy sessions ignoring broader functional family dynamics
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Haley's strategic therapy: therapist takes an active, directive role designing interventions (homework tasks, paradoxical directives, reframing, ordeal therapy) to disrupt dysfunctional family interaction sequences.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Reflective listening = person-centered (Rogers); strategic therapy is highly directive
(C) Psychoanalytic interpretation = psychodynamic approach, not strategic
(D) Strategic therapy works with the FAMILY system, not just individuals
references: Haley, J. (1976). Problem-solving therapy. Jossey-Bass.

reviewQueue.prompt: Contingency management uses:
choices: Specific subjective complex psychoanalytic highly intensive formal dream analysis resolving the unconscious
Tangible reinforcers (vouchers, prizes) contingent on verified behavioral change (e.g., negative drug tests)
Highly unstructured spontaneous unrestricted free association fundamentally focused on latent core meaning
Formal intensive specific clinical psychodynamic analysis and strict interpretation of relational transference
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Contingency management: evidence-based behavioral approach using reinforcement (vouchers exchangeable for goods, prize drawings) contingent on objective verification of target behaviors (clean urine samples, treatment attendance).

Why others are wrong:
(A) Dream analysis = psychoanalytic technique
(C) Free association = psychoanalytic technique
(D) Transference interpretation = psychoanalytic technique
references: Higgins, S. T., Silverman, K., & Heil, S. H. (Eds.). (2008). Contingency management in substance abuse treatment. Guilford Press.

reviewQueue.prompt: The miracle question in SFBT asks clients:
choices: To specifically vividly explicitly describe their absolute worst nightmare
To imagine waking up and the problem is solved — what would be different?
To exhaustively fundamentally analyze profoundly damaging childhood trauma
To systematically distinctly identify deep internal cognitive distortions
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) The miracle question (de Shazer): 'Suppose tonight while you sleep a miracle happens and the problem is solved. When you wake up, how would you know? What would be different?' This shifts focus from problems to desired outcomes.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Describing nightmares = might occur in trauma therapy, not SFBT
(C) Childhood trauma analysis = psychodynamic approach; SFBT is future/solution-focused
(D) Identifying cognitive distortions = CBT technique, not SFBT
references: de Shazer, S. (1988). Clues: Investigating solutions in brief therapy. W. W. Norton.

reviewQueue.prompt: Pharmacotherapy for ADHD in children typically involves:
choices: Potent major atypical antipsychotic medications prioritizing dopamine blockade
Stimulant medications (methylphenidate, amphetamine) as first-line treatment
Sedating anxiolytic benzodiazepines prescribed exclusively for severe anxiety
Strictly regulated complex MAOI antidepressants carrying high dietary warnings
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Stimulants (methylphenidate/Ritalin, amphetamine/Adderall) are first-line for ADHD. They increase dopamine and norepinephrine availability, paradoxically improving focus and reducing hyperactivity/impulsivity.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Antipsychotics are not first-line for ADHD (though sometimes used for severe aggression)
(C) Benzodiazepines treat anxiety, not ADHD — they could worsen ADHD symptoms
(D) MAOIs are rarely used for ADHD due to dietary restrictions and side effect profile
references: Wolraich, M. L., Hagan, J. F., Allan, C., et al. (2019). Clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis, evaluation, and treatment of ADHD in children and adolescents. Pediatrics, 144(4), e20192528. https://doi.org/10.1542/peds.2019-2528

reviewQueue.prompt: Thought stopping is a technique where:
choices: The clinical practitioner formally unilaterally abruptly constantly actively interrupts the session
The client learns to interrupt intrusive thoughts by saying 'STOP' and redirecting their attention
All spontaneous mental cognition is formally fully permanently strictly abruptly completely stopped
Exclusively strictly solely uniquely only highly profoundly incredibly positive thoughts are allowed
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Thought stopping: when an unwanted thought occurs, the client shouts 'STOP!' (initially aloud, then subvocally), then redirects attention to a neutral or positive thought. Simple but increasingly considered less effective than acceptance-based approaches.

Why others are wrong:
(A) The CLIENT interrupts their own thoughts, not the therapist interrupting the session
(C) Only INTRUSIVE/unwanted thoughts are targeted — normal thinking continues
(D) The technique is about interrupting unwanted thoughts, not filtering all thought content
references: Wolpe, J. (1958). Psychotherapy by reciprocal inhibition. Stanford University Press.

reviewQueue.prompt: A mediator variable explains:
choices: When or for whom a particular effect occurs by specifying boundary conditions and interactions
HOW or WHY an independent variable produces its effect on the dependent variable mechanistically
That two variables under investigation are completely unrelated and share no common variance
Only random unsystematic measurement error variance that obscures true relationships between variables
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Mediator: the mechanism through which X affects Y. X → M → Y. Example: Exercise (X) → improved mood (M) → reduced depression (Y). Mediators explain the causal pathway.

Why others are wrong:
(A) When/for whom an effect occurs = moderator variable (interaction effect).
(C) A mediator specifically establishes a RELATIONSHIP pathway between variables.
(D) Mediators explain systematic variance, not random error.
references: Baron, R. M., & Kenny, D. A. (1986). The moderator–mediator variable distinction in social psychological research: Conceptual, strategic, and statistical considerations. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 51(6), 1173–1182. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.51.6.1173

reviewQueue.prompt: A moderator variable specifies:
choices: The underlying causal mechanism through which an independent variable produces its observed effect
Under WHAT CONDITIONS or FOR WHOM the relationship between two variables changes in direction or strength
That the independent variable definitively and directly causes changes in the dependent variable
That the dependent variable actually causes changes in the independent variable through reverse causation
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Moderator: a variable that changes the STRENGTH or DIRECTION of the relationship between X and Y. Example: Age moderates the relationship between stress and health (effect is stronger for older adults).

Why others are wrong:
(A) Mechanism = mediator; moderators specify WHEN, not HOW.
(C) Moderators don't establish causation — they specify boundary conditions.
(D) Moderators don't indicate reverse causation.
references: Baron, R. M., & Kenny, D. A. (1986). The moderator–mediator variable distinction in social psychological research. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 51(6), 1173–1182. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.51.6.1173

reviewQueue.prompt: Effect size measures:
choices: Only statistical significance as determined by the p-value relative to the chosen alpha level
The magnitude and practical importance of a finding independent of sample size considerations
The minimum required sample size needed to achieve adequate statistical power for detection
Whether the null hypothesis is definitively true or false in the target population of interest
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Effect size quantifies the magnitude of an effect (Cohen's d, η², r²), conveying practical significance independent of sample size. A finding can be statistically significant but have a trivial effect size.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Statistical significance (p-value) is separate from effect size — they answer different questions.
(C) Sample size requirements are determined through power analysis, which USES effect size as an input.
(D) Effect sizes quantify the magnitude of an effect — they don't prove or disprove null hypotheses.
references: Cohen, J. (1988). Statistical power analysis for the behavioral sciences (2nd ed.). Erlbaum.

reviewQueue.prompt: Intention-to-treat analysis includes:
choices: Only participants who successfully completed the entire study protocol without any protocol deviations
ALL participants originally randomized regardless of whether they completed or complied with treatment
Only participants who demonstrated measurable clinical improvement during the course of the study
Only participants assigned to the control group excluding all participants in active treatment conditions
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) ITT analysis includes ALL randomized participants in their original groups, even if they dropped out, didn't comply, or switched groups. This preserves the benefits of randomization and provides a more realistic effectiveness estimate.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Including only completers = per-protocol analysis, which can introduce attrition bias.
(C) Including only improvers = extreme bias violating the purpose of the trial.
(D) ITT includes ALL groups, not just the control.
references: Gupta, S. K. (2011). Intention-to-treat concept: A review. Perspectives in Clinical Research, 2(3), 109–112. https://doi.org/10.4103/2229-3485.83221

reviewQueue.prompt: Ceiling and floor effects reduce:
choices: Only the reliability of the test without affecting any other psychometric properties or statistical analyses
The ability to detect true differences by restricting variability and attenuating statistical power
The minimum sample size required to achieve adequate statistical power for detecting meaningful effects
The necessity for including appropriate control groups in experimental and quasi-experimental research designs
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Ceiling/floor effects restrict score variability — if everyone scores at the top or bottom, the measure can't differentiate among individuals, reducing the ability to detect true differences (attenuated correlations, reduced power).

Why others are wrong:
(A) They affect both reliability AND the ability to detect differences — not only reliability.
(C) They don't reduce sample size needs — if anything, they require LARGER samples to detect effects.
(D) They have no relationship to the need for control groups.
references: Anastasi, A., & Urbina, S. (1997). Psychological testing (7th ed.). Prentice Hall.

reviewQueue.prompt: Cohen's kappa measures:
choices: Effect size indicating the magnitude of a treatment outcome or group difference in a study
Inter-rater agreement for categorical judgments corrected for the probability of chance agreement
Test-retest temporal stability reliability assessed by correlating scores from two administration occasions
Internal consistency reliability assessed through Cronbach's alpha or split-half correlation methodologies
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Cohen's κ measures agreement between two raters for categorical judgments, correcting for the probability of chance agreement. κ = 1.0 = perfect agreement; κ = 0 = chance-level agreement.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Effect size measures (Cohen's d, η²) quantify magnitude of findings, not inter-rater agreement.
(C) Test-retest reliability = correlating scores from two administrations over time.
(D) Internal consistency = Cronbach's alpha or split-half reliability, measuring item intercorrelation.
references: Cohen, J. (1960). A coefficient of agreement for nominal scales. Educational and Psychological Measurement, 20(1), 37–46. https://doi.org/10.1177/001316446002000104

reviewQueue.prompt: A confounding variable threatens internal validity because it:
choices: Is explicitly measured accurately across all independent test conditions
Provides an alternative explanation for the relationship between IV and DV
Directly explicitly and consistently increases overall broad external validity
Is methodologically strictly explicitly and completely always controlled for
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) A confound covaries with the IV, making it impossible to determine whether the IV or the confound caused changes in the DV. This eliminates the ability to make causal inferences.

Why others are wrong:
(A) How accurately a confound is measured is irrelevant — its existence as an alternative explanation is the threat
(C) Confounds THREATEN validity — they don't increase external validity
(D) Confounds are NOT always controlled for — that's why they're a threat. Good designs aim to control them
references: Shadish, W. R., Cook, T. D., & Campbell, D. T. (2002). Experimental and quasi-experimental designs for generalized causal inference. Houghton Mifflin.

reviewQueue.prompt: Counterbalancing is used in within-subjects designs to control for:
choices: Significant systematic structural selection bias
Order effects (practice, fatigue, carryover)
Insufficient distinct targeted raw sample size
Targeted generalized overall external validity
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Counterbalancing: varying the order of conditions across participants (e.g., AB for half, BA for the other half) to distribute order effects equally across conditions, preventing them from confounding results.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Selection bias is a between-subjects concern controlled by random assignment
(C) Counterbalancing doesn't affect sample size — it's about ORDER of conditions
(D) Counterbalancing is an internal validity control, not directly about external validity
references: Rosenthal, R., & Rosnow, R. L. (2008). Essentials of behavioral research: Methods and data analysis (3rd ed.). McGraw-Hill.

reviewQueue.prompt: Meta-analysis is a statistical technique that:
choices: Qualitatively studies a single unique target participant in thorough extreme deep detail
Quantitatively combines results from multiple studies to estimate an overall effect size
Fundamentally explicitly definitively thoroughly replaces the need for any new research
Exclusively systematically integrates strictly subjective qualitative narrative text data
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Meta-analysis (Glass, 1976) uses statistical methods to combine findings across studies, calculating a weighted average effect size. It increases statistical power and identifies patterns not visible in individual studies.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Single participant in depth = case study methodology, not meta-analysis
(C) Meta-analysis complements new research — it doesn't replace the need for primary studies
(D) Meta-analysis is fundamentally QUANTITATIVE — it uses numerical effect sizes from published studies
references: Glass, G. V. (1976). Primary, secondary, and meta-analysis of research. Educational Researcher, 5(10), 3–8. https://doi.org/10.3102/0013189X005010003

reviewQueue.prompt: A single-case experimental design such as ABA (reversal) includes:
choices: Statistically analyzing and explicitly comparing large-scale independent massive comprehensive standardized clinical groups
Establishing baseline (A), introducing treatment (B), then withdrawing treatment (A) to demonstrate experimental control
Providing absolutely no consistent continuous quantitative or qualitative specific structured measurements of target behavior
Exclusively evaluating explicitly subjective completely historical retrospective test data systematically gathered after treatment
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) ABA reversal design: (A) baseline measurement, (B) treatment introduction with continued measurement, (A) treatment withdrawal to see if behavior returns to baseline. If behavior reverses, it demonstrates the treatment caused the change.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Single-case designs study individual participants, not large groups
(C) Continuous, repeated measurement is essential to single-case designs
(D) ABA designs use prospective, ongoing measurement, not retrospective reports
references: Barlow, D. H., Nock, M. K., & Hersen, M. (2009). Single case experimental designs (3rd ed.). Allyn & Bacon.

reviewQueue.prompt: ANOVA is used to compare:
choices: Two group means only
Means of THREE or more groups
Correlations between variables
Frequencies of categorical outcomes
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) ANOVA (Analysis of Variance) tests whether means differ among three or more groups. It controls the familywise error rate compared to multiple t-tests. Significant F-tests are followed by post-hoc comparisons.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Two means = t-test (though ANOVA can handle two groups, it's designed for 3+)
(C) Correlations use Pearson's r, Spearman's ρ, or regression
(D) Categorical outcome frequencies = chi-square test
references: Fisher, R. A. (1925). Statistical methods for research workers. Oliver & Boyd.

reviewQueue.prompt: A correlation coefficient of r = -.85 indicates:
choices: A distinctly weak positive relationship where variables systematically increase together
A strong NEGATIVE relationship — as one variable increases, the other tends to decrease
Absolutely no distinct measurable statistical relationship between the specific variables
A specifically perfect positive relationship where both variables rigidly align together
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) r = -.85 indicates a strong inverse relationship. The sign (negative) indicates direction (inverse); the absolute value (.85) indicates strength (strong). Correlation strength: .10 small, .30 medium, .50+ large.

Why others are wrong:
(A) The relationship is NEGATIVE and STRONG, not weak and positive
(C) r = 0 indicates no relationship; -.85 is far from zero
(D) r = +1.0 indicates a perfect positive relationship; -.85 is negative
references: Cohen, J. (1988). Statistical power analysis for the behavioral sciences (2nd ed.). Erlbaum.

reviewQueue.prompt: Regression analysis allows researchers to:
choices: Exclusively summarize specifically defined categorical data without precise predictions
Predict the value of a dependent variable based on one or more independent variables
Definitively unequivocally specifically firmly establish exact causation with certainty
Exclusively distinctly specifically objectively simply statistically compare group means
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Regression: models the relationship between predictor(s) and an outcome variable, generating an equation to predict DV values from IV values. Simple regression uses one predictor; multiple regression uses two or more.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Regression PREDICTS outcomes, going beyond mere description
(C) Regression shows prediction/association but doesn't establish causation without experimental design
(D) Comparing group means = ANOVA/t-test; regression examines continuous predictive relationships
references: Tabachnick, B. G., & Fidell, L. S. (2019). Using multivariate statistics (7th ed.). Pearson.

reviewQueue.prompt: Ecological validity in research refers to:
choices: Specifically thoroughly investigating highly complex natural diverse biological ecosystems
The extent to which research findings generalize to real-world settings and everyday behavior
Strictly exclusively evaluating explicitly and profoundly isolated robust internal validity
Rigorously confirming appropriately precise explicit direct statistical conclusion validity
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Ecological validity: whether findings obtained in the lab (or other research settings) apply to natural, everyday environments and behaviors. High ecological validity = real-world relevance.

Why others are wrong:
(A) 'Ecological' refers to natural/real-world settings, not biological ecosystems
(C) Ecological validity is a component of EXTERNAL validity, not internal validity
(D) Statistical conclusion validity concerns the appropriate use of statistics, a different validity type
references: Bronfenbrenner, U. (1979). The ecology of human development. Harvard University Press.

reviewQueue.prompt: A longitudinal study follows:
choices: Many different age groups at one time point
The SAME participants over an extended period of time
Only cross-sectional data
No participants over time
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Longitudinal designs track the SAME individuals over time (months, years, decades), measuring changes within individuals. This allows study of development, aging, treatment effects, and causal processes.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Many age groups at one time = cross-sectional design
(C) Longitudinal is the opposite of cross-sectional — it follows people OVER time
(D) Longitudinal designs specifically track participants OVER time
references: Baltes, P. B. (1968). Longitudinal and cross-sectional sequences in the study of age and generation effects. Human Development, 11(3), 145–171. https://doi.org/10.1159/000270604

reviewQueue.prompt: Informed consent must include:
choices: Exclusively the active treating therapist's explicitly required academic and formal clinical credentials
The nature of treatment, potential risks and benefits, alternatives, and the right to withdraw at any time
Absolutely nothing whatsoever, since explicit formal diagnostic treatment consent is constantly assumed
Exclusively and directly only the explicitly established absolute primary categorical clinical diagnosis
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Informed consent requires: nature/purpose of treatment, expected benefits, risks/side effects, alternative treatments, limits of confidentiality, fees, and the right to withdraw without penalty.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Credentials are one component but grossly insufficient for full informed consent
(C) Consent must be INFORMED and DOCUMENTED — it's never simply assumed
(D) Diagnosis alone doesn't constitute informed consent without treatment information
references: American Psychological Association. (2017). Ethical principles of psychologists and code of conduct, Standard 3.10. https://www.apa.org/ethics/code

reviewQueue.prompt: Group therapy confidentiality differs from individual therapy because:
choices: Strict formal professional confidentiality fundamentally doesn't apply within group contexts
The primary clinical therapist explicitly guarantees complete confidentiality from group members
The therapist CANNOT guarantee that group members will maintain each other's confidentiality
Active participating group members remain totally uninformed regarding confidentiality boundaries
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (C) In groups, the therapist can maintain their own confidentiality obligations but cannot control other group members' behavior. Therapists must discuss this limitation during informed consent and emphasize confidentiality expectations.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Confidentiality still applies — the therapist maintains their obligation
(B) The therapist CANNOT guarantee other members' behavior — only their own
(D) Members SHOULD be informed about confidentiality limits during group informed consent
references: Lasky, G. B., & Riva, M. T. (2006). Confidentiality and privileged communication in group psychotherapy. International Journal of Group Psychotherapy, 56(4), 455–476. https://doi.org/10.1521/ijgp.2006.56.4.455

reviewQueue.prompt: When a psychologist discovers they lack competence in a needed area, they should:
choices: Continue treating the client without disclosing the limitation
Obtain appropriate training, consultation, or supervision, or refer the client
Ignore the limitation
Tell the client it doesn't matter
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Standard 2.01: psychologists provide services only within their areas of competence. When facing novel areas, they obtain relevant education, training, consultation, or supervised experience — or refer to a qualified colleague.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Continuing without disclosure or competence development = practicing outside competence (ethical violation)
(C) Ignoring limitations risks client harm and violates competence standards
(D) Minimizing the limitation is dishonest and potentially harmful
references: American Psychological Association. (2017). Ethical principles of psychologists and code of conduct, Standard 2.01. https://www.apa.org/ethics/code

reviewQueue.prompt: A psychologist who has a sexual relationship with a current client is:
choices: Violating precise therapeutic professional clinical ethics explicitly if fully consented
Always violating Standard 10.05 — sexual intimacies with current clients are prohibited
Only objectively formally exclusively in complete violation if the therapist initiated
Absolutely not explicitly empirically formally in violation if the therapy is going well
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Standard 10.05: Sexual intimacies with current therapy clients are prohibited. Period. No exceptions for consent, therapeutic progress, client initiation, or mutual attraction. This is an absolute prohibition.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Client consent does NOT make sexual contact ethical — the power differential makes true consent questionable
(C) Regardless of who initiated, the therapist bears professional responsibility
(D) Quality of therapy is irrelevant — the prohibition is absolute
references: American Psychological Association. (2017). Ethical principles of psychologists and code of conduct, Standard 10.05. https://www.apa.org/ethics/code

reviewQueue.prompt: Psychologists must report their own ethical violations or impairment because:
choices: Formal systematic ethical reporting of specific personal subjective true impairment remains fully optional
Specific standards require explicitly reporting actual violations alongside addressing personal impairment
The strict extremely formal continuous clinical explicit professional defining mandate binds only students
Proactive independent objective individual clinical formal systematic ethical reporting is entirely optional
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Standard 1.05: psychologists take reasonable steps to address ethical violations they become aware of. Standard 2.06: psychologists refrain from practice when personal problems may impair their competence. Both obligations apply.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Self-reporting and addressing impairment is a professional OBLIGATION
(C) Standards apply to ALL psychologists, not just students
(D) The obligation exists regardless of whether anyone else has reported — it's proactive
references: American Psychological Association. (2017). Ethical principles of psychologists and code of conduct, Standards 1.05 & 2.06. https://www.apa.org/ethics/code

reviewQueue.prompt: When psychologists provide services via telehealth, they must:
choices: Operate exactly identically parallel precisely smoothly doing strictly nothing different from formal in-person practice
Ensure telehealth competence, comply with all jurisdictions, address security, and obtain telehealth-specific consent
Specifically reliably carefully exactly safely exclusively use video platforms while explicitly never offering any phone
Systematically explicitly profoundly extensively broadly entirely carefully avoid providing any telehealth truly forever
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Telehealth requires: competence in technology-mediated service delivery, compliance with laws in both the psychologist's and client's jurisdictions, secure technology platforms, and informed consent addressing telehealth-specific risks.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Telehealth involves unique considerations (technology, jurisdiction, security) that differ from in-person
(C) Both video and phone can be appropriate depending on clinical needs and regulations
(D) Telehealth is an accepted service delivery modality — avoidance isn't necessary or practical
references: Joint Task Force for the Development of Telepsychology Guidelines for Psychologists. (2013). Guidelines for the practice of telepsychology. American Psychologist, 68(9), 791–800. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0035001

reviewQueue.prompt: Principle A (Beneficence and Nonmaleficence) directs psychologists to:
choices: Strictly explicitly consistently uniquely and exclusively constantly focus upon direct financial gain
Actively strive to directly constructively benefit clients and take extreme care to do absolutely no harm
Exclusively explicitly strictly completely rigorously unequivocally conduct systematic peer research
Actively fundamentally formally deliberately carefully entirely constantly avoid all professional relations
reviewQueue.rationale:
Correct: (B) Principle A: psychologists strive to benefit clients and minimize harm. They guard against personal, financial, social, organizational, and political factors that might lead to misuse of their influence.

Why others are wrong:
(A) Financial gain is secondary to client welfare — Principle A prioritizes beneficence
(C) Principle A applies to ALL professional activities, not just research
(D) Being helpful requires professional relationships — avoidance would contradict the principle
references: American Psychological Association. (2017). Ethical principles of psychologists and code of conduct — General Principles. https://www.apa.org/ethics/code
